board_events.text: Before Mendel: the blending guess
True-breeding line: on self-pollination, hands down the same trait generation after generation.

board_events.text: Blending idea: purple crossed with green should give a muddy purplish green.
Blending is wrong. Traits are not paint.
Gregor Mendel: garden pea (Pisum sativum), seven years, 1856 to 1863.
His real innovation: he counted. Statistics and mathematical logic applied to inheritance.
Seven pairs of contrasting traits. Pure lines crossed. Thousands of offspring tallied.
Cross two pure parents: what actually happens
P generation: two pure, contrasting parents.
F1: every offspring resembles ONE parent. The dominant trait shows; the recessive seems to vanish.

board_events.text: F2 (F1 selfed): the hidden trait reappears, in a regular ratio of about 3 dominant : 1 recessive.
It never vanished. It was masked.
Alleles stay pure. They are masked, never mixed or diluted.
From 3 : 1 came the Law of Dominance and the Law of Segregation. From 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 came Independent Assortment.
Terms you will use in every single question
Gene, or factor: the unit of inheritance that codes for a trait. Mendel called them factors.
Allele: one alternative form of a gene. Capital letter = dominant (T); same letter, lower case = recessive (t).
Genotype: the genetic constitution, e.g. Tt. Phenotype: the observable expression, e.g. tall.

board_events.text: Homozygous: both alleles identical — TT or tt. A true-breeding line is homozygous.
Heterozygous: the two alleles differ — Tt. Such an individual is called a hybrid.
Dominant expresses in TT and in Tt. Recessive expresses only in tt.
So TT and Tt look identical. Phenotype alone can never separate them.
Four crosses you must name on sight
Monohybrid cross: a cross tracking a single gene pair, e.g. Tt × Tt.
Dihybrid cross: a cross tracking two gene pairs simultaneously, e.g. RrYy × RrYy.

board_events.text: Test cross: an individual of unknown genotype showing the dominant phenotype × a homozygous recessive partner.
Back cross: crossing an F1 individual with either parental type.
Punnett square: the checkerboard grid, devised by R. C. Punnett, for laying out gamete combinations and reading off ratios.
Every test cross is a back cross. Not every back cross is a test cross.
The three principles, and the ratio each came from
Law of Dominance: in a heterozygote, only the dominant allele expresses; the recessive is masked.
It explains why F1 resembles one parent, and why F2 shows 3 : 1.
Law of Segregation, also called the Law of Purity of Gametes: the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation.

board_events.text: Each gamete carries only ONE allele, pure and uncontaminated. Tt makes half T and half t gametes.
Law of Independent Assortment: alleles of different genes, on different chromosomes, segregate independently of one another.
Deduced from the dihybrid ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
Segregation is within one gene. Independent assortment is between two genes.

board_events.text: Monohybrid F2 (Tt × Tt): phenotype 3 : 1, genotype 1 : 2 : 1.
Dihybrid F2: phenotype 9 : 3 : 3 : 1; genotype 1:2:1:2:4:2:1:2:1 — nine distinct genotypes across sixteen boxes.
Monohybrid test cross: 1 : 1 both ways. Dihybrid test cross: 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 both ways.
Incomplete dominance F2 and codominance F2: 1 : 2 : 1 by phenotype AND by genotype.
Genetics ratios are pure numbers. No units to check — the quantity is proportion of offspring.
In both deviations, phenotype ratio equals genotype ratio, because every genotype looks different.
Procedure A: predict offspring ratios for one gene
Step 1. Assign symbols: capital = dominant, lower case = recessive. Write each parent's genotype.
Genotype, not phenotype, decides what gametes form. Two purple plants can be PP or Pp.
Step 2. Determine the gametes. By segregation, each parent contributes one allele per gamete: PP makes only P; Pp makes half P and half p.

board_events.text: Step 3. Draw the Punnett square: one parent's gametes across the top, the other's down the side. Fill each cell by combining row and column.
The grid enumerates every equally likely fertilisation event — that is why the counts come out as ratios.
Step 4. Read the genotype ratio: 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp.
Then collapse to phenotype using dominance: 3 purple : 1 green.
Procedure B: two genes at once, without the pain
A heterozygote RrYy makes $2^n$ gamete types, where n = the number of heterozygous gene pairs.
Here n = 2, so four gametes: RY, Ry, rY, ry — each in equal proportion.
A 4 × 4 Punnett square of RrYy × RrYy yields the classic 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, confirming the two genes assort independently.

Product rule: the probability of two independent events both happening is the product of their separate probabilities.
Sum rule: the probability of either of two mutually exclusive outcomes is their sum.
P(round and yellow) = 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16 — the 9 in 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, with no grid at all.
Procedure C: make the unknown confess
A purple plant is either PP or Pp. Phenotype alone cannot tell which.
Cross it with the homozygous recessive, pp.

board_events.text: If the unknown is PP: all offspring are Pp, so all are purple — a 1 : 0 result.
If the unknown is Pp: offspring are half Pp and half pp — 1 purple : 1 green.
The appearance of ANY recessive offspring proves the parent was heterozygous.
Why a homozygous recessive partner: it contributes only recessive alleles, so the offspring's phenotype directly mirrors the unknown parent's gamete types.

segments.text: <curious>Picture a sabziwala sorting brinjals — some deep purple, some pale green. He saves seed only from the purple ones, and every single year, purple comes back.
That is a true-breeding line. On self-pollination it hands down the same trait, generation after generation, with no surprises. Do the same with green, and you get a second true-breeding line.

Here they are side by side. Purple parent, purple offspring, purple grandchildren; green parent, green offspring, green grandchildren. Nothing drifts, nothing dilutes. That stability is what true-breeding means.
Now cross a true-breeding purple with a true-breeding green. Common sense borrowed from mixing paint says you should get something in between — a muddy purplish green. That guess is called blending.
And it is flatly wrong. Traits are not paint. Hold on to that, because almost every mistake in this chapter is a quiet return to blending thinking.
Gregor Mendel worked on garden pea, Pisum sativum, for seven patient years, from eighteen fifty six to eighteen sixty three — a plant with clean contrasting traits that self-pollinates easily.
But the plant was not his real innovation. Mendel counted. He brought statistics and mathematical logic to inheritance, something nobody had ever done with living things.
Seven pairs of contrasting traits, pure lines crossed, thousands of offspring tallied. Out of those numbers came a story that blending could never explain.
<curious>Mendel crossed two pure contrasting parents — the P generation. If blending were right, the children should have landed exactly halfway between them. They did not.
The P generation is that starting pair: one true-breeding purple, one true-breeding green. Both are pure, so each can hand only one kind of factor to its offspring.

The first hybrid offspring, the F one generation, were not intermediate at all. Every single one looked like one parent. That expressed trait is called dominant; the other, apparently gone, is recessive.
Follow the picture. P: purple crossed with green. F one: all purple, with green nowhere in sight. Then Mendel let the F one self-pollinate, and watch what walks back in.
In the F two generation the green reappears — and in a strikingly regular ratio, about three dominant to one recessive. Something that had truly vanished could never come back that cleanly.
So it never vanished. It was masked. Think of a recessive allele as a quiet cousin at a loud family dinner: with the loud cousin at the table, you barely notice him.
Move that quiet cousin to a table where he sits only with another quiet cousin — the recessive homozygote in F two — and suddenly his voice is the only one you hear. Nothing mixed, nothing diluted.
That is the heart of Mendelian inheritance. From three to one Mendel deduced dominance and segregation; from a two-trait cross giving nine to three to three to one, he deduced independent assortment.
This section is pure vocabulary, and it is worth being ruthless about it. Almost every mark lost in genetics is a term read carelessly, not a concept missed.
A gene, or factor, is the unit of inheritance that codes for a trait. Mendel had no idea what a gene was made of — he simply called them factors, and reasoned about them as invisible units.

An allele is one alternative form of a gene. Tall and dwarf are two alleles of the same height gene. The convention: capital letter for the dominant allele, the same letter in lower case for the recessive.
Genotype is the genetic constitution — what the organism actually carries, written as T T or T small t. Phenotype is the observable expression of that genotype: tall, or dwarf. Carried versus shown.
Look at the three possible genotypes. Capital T capital T is tall. Capital T small t is tall as well. Small t small t is dwarf. Three genotypes, but only two phenotypes.
Homozygous means both alleles are identical — capital T capital T is homozygous dominant, small t small t is homozygous recessive. And notice: a true-breeding line is exactly a homozygous line.
Heterozygous means the two alleles differ — capital T small t. Such an individual is called a hybrid, which is where the word monohybrid in monohybrid cross comes from.
A dominant allele expresses itself in both the homozygous and the heterozygous state. A recessive allele expresses only in the homozygous state; in the heterozygote it is masked.

Which leaves you with the single most useful consequence of this vocabulary: capital T capital T and capital T small t look identical. Phenotype alone can never separate them — you will need a test cross.
Exam questions rarely say which cross they mean; they describe it and expect you to name it. So let us fix the four names, and the one distinction students lose marks on.
A monohybrid cross tracks a single gene pair. Capital T small t crossed with capital T small t is the classic. One gene, one pair of contrasting alleles, and the F two ratio you already know.

A dihybrid cross tracks two gene pairs at the same time — R small r capital Y small y crossed with the same. Two genes travelling together through one cross, which is where independent assortment shows up.
Here they are together. Top row, the two selfing crosses that give you ratios. Bottom row, the two crosses that use a parent deliberately, to find something out.

A test cross takes an individual of unknown genotype — one showing the dominant phenotype — and crosses it with a homozygous recessive partner. Its whole purpose is to reveal whether that unknown is homozygous or heterozygous.
A back cross is broader: it is crossing an F one individual with either parental type. So you could back cross to the dominant parent, or to the recessive parent.
And a Punnett square is not a cross at all — it is the tool. R C Punnett's checkerboard grid, where gametes go along the edges and every cell is one equally likely fertilisation event.

Now the distinction. Cross the F one with the recessive parent and you have done both a back cross and a test cross. Cross it with the dominant parent and it is a back cross only — it tells you nothing.
Mendel's three laws are not three separate discoveries — they are three conclusions read off his counts. Each law has a ratio behind it, and knowing which ratio came from which law is exam gold.
The Law of Dominance says that in a heterozygote, only the dominant allele expresses itself; the recessive one is masked. It is a statement about expression, not about inheritance.
That one law explains two observations at once: why the F one resembles only one parent, and why the F two collapses from three genotype classes down to a phenotype ratio of three to one.
The Law of Segregation — also called the Law of Purity of Gametes — says the two alleles of a gene separate cleanly from each other during gamete formation. This is the law about inheritance itself.
Watch the cell. A capital T small t parent goes into meiosis carrying both alleles. They separate, and each gamete walks out with exactly one of them.

So each gamete carries only one allele, pure and uncontaminated. A capital T small t heterozygote makes half capital T gametes and half small t gametes. Never both, never a mixture — that word purity is doing real work.

The Law of Independent Assortment says that alleles of different genes, sitting on different chromosomes, segregate independently of one another during gamete formation. How one gene splits says nothing about how the other splits.
<excited>And Mendel deduced that purely from a number — the dihybrid ratio nine to three to three to one. He could not see chromosomes. He inferred their behaviour from a tally sheet.

Keep the two apart in your head. Segregation is about what happens within one gene — its two alleles part company. Independent assortment is about what happens between two genes — they part company without consulting each other.
This table is the highest-yield object in the subtopic. If it is not automatic, every numerical becomes a derivation under time pressure. So read it once as a structure, not as six unrelated facts.
Six crosses, two columns. Left column is what you see, right column is what is carried. The whole table is really one question: do the numbers on the left and the right agree, or not?
Monohybrid F two, capital T small t crossed with capital T small t: phenotype three to one, genotype one to two to one. The two disagree because the heterozygote hides behind the dominant.
Dihybrid F two: phenotype nine to three to three to one; genotype one, two, one, two, four, two, one, two, one — that is nine distinct genotypes, spread across sixteen boxes of the grid.

The test crosses are the friendly ones. Monohybrid test cross is one to one both ways. Dihybrid test cross is one to one to one to one both ways. Nothing hides, because the recessive parent contributes nothing to hide behind.
Now the two deviations. Incomplete dominance F two and codominance F two both give one to two to one — and here the phenotype ratio and the genotype ratio are the same number.

One housekeeping point that examiners like to test indirectly: there are no units anywhere in this subtopic. Genetics ratios are pure numbers. The quantity being tracked is a proportion of offspring, and nothing needs dimension checking.

And the pattern to carry away: in the deviations, phenotype equals genotype because every genotype looks different. Whenever the ratios agree, you are looking at a deviation, not at ordinary dominance.
Every monohybrid question in this chapter is the same four steps in the same order. Learn the order once and you will never stare at a blank page.
Step one: assign symbols. Choose a letter, capital for the dominant allele, lower case for the recessive. Then write each parent's genotype — not its description, its genotype.

And here is the reason that step matters. Genotype, not phenotype, determines what gametes form. Two purple plants that look identical can be capital P capital P or capital P small p, and they behave completely differently.

Step two: determine the gametes. By the Law of Segregation each parent contributes one allele per gamete. Capital P capital P makes only capital P. Capital P small p makes half capital P and half small p. Alleles stay pure — they never blend inside a gamete.
Step three, and here is the grid for capital P small p crossed with capital P small p. Gametes of one parent across the top, gametes of the other down the side.
Fill each cell by combining its row allele with its column allele. Top left, capital P meets capital P, giving capital P capital P. Bottom right, small p meets small p, giving small p small p.
Why does a grid give a ratio at all? Because it enumerates every equally likely fertilisation event exactly once. Four boxes, four equally likely outcomes — so counting boxes is counting probability.
Step four, first half: read the genotype ratio straight off the boxes. One capital P capital P, two capital P small p, one small p small p. That is one to two to one.
Then, and only then, collapse to phenotype using dominance. The first three boxes all carry at least one capital P, so all three are purple. Only small p small p is green. Three purple to one green.
Two genes at once is where students start drawing enormous grids and losing marks to arithmetic. There is a grid method and a fast method, and you should know both, but use the fast one.

Start with the gametes. A heterozygote capital R small r capital Y small y makes two to the power n gamete types, where n is the number of heterozygous gene pairs. That formula will come back in almost every numerical.
Here n equals two, so four gamete types: capital R capital Y, capital R small y, small r capital Y, small r small y — each in equal proportion, one quarter each.

Feed those four gametes into a four by four Punnett square for capital R small r capital Y small y crossed with itself, and out comes the classic nine to three to three to one. That ratio is the evidence the two genes assort independently.
But look at the two routes side by side. On the left, sixteen boxes to fill and classify. On the right, two little monohybrid crosses. Same answer, very different failure rate under exam pressure.
So skip the grid. Sixteen boxes is slow, and an eight by eight for three genes is a guaranteed mistake. Multiply instead.

The product rule: the probability of two independent events both happening is the product of their separate probabilities. Round and yellow are governed by different genes, so they qualify as independent.
The sum rule is its partner: the probability of either of two mutually exclusive outcomes is their sum. Use product for and, use sum for or.

<excited>Watch it work. Probability of round is three quarters. Probability of yellow is three quarters. Probability of round and yellow is three quarters times three quarters, which is nine sixteenths — the nine in nine to three to three to one, with no grid at all.
<curious>You are standing in front of a purple brinjal plant. It is either capital P capital P or capital P small p, and nothing about looking at it will ever tell you which. So how do you find out?
This is the problem the test cross exists to solve. Both genotypes give the identical purple phenotype, because one capital P is enough. The information is there in the plant; it is just hidden.
So you cross it with the homozygous recessive — small p small p, a green plant. Not with another purple, not with the dominant parent. With the double recessive, deliberately.
And now there are exactly two things that can happen, depending on which genotype the unknown really had. The two branches look completely different, which is the whole point.

Branch one: if the unknown is capital P capital P, it can only give capital P gametes. Every offspring gets capital P from it and small p from the green partner, so every offspring is capital P small p — all purple. A one to zero result.
Branch two: if the unknown is capital P small p, it gives half capital P and half small p. Half the offspring are capital P small p, purple; half are small p small p, green. One purple to one green.

So you do not even need to count carefully. The appearance of any recessive offspring at all — one green brinjal — proves the parent was heterozygous. A homozygous dominant parent simply cannot produce one.

And now the reason the recessive partner is compulsory. It contributes only recessive alleles, so it never masks anything. The offspring's phenotype becomes a direct read-out of the unknown parent's gamete types — which is exactly the information you wanted.
<curious>ज़रा सोचिए एक sabziwala brinjals sort कर रहा है — कुछ deep purple, कुछ pale green। वो सिर्फ purple वालों का seed रखता है, और हर साल purple ही वापस आता है।
यही है एक true-breeding line। Self-pollination पर वही trait generation के बाद generation हाथ आता है, बिना किसी surprise के। Green के साथ भी वही कीजिए, दूसरी true-breeding line मिल जाएगी।

देखिए दोनों lines साथ में। Purple parent, purple offspring, purple grandchildren; green parent, green offspring, green grandchildren। कुछ भी drift या dilute नहीं होता — यही stability true-breeding का मतलब है।
अब true-breeding purple को true-breeding green से cross कीजिए। Paint मिलाने वाली common sense कहती है कुछ बीच का मिलेगा — muddy purplish green। इसी guess को blending कहते हैं।
और ये बिलकुल ग़लत है। Traits paint नहीं होते। इसे पकड़ कर रखिए, क्योंकि इस chapter की लगभग हर ग़लती चुपके से blending thinking पर लौट जाती है।
Gregor Mendel ने garden pea, Pisum sativum, पर सात साल काम किया, अठारह सौ छप्पन से अठारह सौ तिरेसठ तक — एक ऐसा plant जिसमें clean contrasting traits हैं और self-pollination आसान है।
लेकिन असली innovation plant नहीं था। Mendel ने counting की। उन्होंने inheritance में statistics और mathematical logic लाई, जो living things के साथ पहले किसी ने नहीं किया था।
सात pairs के contrasting traits, pure lines का cross, हज़ारों offspring की tally। इन्हीं numbers से वो कहानी निकली जो blending कभी explain नहीं कर सकती थी।
<curious>Mendel ने दो pure contrasting parents cross किए — ये है P generation। अगर blending सही होती, तो children ठीक बीच में होने चाहिए थे। पर ऐसा नहीं हुआ।
P generation वही starting pair है: एक true-breeding purple, एक true-breeding green। दोनों pure हैं, तो हर एक अपने offspring को सिर्फ एक ही तरह का factor दे सकता है।
पहली hybrid offspring, यानी F one generation, बिलकुल intermediate नहीं थी। हर एक एक ही parent जैसी दिखी। वो express होने वाला trait dominant कहलाता है; दूसरा, जो गायब लगता है, recessive।
Picture देखिए। P: purple cross with green। F one: सब purple, green कहीं दिख ही नहीं रहा। फिर Mendel ने F one को self-pollinate होने दिया — अब देखिए कौन वापस आता है।
F two generation में green वापस आ जाता है — और एक बेहद regular ratio में, लगभग तीन dominant to एक recessive। जो चीज़ सच में ख़त्म हो गई हो, वो इतनी साफ़ वापस नहीं आ सकती।
तो वो कभी गया ही नहीं था — बस mask हो गया था। Recessive allele को ऐसे सोचिए जैसे शोर वाले family dinner में एक शांत cousin: loud cousin के साथ बैठा हो तो आप उसे notice ही नहीं करते।
उसी शांत cousin को ऐसी table पर बिठाइए जहाँ सिर्फ दूसरा शांत cousin हो — यानी F two का recessive homozygote — और अचानक सिर्फ उसी की आवाज़ सुनाई देती है। कुछ mix नहीं हुआ, कुछ dilute नहीं हुआ।
यही Mendelian inheritance का दिल है। तीन to एक से Mendel ने dominance और segregation निकाला; और dihybrid के नौ to तीन to तीन to एक से independent assortment।
ये section pure vocabulary है, और इसमें बिलकुल कड़ाई रखिए। Genetics में ज़्यादातर marks concept miss होने से नहीं, term को लापरवाही से पढ़ने से जाते हैं।
Gene, या factor, inheritance की वो unit है जो किसी trait को code करती है। Mendel को पता ही नहीं था कि gene किस चीज़ का बना है — उन्होंने इन्हें बस factors कहा, और invisible units की तरह सोचा।
Allele किसी gene का एक alternative form है। Tall और dwarf एक ही height gene के दो alleles हैं। Convention ये है: dominant allele के लिए capital letter, recessive के लिए वही letter lower case में।
Genotype मतलब genetic constitution — organism असल में carry क्या कर रहा है, जैसे T T या T small t। Phenotype उसी genotype का observable expression है: tall या dwarf। यानी carry versus dikhna।
तीनों possible genotypes देखिए। Capital T capital T tall है। Capital T small t भी tall है। Small t small t dwarf है। तीन genotypes, लेकिन सिर्फ दो phenotypes।
Homozygous मतलब दोनों alleles identical — capital T capital T homozygous dominant, small t small t homozygous recessive। और ध्यान दीजिए: true-breeding line असल में homozygous line ही है।
Heterozygous मतलब दोनों alleles अलग — capital T small t। ऐसे individual को hybrid कहते हैं, और यहीं से monohybrid cross वाला शब्द hybrid आता है।
Dominant allele homozygous और heterozygous, दोनों states में express होता है। Recessive allele सिर्फ homozygous state में express होता है; heterozygote में वो mask रहता है।
और इससे निकलता है इस vocabulary का सबसे काम का नतीजा: capital T capital T और capital T small t दिखने में एक जैसे हैं। सिर्फ phenotype से इन्हें अलग नहीं किया जा सकता — इसके लिए test cross चाहिए।
Exam questions शायद ही बताती हैं कि कौन सा cross है; वो describe करती हैं और उम्मीद करती हैं कि आप नाम पहचानें। तो चारों names fix कर लीजिए, और वो एक distinction जिसमें marks जाते हैं।
Monohybrid cross एक single gene pair track करता है। Capital T small t cross with capital T small t — classic। एक gene, contrasting alleles की एक जोड़ी, और वही F two ratio जो आप जानते हैं।
Dihybrid cross एक साथ दो gene pairs track करता है — R small r capital Y small y का उसी से cross। दो genes एक ही cross में साथ चलते हैं, और यहीं independent assortment दिखता है।
यहाँ चारों साथ में हैं। ऊपर वाली row में selfing crosses जो ratios देते हैं। नीचे वाली row में वो crosses जो जानबूझ कर एक parent इस्तेमाल करते हैं, कुछ पता करने के लिए।

Test cross में unknown genotype वाला individual — जो dominant phenotype दिखा रहा है — homozygous recessive partner से cross किया जाता है। इसका पूरा मक़सद यही है: वो unknown homozygous है या heterozygous।
Back cross थोड़ा broader है: F one individual का किसी भी parental type से cross। यानी आप dominant parent से भी back cross कर सकते हैं, और recessive parent से भी।
और Punnett square तो cross है ही नहीं — वो tool है। R C Punnett का checkerboard grid, जिसमें gametes किनारों पर जाते हैं और हर cell एक equally likely fertilisation event है।
अब distinction। F one को recessive parent से cross किया, तो आपने back cross भी किया और test cross भी। Dominant parent से किया, तो सिर्फ back cross — उससे कुछ पता नहीं चलता।
Mendel के तीन laws तीन अलग discoveries नहीं हैं — ये उनके counts से पढ़े गए तीन conclusions हैं। हर law के पीछे एक ratio है, और कौन सा ratio किस law से आया, यही exam gold है।
Law of Dominance कहता है कि heterozygote में सिर्फ dominant allele express होता है; recessive mask हो जाता है। ये expression के बारे में statement है, inheritance के बारे में नहीं।
यही एक law दो observations एक साथ explain करता है: F one सिर्फ एक parent जैसा क्यों दिखता है, और F two तीन genotype classes से सिमट कर phenotype ratio तीन to एक क्यों बन जाता है।
Law of Segregation — जिसे Law of Purity of Gametes भी कहते हैं — कहता है कि gamete formation के दौरान किसी gene के दोनों alleles साफ़-साफ़ अलग हो जाते हैं। ये असली inheritance वाला law है।
Cell देखिए। Capital T small t parent दोनों alleles लेकर meiosis में जाता है। वो separate होते हैं, और हर gamete ठीक एक allele लेकर बाहर निकलता है।

तो हर gamete सिर्फ एक allele carry करता है, pure और uncontaminated। Capital T small t heterozygote आधे capital T और आधे small t gametes बनाता है। कभी दोनों नहीं, कभी mixture नहीं — purity शब्द यहाँ असली काम कर रहा है।

Law of Independent Assortment कहता है कि अलग-अलग genes के alleles, जो अलग chromosomes पर बैठे हैं, gamete formation में एक-दूसरे से independently segregate करते हैं। एक gene कैसे बँटा, इससे दूसरे का कोई लेना-देना नहीं।
<excited>और Mendel ने ये सिर्फ एक number से निकाला — dihybrid ratio नौ to तीन to तीन to एक। उन्होंने chromosomes देखे तक नहीं थे। उन्होंने एक tally sheet से उनका behaviour infer कर लिया।
दोनों को अलग रखिए। Segregation एक ही gene के अंदर की बात है — उसके दो alleles अलग होते हैं। Independent assortment दो genes के बीच की बात है — वो एक-दूसरे से पूछे बिना अलग होते हैं।
ये table इस subtopic की सबसे high-yield चीज़ है। अगर ये automatic नहीं है, तो हर numerical time pressure में derivation बन जाता है। तो इसे एक structure की तरह पढ़िए, छह अलग-अलग facts की तरह नहीं।
छह crosses, दो columns। बायाँ column वो जो दिखता है, दायाँ वो जो carry होता है। पूरी table असल में एक ही सवाल है: बाएँ और दाएँ के numbers मिलते हैं या नहीं?
Monohybrid F two, capital T small t cross with capital T small t: phenotype तीन to एक, genotype एक to दो to एक। दोनों अलग हैं क्योंकि heterozygote dominant के पीछे छुप जाता है।
Dihybrid F two: phenotype नौ to तीन to तीन to एक; genotype एक, दो, एक, दो, चार, दो, एक, दो, एक — यानी नौ distinct genotypes, grid के सोलह boxes में फैले हुए।

Test crosses सबसे आसान हैं। Monohybrid test cross दोनों तरह से एक to एक। Dihybrid test cross दोनों तरह से एक to एक to एक to एक। यहाँ कुछ छुपता नहीं, क्योंकि recessive parent छुपने के लिए कुछ देता ही नहीं।
अब दोनों deviations। Incomplete dominance F two और codominance F two, दोनों एक to दो to एक देते हैं — और यहाँ phenotype ratio और genotype ratio एक ही number हैं।

एक छोटी सी बात जो examiners घुमा कर पूछते हैं: इस पूरे subtopic में कोई units हैं ही नहीं। Genetics ratios pure numbers हैं। जो quantity track हो रही है वो offspring का proportion है, dimension check की ज़रूरत नहीं।
और pattern याद रखिए: deviations में phenotype बराबर genotype होता है क्योंकि हर genotype अलग दिखता है। जब भी दोनों ratios मिल जाएँ, समझ जाइए ये deviation है, ordinary dominance नहीं।
इस chapter का हर monohybrid question वही चार steps है, उसी order में। Order एक बार सीख लीजिए, फिर आप कभी blank page को नहीं घूरेंगे।
Step one: symbols assign कीजिए। एक letter चुनिए — dominant allele के लिए capital, recessive के लिए lower case। फिर हर parent का genotype लिखिए — उसका description नहीं, genotype।

और यही step क्यों ज़रूरी है, ये समझिए। Gametes genotype से बनते हैं, phenotype से नहीं। दो purple plants जो एक जैसे दिखते हैं, capital P capital P या capital P small p हो सकते हैं — और behaviour बिलकुल अलग।

Step two: gametes निकालिए। Law of Segregation से हर parent एक gamete में एक allele देता है। Capital P capital P सिर्फ capital P बनाता है। Capital P small p आधा capital P और आधा small p। Alleles pure रहते हैं — gamete के अंदर कभी blend नहीं होते।
Step three — और यहाँ grid है capital P small p cross with capital P small p का। एक parent के gametes ऊपर, दूसरे के gametes साइड में।
हर cell उसकी row वाले allele और column वाले allele को जोड़ कर भरिए। ऊपर बाएँ capital P और capital P मिलकर capital P capital P। नीचे दाएँ small p और small p मिलकर small p small p।
Grid से ratio आता ही क्यों है? क्योंकि वो हर equally likely fertilisation event को ठीक एक बार गिनता है। चार boxes, चार equally likely outcomes — तो boxes गिनना probability गिनना है।
Step four का पहला हिस्सा: genotype ratio सीधे boxes से पढ़िए। एक capital P capital P, दो capital P small p, एक small p small p। यानी एक to दो to एक।
और उसके बाद ही dominance लगाकर phenotype पर collapse कीजिए। पहले तीनों boxes में कम से कम एक capital P है, तो तीनों purple। सिर्फ small p small p green है। तीन purple to एक green।
दो genes एक साथ — यहीं students बड़े-बड़े grids बनाने लगते हैं और arithmetic में marks गँवाते हैं। एक grid method है और एक fast method; दोनों जानिए, इस्तेमाल fast वाला कीजिए।
Gametes से शुरू कीजिए। Heterozygote capital R small r capital Y small y दो to the power n gamete types बनाता है, जहाँ n है heterozygous gene pairs की संख्या। ये formula लगभग हर numerical में लौटेगा।
यहाँ n बराबर दो, तो चार gamete types: capital R capital Y, capital R small y, small r capital Y, small r small y — हर एक बराबर proportion में, एक-चौथाई।

इन चार gametes को चार by चार Punnett square में डालिए, capital R small r capital Y small y का अपने आप से cross, और निकलता है classic नौ to तीन to तीन to एक। यही ratio सबूत है कि दोनों genes independently assort कर रहे हैं।
पर दोनों रास्ते साथ में देखिए। बाईं तरफ़ सोलह boxes भरने और classify करने हैं। दाईं तरफ़ दो छोटे monohybrid crosses। जवाब वही, पर exam pressure में failure rate बिलकुल अलग।
तो grid छोड़िए। सोलह boxes slow हैं, और तीन genes के लिए आठ by आठ तो पक्की ग़लती है। बजाय इसके multiply कीजिए।
Product rule: दो independent events के एक साथ होने की probability उनकी अलग-अलग probabilities का product होती है। Round और yellow अलग genes से control होते हैं, तो ये independent qualify करते हैं।
Sum rule इसका साथी है: दो mutually exclusive outcomes में से किसी एक की probability उनका sum होती है। And के लिए product, or के लिए sum।

<excited>चलकर देखिए। Round की probability तीन-चौथाई। Yellow की probability तीन-चौथाई। Round and yellow की probability हुई तीन-चौथाई into तीन-चौथाई, यानी नौ बटा सोलह — वही नौ जो नौ to तीन to तीन to एक में है, बिना grid के।
<curious>आप एक purple brinjal plant के सामने खड़े हैं। वो या तो capital P capital P है या capital P small p, और देखने से आपको कभी पता नहीं चलेगा। तो पता कैसे करें?
यही problem solve करने के लिए test cross है। दोनों genotypes वही identical purple phenotype देते हैं, क्योंकि एक capital P काफ़ी है। Information plant में है ही — बस छुपी हुई है।
तो उसे homozygous recessive से cross कीजिए — small p small p, एक green plant। किसी और purple से नहीं, dominant parent से नहीं। जानबूझ कर double recessive से।
और अब ठीक दो ही चीज़ें हो सकती हैं, इस पर कि unknown असल में कौन सा genotype था। दोनों branches बिलकुल अलग दिखती हैं — यही तो पूरा मक़सद है।

पहली branch: अगर unknown capital P capital P है, तो वो सिर्फ capital P gametes दे सकता है। हर offspring को उससे capital P और green partner से small p मिलेगा, तो हर offspring capital P small p — सब purple। यानी एक to शून्य।
दूसरी branch: अगर unknown capital P small p है, तो आधा capital P और आधा small p देता है। आधे offspring capital P small p, purple; आधे small p small p, green। एक purple to एक green।
तो आपको ध्यान से गिनने की ज़रूरत भी नहीं। एक भी recessive offspring का दिखना — एक हरा brinjal — साबित कर देता है कि parent heterozygous था। Homozygous dominant parent उसे पैदा कर ही नहीं सकता।

और अब समझिए recessive partner क्यों compulsory है। वो सिर्फ recessive alleles देता है, तो कुछ mask करता ही नहीं। Offspring का phenotype सीधे unknown parent के gamete types का read-out बन जाता है — यही तो चाहिए था।

board_events.text: When neither allele fully dominates
Incomplete dominance: neither allele fully dominates; the heterozygote shows a new, intermediate phenotype.
Classic cases: flower colour in Mirabilis jalapa (the four o'clock plant) and in Antirrhinum (snapdragon).

board_events.text: Red (RR) × white (rr) gives pink (Rr) in F1. Selfing the F1 gives 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.
Phenotypic ratio now EQUALS genotypic ratio, because every genotype looks different.
Mechanism: the recessive allele makes a non-functional or reduced enzyme, so one dose of the functional allele cannot make full pigment.
This is NOT blending. Red and white parents reappear unchanged in F2, proving the alleles stayed pure.
Segregation still holds perfectly. The deviation is in how alleles express, not in how they are inherited.
When both alleles speak at once
Codominance: both alleles express fully and independently in the heterozygote — you see both parental products, not a blend.
The textbook case: the human ABO blood group, governed by one gene $I$ with three alleles — $I^A$, $I^B$ and $i$.

board_events.text: $I^A$ and $I^B$ are codominant — each makes its own surface sugar. Both are dominant over $i$.
$I^AI^A$ and $I^Ai$ give A. $I^BI^B$ and $I^Bi$ give B. $I^AI^B$ gives AB. $ii$ gives O.
Multiple allelism: a gene with more than two alleles in the population — here three.
Three alleles produce six genotypes and four phenotypes.
One example, two ideas: multiple allelism, and codominance visible in the AB heterozygote.
Four gates a clean Mendelian ratio must pass
Condition 1: the genes must lie on different chromosomes, or far apart, so they assort independently.
Genes physically close together are linked, and linkage breaks the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.
Condition 2: one allele must be fully dominant. Incomplete dominance and codominance shift the phenotypic ratio.

board_events.text: Condition 3: all genotypes must survive and reproduce equally — no lethal alleles, no selection.
Condition 4: the sample must be large enough for ratios to emerge. With three or four offspring you will rarely see a clean 3 : 1.
Mendel partly got lucky: the seven pea genes he studied sit on only four chromosomes, yet behaved as independent.
Example one [C B S E Board]
In brinjal, purple fruit colour (P) is dominant over green (p). A true-breeding purple plant is crossed with a true-breeding green plant. Give the F1 and F2 ratios.

Example two [N E E T speed trap]
(a) How many gamete types does an individual of genotype AaBBCcDd produce? (b) In the cross AaBbCc × AaBbCc, what fraction of offspring are aabbcc?

board_events.text: Speed logic: only heterozygous gene pairs generate gamete variety. Use $2^n$.
Heterozygous pairs in AaBBCcDd: Aa, Cc and Dd. So n = 3.
$2^3 = 8$ gamete types.
BB is homozygous and contributes nothing. The classic trap is counting it and answering $2^4 = 16$.
(b) Take one gene at a time. For each gene, P(recessive homozygote) = 1/4.
By the product rule, $(1/4)^3 = 1/64$.
Example three [N E E T]
A man with blood group AB marries a woman with blood group O. What blood groups can their children have, and what is the probability that a given child is group A?

<rect x="140" y="92" width="120" height="60" fill="#ede9fe" stroke="#1f2937"/>

<rect x="60" y="198" width="380" height="42" rx="8" fill="#fef2f2" stroke="#dc2626"/>
<text x="250" y="224" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">AB and O are the two groups that are impossible</text>
<text x="250" y="264" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#6b7280">The father has no i to give; the mother has no I A or I B to give</text>

</svg>

board_events.text: Genotypes: the AB man is $I^AI^B$; the O woman is $ii$.
Gametes: the man gives half $I^A$ and half $I^B$. The woman gives only $i$.
Offspring: half $I^Ai$, which is group A, and half $I^Bi$, which is group B.
So children can be only A or B, in a 1 : 1 ratio, and P(group A) = 1/2.
Neither AB nor O is possible. The two groups people guess are exactly the two that are excluded.
Example four [N E E T high difficulty]
In snapdragon, flower colour shows incomplete dominance: RR = red, Rr = pink, rr = white. Height shows complete dominance: T (tall) over t (dwarf). Cross RrTt × RrTt.
(a) What is the probability of a pink, tall offspring? (b) How many distinct phenotypic classes appear?

board_events.text: Treat each gene independently and use the product rule.
Colour (Rr × Rr): 1/4 red : 1/2 pink : 1/4 white, so P(pink) = 1/2.
Height (Tt × Tt): 3/4 tall : 1/4 dwarf, so P(tall) = 3/4.
(a) P(pink and tall) = 1/2 × 3/4 = 3/8.
(b) 3 colour classes × 2 height classes = 6 phenotypic classes — not the 4 of an ordinary dihybrid.
Common student pitfalls
Pitfall 1: mixing up genotypic and phenotypic ratios. Monohybrid F2 is 3 : 1 by phenotype, but 1 : 2 : 1 by genotype. Read the wording before answering.
Pitfall 2: confusing incomplete dominance with codominance. Both give a 1 : 2 : 1 phenotypic ratio, so the ratio can never separate them.

board_events.caption: The heterozygote is the only reliable clue

<text x="139" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">Mirabilis, snapdragon</text>

board_events.text: The difference is the heterozygote: incomplete dominance shows a blended intermediate (pink); codominance shows both parental traits fully and separately (group AB).
Intermediate = incomplete. Both-at-once = co.
Pitfall 3: forgetting that a test cross needs a homozygous recessive partner. Crossing with any other parental type is a back cross, not necessarily a test cross.
Pitfall 4: treating blood group O as dominant, or counting homozygous pairs like BB as a source of gamete variety. $i$ is recessive, and homozygous pairs contribute zero variety.
Pro-tips and memory aids
For any multi-gene cross, never draw a giant Punnett square.
Split it into separate monohybrid crosses, find each single-gene probability, and multiply.
P(a specific multi-trait offspring) is just the product of the single-gene probabilities — faster, and far fewer arithmetic slips under exam pressure.
Pair this with $2^n$ for counting gamete types, where n = the number of heterozygous gene pairs only.
Memory aid: "Cross the unknown with the double-recessive to make it confess."
Memory aid: "Intermediate = incomplete; both-at-once = co."
Deviation check: whenever the phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio, you are looking at incomplete dominance or codominance, not ordinary dominance.
From invisible factors to visible chromosomes
Mendel handed us factors that segregate and assort — but he never knew where they physically sat.
By 1900, microscopes had improved enough that biologists could watch chromosomes pair up and separate during meiosis.

board_events.text: Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri noticed it: chromosome behaviour in gamete formation runs exactly parallel to how Mendel's factors segregate.
Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance (Sutton and Boveri, 1902): genes are carried on chromosomes.
The movement of chromosomes during meiosis is the physical machinery behind Mendel's laws.
Pairing, then separating, one of each pair into each gamete — that IS segregation, made visible.

segments.text: Mendel picked seven traits where one allele fully dominates. Nature is richer than that. The next two sections are the two famous places where the dominance rule bends — but, and this matters, the inheritance rule does not.
Incomplete dominance is the first. Neither allele fully dominates the other, and the heterozygote shows a brand new, intermediate phenotype — something that looks like neither parent.

The classic cases are flower colour in Mirabilis jalapa, the four o'clock plant, and in Antirrhinum, the snapdragon. If a question mentions either plant with flower colour, this is almost certainly what it is testing.
Follow the cross. Red, capital R capital R, crossed with white, small r small r. And the F one is neither — it is pink.

Red crossed with white gives pink in the F one, every time. Self the F one and the F two comes out one red to two pink to one white. Notice that is not three to one. The ratio itself has changed shape.

And here is the structural point. The phenotypic ratio now equals the genotypic ratio — both are one to two to one. That happens because every genotype looks different: capital R capital R is red, capital R small r is pink, small r small r is white. Nothing hides.

The mechanism is worth one line, because boards ask for it. The recessive allele produces a non-functional, or reduced, enzyme. So a heterozygote has only one working dose, and one dose cannot manufacture full pigment. Half the pigment machinery, half the colour.

<curious>Now the trap that this looks exactly like. Pink is not a blend. If red and white had truly mixed, they could never separate again — and yet pure red and pure white walk right back into the F two, unchanged.

So segregation holds perfectly here. The alleles stayed pure, separated cleanly, and recombined. The deviation is only in how the alleles express, not in how they are inherited. Mendel's logic survives; only the dominance assumption fails.

The second deviation is codominance, and the difference from incomplete dominance is one word: both. Both alleles express fully and independently in the heterozygote, so you see both parental products — side by side, not blended into one.
Say that carefully, because it is the exact line examiners test. Not an intermediate. Not a compromise. Both products, each made at full strength, both visible in the same individual.
The textbook case is the human A B O blood group. It is governed by one gene, called capital I, but that gene has three alleles in the population — I A, I B, and small i.
Look at the red cell surfaces. Group A carries one kind of sugar. Group B carries another. Group A B carries both kinds, at once, in full — and that is what codominance looks like physically.

The rules are two lines. I A and I B are codominant with each other — each makes its own surface sugar, and neither hides the other. And both of them are dominant over small i, which makes no sugar at all.
Now read the table. I A with I A, or I A with small i, gives group A. I B with I B, or I B with small i, gives group B. I A with I B gives group A B. And small i with small i gives group O.

This example also carries a second idea, and questions love to bundle them. Multiple allelism means a gene with more than two alleles present in the population — here, three. Any one person still carries only two of them.

<excited>And the arithmetic falls out beautifully. Three alleles taken two at a time give six genotypes, and those six collapse into four phenotypes — because I A I A and I A small i both look like group A, and likewise for B.

So hold this one example in mind for two separate questions. Ask about the three alleles, and the answer is multiple allelism. Ask about the A B individual specifically, and the answer is codominance.

Mendel's ratios are not laws of nature that hold everywhere. They are outputs of a model, and the model has assumptions. Knowing where it breaks is exactly what separates a board-level answer from a rank.

Condition one: the genes must lie on different chromosomes, or at least far apart on the same one, so that they assort independently. Independent assortment was never a guarantee — it was a condition.

Break that condition and you get linkage. Genes sitting physically close together travel together, and the nine to three to three to one ratio collapses. That is the entire next subtopic, so file it here.

Condition two: one allele must be fully dominant. You have just seen the two ways this fails — incomplete dominance and codominance — and both of them shift the phenotypic ratio from three to one over to one to two to one.
Here are all four gates together. A cross must pass every one of them for the textbook numbers to appear. Fail any single gate and the ratio you were expecting simply does not show up.

Condition three: all genotypes must survive and reproduce equally. If one genotype is lethal, or is selected against, the survivors are a biased sample and the counted ratio shifts. You are counting who lived, not who was conceived.

Condition four is the quietly practical one: the sample must be large. Ratios are statistical statements. With three or four offspring you will almost never see a clean three to one — which is precisely why Mendel counted thousands.

<chuckle>And one honest footnote the exam sometimes rewards. Mendel partly got lucky. His seven pea genes sit on only four chromosomes, so some of them should have been linked — and yet they behaved as independent.

First worked example, and it is a C B S E board favourite. In brinjal, purple fruit colour, capital P, is dominant over green, small p. A true-breeding purple plant is crossed with a true-breeding green plant. Give the F one and F two ratios.

Before any arithmetic, translate the words. True-breeding purple is not just purple — true-breeding means homozygous, so it must be capital P capital P. True-breeding green is small p small p. That translation is step one of Procedure A, and it is where careless answers die.
Here is the whole solution laid out. Left half is the F one step, right half is the F two Punnett square. In a board answer, you draw both — the marks are for the working, not just the final ratio.
So, given: the parents are capital P capital P, purple, and small p small p, green.

The F one: capital P capital P crossed with small p small p. The first parent can give only capital P, the second only small p. So every offspring is capital P small p, and since capital P is dominant, the entire F one is purple.

Now the F two, which is the F one selfed: capital P small p crossed with capital P small p. Both parents give half capital P and half small p, and the four boxes come out capital P capital P, capital P small p, capital P small p, and small p small p.
Read the genotype ratio straight off the grid: one capital P capital P to two capital P small p to one small p small p. One to two to one.

Then collapse using dominance: the three boxes carrying at least one capital P are purple, and only small p small p is green. Three purple to one green. And the exam point is right here — the question said ratios, plural, so write both, and always check which one is being asked.

This one is a N E E T speed trap, which means it is designed so that the fast wrong answer is easier to reach than the fast right answer. Two parts. Part a: how many gamete types does an individual of genotype capital A small a, capital B capital B, capital C small c, capital D small d produce? Part b: in the cross capital A small a capital B small b capital C small c with itself, what fraction of offspring are small a small a small b small b small c small c?
Look at the genotype broken up gene pair by gene pair. Three of the four pairs are heterozygous. One of them is not. That single homozygous pair is the entire question.
The speed logic is one sentence: only heterozygous gene pairs generate gamete variety, so use two to the power n, where n counts those pairs and nothing else.
So identify them. Capital A small a is heterozygous. Capital B capital B is not. Capital C small c is heterozygous. Capital D small d is heterozygous. That gives n equals three.
And the answer to part a is two cubed, which is eight gamete types.

Why is capital B capital B excluded? Because it can only ever give capital B. It multiplies your gamete count by one, not by two. It adds no variety, so it does not enter the exponent. The classic trap is to count all four letters and answer two to the fourth, sixteen — and sixteen will absolutely be on the option list.

Now part b, which is a completely different idea wearing the same clothes. Here you want a specific offspring genotype from a triple heterozygous cross. Do not touch two to the power n — that formula counts gametes, not offspring.

Instead take one gene at a time. Capital A small a crossed with capital A small a gives small a small a with probability one quarter. The same is true for the b gene, and for the c gene, independently.

So by the product rule, the probability of small a small a and small b small b and small c small c together is one quarter times one quarter times one quarter — one quarter cubed, which is one over sixty four.

This question is a N E E T regular, and it is worth doing slowly, because the wrong answer feels so natural that students pick it confidently. A man with blood group A B marries a woman with blood group O. What blood groups can their children have, and what is the probability that a given child is group A?
The instinct is to say A B and O — the parents' own groups, one each, nice and symmetric. Hold that thought, because it is not just wrong, it is exactly inverted.
Look at the grid. Two boxes, and neither of them says A B, and neither says O. Everything below is just working out why.

Start where you always start: convert phenotypes to genotypes. Blood group A B has to be I A with I B — there is no other way to be A B. Blood group O has to be small i small i, because small i is recessive and O means no sugar at all.

Now the gametes. The man is heterozygous for two codominant alleles, so he gives half I A and half I B. The woman is homozygous small i small i, so she gives only small i — she has nothing else to give.
Combine them. Half the children get I A from the father and small i from the mother, giving I A small i, which is group A. The other half get I B and small i, giving I B small i, which is group B.
So children can be only A or B, in a one to one ratio, and the probability that a given child is group A is one half. That answers both parts of the question.

<curious>And now the reason the instinct fails. For a child to be A B, it would need an I A and an I B — but the mother has neither. For a child to be O, it would need a small i from each parent — but the father has no small i to give. The A B father cannot pass on small i, and the O mother cannot pass on I A or I B, so the very two groups people guess are the two that are excluded.
This is the hard one, and it is hard for a specific reason: it hides a deviation inside a perfectly ordinary-looking dihybrid.

Here is the setup. In snapdragon, flower colour shows incomplete dominance — capital R capital R is red, capital R small r is pink, small r small r is white. Height shows ordinary complete dominance, capital T tall over small t dwarf. Cross capital R small r capital T small t with itself.

Two parts. Part a: what is the probability of a pink, tall offspring? Part b: how many distinct phenotypic classes appear? And if your reflex is to reach for nine to three to three to one, this question has already caught you.
Look at the split — colour handled on the left, height on the right. Two small monohybrids instead of one sixteen-box grid.
The method is the same as any dihybrid: solve each gene independently, then multiply. The only difference is that one of the two monohybrids does not follow the usual dominance rule.

So take colour first. Capital R small r crossed with capital R small r gives one quarter red, one half pink, one quarter white. That is the incomplete dominance ratio, one to two to one, not three to one. So the probability of pink is one half.
Now height, which is completely ordinary. Capital T small t crossed with capital T small t gives three quarters tall to one quarter dwarf. So the probability of tall is three quarters.

Part a is now one multiplication. Probability of pink and tall equals one half times three quarters, which is three eighths. Notice it is not nine sixteenths — the deviation changed one of the factors, and the answer moved with it.

<excited>Part b is the deeper half. Colour gives three visible classes — red, pink and white — because incomplete dominance makes the heterozygote look different; height gives two, tall and dwarf. So total classes equals three times two, which is six, not the four of an ordinary dihybrid. One deviation in one gene rewrote the familiar answer, and that is precisely what this question is testing.
These four pitfalls are not exotic. They are the ordinary ways a student who understands the chapter still loses marks — so read them as a checklist to run before you write any final answer.

Pitfall one: mixing up genotypic and phenotypic ratios. Monohybrid F two is three to one by phenotype, but one to two to one by genotype. Both are correct answers to different questions. Read the wording, underline the word phenotypic or genotypic, and then answer.

Pitfall two is the big one: confusing incomplete dominance with codominance. Both give a one to two to one phenotypic ratio, so students treat them as the same thing. And notice what that means — the ratio can never tell you which one you are looking at.
So look at the picture instead, specifically at the middle individual in each case. That heterozygote is the only reliable clue you have.

The difference lives entirely there. In incomplete dominance the heterozygote is a blended intermediate — pink, a shade neither parent had. In codominance the heterozygote shows both parental traits fully and separately — group A B carries both sugars, side by side, neither diluted.
So carry the one-line test. Intermediate equals incomplete. Both-at-once equals co. Say it in that order, and check it against the heterozygote, never against the numbers.

Pitfall three: forgetting that a test cross needs a homozygous recessive partner. Crossing your unknown with a recessive-looking plant, or with either parental type generally, is a back cross — and only the homozygous recessive version cleanly reveals the unknown genotype.

Pitfall four is really two habits in one. Do not treat blood group O as dominant — small i is recessive, and O is the double recessive. And do not count homozygous gene pairs like capital B capital B when working out gamete variety, because a homozygous pair contributes exactly zero variety.
Close the subtopic with the habits, not the facts. These are the things that decide whether you finish the paper, not just whether you understand the biology.
First and biggest: for any multi-gene cross, never draw a giant Punnett square. Sixteen boxes is slow. Sixty four boxes is a mistake with extra steps. The grid is a teaching tool, not an exam tool.

Instead, split the cross into separate monohybrid crosses, find each single-gene probability, and multiply. Every dihybrid and trihybrid question in this chapter dissolves into two or three tiny crosses you can do in your head.

The rule underneath it is simple: the probability of a specific multi-trait offspring is just the product of the single-gene probabilities. Faster, and far fewer arithmetic slips under exam pressure — which is where marks actually leak.
Pair that with two to the power n for counting gamete types, and remember the one restriction that makes it a trap: n counts heterozygous gene pairs only. Homozygous pairs never enter the exponent.

For the test cross, keep the sentence that carries both the method and the reason. Cross the unknown with the double-recessive to make it confess. The double recessive hides nothing, so the offspring report the truth.
And the deviation line, which you will use in almost every deviation question. Intermediate equals incomplete; both-at-once equals co. Check it against the heterozygote, never against the ratio.

One last diagnostic to carry into the next subtopic. Whenever the phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio, you are not looking at ordinary dominance — you are looking at incomplete dominance or codominance. And when the dihybrid ratio itself refuses to be nine to three to three to one, that is linkage, which is exactly where we go next.

In the last subtopic Mendel handed us factors that segregate and assort. But notice what he never told us: where those factors actually are. He was reasoning about invisible units he could not point at.
That is the gap this subtopic closes. Mendel's factors get a street address — and the address is the chromosome.

By around nineteen hundred, microscopes had improved enough that biologists could actually watch chromosomes during meiosis. They saw them pair up, line up, and separate, one of each pair into each gamete.
Now put the two pictures side by side, which is exactly what the diagram does. On top, Mendel's factors separating. Below, chromosomes separating. Look at how similar the two stories are.

Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri noticed precisely that. The way chromosomes behave during gamete formation — pairing, then separating, one of each pair into each gamete — runs exactly parallel to the way Mendel's factors segregate.

So they put the two ideas together into the Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance, in nineteen oh two: genes are carried on chromosomes. Sutton and Boveri — that pairing of names is a guaranteed recall question.
And the claim is stronger than it first sounds. It says the movement of chromosomes during meiosis is not merely similar to Mendel's laws — it is the physical machinery behind them.

Read the last line carefully, because it is the whole theory in one sentence. Chromosomes pairing and then separating, one of each pair into each gamete, is not an analogy for segregation. It is segregation, made visible.

Mendel ने सात ऐसे traits चुने जहाँ एक allele पूरी तरह dominate करता है। पर nature इससे कहीं ज़्यादा rich है। अगले दो sections वो दो मशहूर जगहें हैं जहाँ dominance rule झुकता है — पर inheritance rule नहीं।
पहली है incomplete dominance। यहाँ कोई भी allele दूसरे को पूरी तरह dominate नहीं करता, और heterozygote एक बिलकुल नया, intermediate phenotype दिखाता है — जो किसी parent जैसा नहीं लगता।

Classic cases हैं Mirabilis jalapa का flower colour, यानी four o'clock plant, और Antirrhinum यानी snapdragon। Question में इनमें से कोई plant flower colour के साथ आए, तो लगभग पक्का यही test हो रहा है।
Cross देखिए। Red, capital R capital R, cross with white, small r small r। और F one दोनों में से कोई नहीं — वो pink है।
Red cross white हर बार F one में pink देता है। F one को self कीजिए और F two निकलता है एक red to दो pink to एक white। ध्यान दीजिए, ये तीन to एक नहीं है। Ratio की shape ही बदल गई।

और यहाँ structural बात है। Phenotypic ratio अब genotypic ratio के बराबर है — दोनों एक to दो to एक। ऐसा इसलिए क्योंकि हर genotype अलग दिखता है: capital R capital R red, capital R small r pink, small r small r white। कुछ छुपता नहीं।

Mechanism की एक line ज़रूरी है, क्योंकि boards यही पूछते हैं। Recessive allele एक non-functional, या कम काम करने वाला, enzyme बनाता है। तो heterozygote के पास सिर्फ एक working dose है, और एक dose पूरा pigment नहीं बना पाता। आधी machinery, आधा colour।

<curious>अब वो trap जिससे ये बिलकुल मिलता-जुलता लगता है। Pink कोई blend नहीं है। अगर red और white सच में mix हो जाते, तो फिर कभी अलग नहीं हो पाते — और यहाँ pure red और pure white F two में वापस चले आते हैं, बिलकुल unchanged।

तो यहाँ segregation पूरी तरह होता है। Alleles pure रहे, साफ़ अलग हुए, और फिर से जुड़े। Deviation सिर्फ इसमें है कि alleles express कैसे होते हैं, इसमें नहीं कि वो inherit कैसे होते हैं। Mendel की logic बची रहती है; सिर्फ dominance assumption टूटता है।

दूसरा deviation है codominance, और incomplete dominance से फ़र्क़ सिर्फ एक शब्द का है: both। Heterozygote में दोनों alleles पूरी तरह और independently express होते हैं, तो आपको दोनों parental products दिखते हैं — साथ-साथ, blend होकर एक नहीं।
इसे ध्यान से बोलिए, क्योंकि examiners यही line test करते हैं। कोई intermediate नहीं। कोई compromise नहीं। दोनों products, हर एक पूरी strength पर, दोनों एक ही individual में दिखते हुए।
Textbook case है human A B O blood group। ये एक ही gene से control होता है, जिसे capital I कहते हैं, पर उस gene के population में तीन alleles हैं — I A, I B, और small i।
Red cell surfaces देखिए। Group A एक तरह की sugar carry करता है। Group B दूसरी। Group A B दोनों तरह की, एक साथ, पूरी — और codominance physically ऐसा ही दिखता है।
Rules दो lines में हैं। I A और I B आपस में codominant हैं — हर एक अपनी surface sugar बनाता है, कोई दूसरे को छुपाता नहीं। और ये दोनों small i पर dominant हैं, जो कोई sugar बनाता ही नहीं।
अब table पढ़िए। I A with I A, या I A with small i, देता है group A। I B with I B, या I B with small i, देता है group B। I A with I B देता है group A B। और small i with small i देता है group O।

ये example एक दूसरा idea भी लेकर आता है, और questions इन्हें साथ में पूछना पसंद करते हैं। Multiple allelism मतलब ऐसा gene जिसके population में दो से ज़्यादा alleles हों — यहाँ तीन। कोई भी एक इंसान फिर भी सिर्फ दो ही carry करता है।

<excited>और arithmetic बहुत सुंदर निकलती है। तीन alleles, दो-दो करके, छह genotypes देते हैं, और वो छह सिमट कर चार phenotypes बनते हैं — क्योंकि I A I A और I A small i दोनों group A दिखते हैं, और यही B के साथ।
तो इस एक example को दो अलग questions के लिए याद रखिए। तीन alleles की बात हो, तो जवाब multiple allelism। सिर्फ A B individual की बात हो, तो जवाब codominance।
Mendel के ratios ऐसे laws नहीं हैं जो हर जगह लागू हों। ये एक model के outputs हैं, और model की assumptions हैं। ये जानना कि model कहाँ टूटता है, यही board-level जवाब और rank में फ़र्क़ है।

Condition one: genes अलग-अलग chromosomes पर होने चाहिए, या कम से कम एक ही chromosome पर बहुत दूर, ताकि वो independently assort करें। Independent assortment कभी guarantee थी ही नहीं — वो एक condition थी।
ये condition टूटी तो linkage मिलता है। Physically पास बैठे genes साथ चलते हैं, और नौ to तीन to तीन to एक वाला ratio बिखर जाता है। यही अगला पूरा subtopic है, तो इसे यहीं note कर लीजिए।

Condition two: एक allele पूरी तरह dominant होना चाहिए। इसके टूटने के दोनों तरीक़े आप अभी देख चुके हैं — incomplete dominance और codominance — और दोनों phenotypic ratio को तीन to एक से खिसका कर एक to दो to एक कर देते हैं।
यहाँ चारों gates साथ में हैं। Textbook numbers दिखने के लिए cross को हर एक gate पास करना होगा। एक भी gate fail हुआ, तो जो ratio आप expect कर रहे थे वो आएगा ही नहीं।

Condition three: सारे genotypes बराबर survive और reproduce करें। अगर कोई genotype lethal है, या उसके ख़िलाफ़ selection है, तो survivors एक biased sample हैं और counted ratio खिसक जाता है। आप गिन रहे हैं कि कौन बचा, ये नहीं कि कौन बना।
Condition four सबसे practical है: sample बड़ा होना चाहिए। Ratios statistical statements हैं। तीन-चार offspring में आपको साफ़ तीन to एक लगभग कभी नहीं दिखेगा — और इसीलिए Mendel ने हज़ारों गिने।

<chuckle>और एक ईमानदार footnote, जिसका exam में कभी-कभी फ़ायदा मिलता है। Mendel थोड़े lucky भी थे। उनके सातों pea genes सिर्फ चार chromosomes पर बैठे हैं, यानी कुछ linked होने चाहिए थे — फिर भी वो independent जैसा behave कर गए।

पहला worked example, और ये C B S E board का favourite है। Brinjal में purple fruit colour, capital P, green यानी small p पर dominant है। एक true-breeding purple plant का true-breeding green से cross कीजिए। F one और F two ratios बताइए।

Arithmetic से पहले शब्दों को translate कीजिए। True-breeding purple सिर्फ purple नहीं है — true-breeding मतलब homozygous, तो वो capital P capital P होगा। True-breeding green small p small p। यही Procedure A का step one है, और यहीं लापरवाह जवाब मरते हैं।
यहाँ पूरा solution रखा है। बायाँ हिस्सा F one step, दायाँ हिस्सा F two Punnett square। Board answer में दोनों बनाइए — marks working के हैं, सिर्फ final ratio के नहीं।
तो given: parents हैं capital P capital P, purple, और small p small p, green।

F one: capital P capital P cross with small p small p। पहला parent सिर्फ capital P दे सकता है, दूसरा सिर्फ small p। तो हर offspring capital P small p, और capital P dominant है, इसलिए पूरी F one purple।

अब F two, यानी F one का selfing: capital P small p cross with capital P small p। दोनों parents आधा capital P और आधा small p देते हैं, और चारों boxes निकलते हैं capital P capital P, capital P small p, capital P small p, और small p small p।
Genotype ratio सीधे grid से पढ़िए: एक capital P capital P to दो capital P small p to एक small p small p। एक to दो to एक।

फिर dominance लगाकर collapse कीजिए: जिन तीन boxes में कम से कम एक capital P है वो purple, और सिर्फ small p small p green। तीन purple to एक green। और exam point यहीं है — question ने ratios कहा, plural में, तो दोनों लिखिए, और हमेशा check कीजिए कौन सा पूछा है।

ये N E E T speed trap है, यानी इसे ऐसे बनाया गया है कि fast ग़लत जवाब, fast सही जवाब से आसान लगे। दो parts। Part a: capital A small a, capital B capital B, capital C small c, capital D small d genotype वाला individual कितने gamete types बनाता है? Part b: capital A small a capital B small b capital C small c का अपने आप से cross — कितने fraction offspring small a small a small b small b small c small c होंगे?
Genotype को gene pair के हिसाब से तोड़ कर देखिए। चार में से तीन pairs heterozygous हैं। एक नहीं है। वही एक homozygous pair पूरा question है।
Speed logic एक line में: सिर्फ heterozygous gene pairs gamete variety बनाते हैं, तो दो to the power n लगाइए, जहाँ n सिर्फ उन्हीं pairs को गिनता है।
तो पहचानिए। Capital A small a heterozygous। Capital B capital B नहीं। Capital C small c heterozygous। Capital D small d heterozygous। यानी n बराबर तीन।
और part a का जवाब है दो का घन, यानी आठ gamete types।

Capital B capital B बाहर क्यों? क्योंकि वो सिर्फ capital B ही दे सकता है। वो आपकी gamete count को एक से multiply करता है, दो से नहीं। कोई variety नहीं जोड़ता, तो exponent में आता ही नहीं। Classic trap है चारों letters गिन कर दो to the fourth, सोलह लिख देना — और सोलह options में ज़रूर होगा।

अब part b, जो बिलकुल अलग idea है पर उन्हीं कपड़ों में। यहाँ triple heterozygous cross से एक specific offspring genotype चाहिए। दो to the power n को हाथ मत लगाइए — वो formula gametes गिनता है, offspring नहीं।
बजाय इसके एक-एक gene लीजिए। Capital A small a cross with capital A small a, small a small a की probability एक-चौथाई। यही b gene के लिए, यही c gene के लिए, independently।
तो product rule से, small a small a और small b small b और small c small c एक साथ आने की probability हुई एक-चौथाई into एक-चौथाई into एक-चौथाई — यानी एक-चौथाई का घन, जो है एक बटा चौंसठ।

ये question N E E T में बार-बार आता है, और इसे धीरे करना चाहिए, क्योंकि ग़लत जवाब इतना natural लगता है कि students confidence से चुन लेते हैं। एक A B blood group वाला आदमी O blood group वाली औरत से शादी करता है। बच्चों के कौन से blood groups हो सकते हैं, और किसी बच्चे के group A होने की probability क्या है?
Instinct कहता है A B और O — यानी parents के अपने groups, एक-एक, बड़ा symmetric। इसे पकड़ के रखिए, क्योंकि ये सिर्फ ग़लत नहीं है, ये बिलकुल उल्टा है।
Grid देखिए। दो boxes, और इनमें से न कोई A B है, न कोई O। नीचे की सारी बात बस ये है कि ऐसा क्यों।

वहीं से शुरू कीजिए जहाँ हमेशा: phenotypes को genotypes में बदलिए। Blood group A B का मतलब I A with I B ही है — A B होने का दूसरा कोई रास्ता नहीं। Blood group O का मतलब small i small i, क्योंकि small i recessive है और O मतलब कोई sugar नहीं।
अब gametes। आदमी दो codominant alleles के लिए heterozygous है, तो वो आधा I A और आधा I B देता है। औरत homozygous small i small i है, तो वो सिर्फ small i देती है — उसके पास देने को और कुछ है ही नहीं।
अब जोड़िए। आधे बच्चों को father से I A और mother से small i मिलता है, यानी I A small i, जो group A है। बाक़ी आधों को I B और small i, यानी I B small i, जो group B है।
तो बच्चे सिर्फ A या B हो सकते हैं, एक to एक ratio में, और किसी बच्चे के group A होने की probability है आधा। यही दोनों parts का जवाब है।

<curious>और अब समझिए instinct fail क्यों हुआ। बच्चा A B होने के लिए उसे I A और I B दोनों चाहिए — पर mother के पास कोई नहीं है। बच्चा O होने के लिए दोनों parents से small i चाहिए — पर father के पास small i है ही नहीं। A B father small i pass नहीं कर सकता, और O mother I A या I B pass नहीं कर सकती, तो जो दो groups लोग guess करते हैं वही दोनों बाहर हो जाते हैं।
ये मुश्किल वाला है, और मुश्किल एक ख़ास वजह से है: ये एक बिलकुल normal दिखने वाले dihybrid के अंदर एक deviation छुपा देता है।

Setup देखिए। Snapdragon में flower colour incomplete dominance दिखाता है — capital R capital R red, capital R small r pink, small r small r white। Height में normal complete dominance है, capital T tall over small t dwarf। Capital R small r capital T small t का अपने आप से cross।

दो parts। Part a: pink और tall offspring की probability क्या है? Part b: कितनी distinct phenotypic classes दिखेंगी? और अगर reflex में आपने नौ to तीन to तीन to एक सोच लिया, तो ये question आपको पकड़ चुका है।
Split देखिए — बाईं तरफ़ colour, दाईं तरफ़ height। एक सोलह-box grid की जगह दो छोटे monohybrids।
Method वही है जो हर dihybrid में: हर gene को independently solve कीजिए, फिर multiply। फ़र्क़ सिर्फ इतना है कि दोनों monohybrids में से एक normal dominance rule नहीं मानता।

तो पहले colour। Capital R small r cross with capital R small r देता है एक-चौथाई red, आधा pink, एक-चौथाई white। ये incomplete dominance वाला ratio है, एक to दो to एक, तीन to एक नहीं। तो pink की probability हुई आधा।
अब height, जो बिलकुल normal है। Capital T small t cross with capital T small t देता है तीन-चौथाई tall to एक-चौथाई dwarf। तो tall की probability हुई तीन-चौथाई।

Part a अब सिर्फ एक multiplication है। Pink and tall की probability बराबर आधा into तीन-चौथाई, यानी तीन बटा आठ। ध्यान दीजिए ये नौ बटा सोलह नहीं है — deviation ने एक factor बदला, और जवाब उसी के साथ हिल गया।

<excited>Part b गहरा हिस्सा है। Colour तीन visible classes देता है — red, pink, white — क्योंकि incomplete dominance heterozygote को अलग दिखा देता है; height दो देता है, tall और dwarf। तो कुल classes हुईं तीन into दो, यानी छह — normal dihybrid वाली चार नहीं। एक gene के एक deviation ने जाना-पहचाना जवाब बदल दिया, और यही तो ये question test कर रहा है।
ये चारों pitfalls कोई exotic चीज़ नहीं हैं। ये वो आम तरीक़े हैं जिनसे chapter समझने वाला student भी marks गँवाता है — तो इन्हें एक checklist की तरह पढ़िए, जो final answer लिखने से पहले चलानी है।

Pitfall one: genotypic और phenotypic ratios में गड़बड़। Monohybrid F two phenotype से तीन to एक है, पर genotype से एक to दो to एक। दोनों सही जवाब हैं — अलग-अलग सवालों के। Wording पढ़िए, phenotypic या genotypic शब्द को underline कीजिए, फिर लिखिए।

Pitfall two सबसे बड़ा है: incomplete dominance और codominance में confusion। दोनों एक to दो to एक phenotypic ratio देते हैं, तो students इन्हें एक ही चीज़ मान लेते हैं। और ध्यान दीजिए इसका मतलब क्या है — ratio आपको कभी नहीं बता सकता कि कौन सा है।
तो ratio की जगह picture देखिए, ख़ासकर हर case के बीच वाले individual को। वही heterozygote आपका इकलौता भरोसेमंद clue है।

फ़र्क़ पूरा वहीं है। Incomplete dominance में heterozygote एक blended intermediate है — pink, ऐसा shade जो किसी parent के पास था ही नहीं। Codominance में heterozygote दोनों parental traits पूरी तरह और अलग-अलग दिखाता है — group A B दोनों sugars carry करता है, साथ-साथ, कोई dilute नहीं।
तो एक line का test साथ रखिए। Intermediate बराबर incomplete। Both-at-once बराबर co। इसी order में बोलिए, और इसे heterozygote पर check कीजिए, numbers पर कभी नहीं।

Pitfall three: भूल जाना कि test cross को homozygous recessive partner चाहिए। अपने unknown का किसी recessive दिखने वाले plant से, या यूँ ही किसी parental type से cross, back cross है — और सिर्फ homozygous recessive वाला version ही unknown genotype साफ़ बताता है।

Pitfall four में असल में दो आदतें हैं। Blood group O को dominant मत मानिए — small i recessive है, और O double recessive है। और gamete variety निकालते वक़्त capital B capital B जैसे homozygous pairs मत गिनिए, क्योंकि homozygous pair बिलकुल शून्य variety देता है।
Subtopic को facts से नहीं, habits से बंद कीजिए। यही चीज़ें तय करती हैं कि आप paper ख़त्म कर पाएँगे या नहीं — सिर्फ ये नहीं कि biology समझ आई या नहीं।
सबसे पहला और सबसे बड़ा: किसी भी multi-gene cross में कभी बड़ा Punnett square मत बनाइए। सोलह boxes slow हैं। चौंसठ boxes तो extra steps वाली ग़लती है। Grid पढ़ाने का tool है, exam का नहीं।

बजाय इसके cross को अलग-अलग monohybrid crosses में तोड़िए, हर single-gene probability निकालिए, और multiply कीजिए। इस chapter का हर dihybrid और trihybrid question दो-तीन छोटे crosses में घुल जाता है, जो आप मन में कर सकते हैं।

इसके नीचे का rule सीधा है: किसी specific multi-trait offspring की probability बस single-gene probabilities का product है। तेज़, और exam pressure में arithmetic की ग़लतियाँ बहुत कम — और असल में marks वहीं रिसते हैं।
इसके साथ दो to the power n रखिए gamete types गिनने के लिए, और वो एक restriction याद रखिए जो इसे trap बनाता है: n सिर्फ heterozygous gene pairs गिनता है। Homozygous pairs कभी exponent में नहीं आते।
Test cross के लिए वो line रखिए जो method और reason दोनों बताती है। Unknown को double-recessive से cross कीजिए ताकि वो confess कर ले। Double recessive कुछ छुपाता नहीं, तो offspring सच बता देते हैं।
और deviation वाली line, जो लगभग हर deviation question में काम आएगी। Intermediate बराबर incomplete; both-at-once बराबर co। इसे heterozygote पर check कीजिए, ratio पर कभी नहीं।

एक आख़िरी diagnostic, अगले subtopic के लिए। जब भी phenotypic ratio genotypic ratio के बराबर हो, वो ordinary dominance नहीं है — वो incomplete dominance या codominance है। और जब dihybrid ratio ख़ुद नौ to तीन to तीन to एक होने से मना कर दे, तो वो linkage है — और हम आगे वहीं जा रहे हैं।

पिछले subtopic में Mendel ने हमें ऐसे factors दिए जो segregate और assort करते हैं। पर ध्यान दीजिए उन्होंने क्या नहीं बताया: वो factors असल में हैं कहाँ। वो ऐसी invisible units पर सोच रहे थे जिन पर उँगली नहीं रख सकते थे।
यही खाई ये subtopic भरता है। Mendel के factors को एक पता मिलता है — और वो पता है chromosome।

लगभग उन्नीस सौ तक microscopes इतने अच्छे हो गए थे कि biologists meiosis के दौरान chromosomes को सच में देख सकते थे। उन्होंने देखा कि वो pair बनाते हैं, line में लगते हैं, और अलग होते हैं — हर pair में से एक हर gamete में।
अब दोनों तस्वीरें साथ रखिए, diagram यही कर रहा है। ऊपर Mendel के factors अलग होते हुए। नीचे chromosomes अलग होते हुए। देखिए दोनों कहानियाँ कितनी मिलती-जुलती हैं।

Walter Sutton और Theodor Boveri ने ठीक यही देखा। Gamete formation में chromosomes का behaviour — pair बनाना, फिर अलग होना, हर pair में से एक हर gamete में — बिलकुल वैसे ही चलता है जैसे Mendel के factors segregate करते हैं।
तो उन्होंने दोनों ideas जोड़ कर Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance बनाई, उन्नीस सौ दो में: genes chromosomes पर carry होते हैं। Sutton और Boveri — ये नामों की जोड़ी पक्का recall question है।
और ये दावा जितना सुनने में लगता है उससे ज़्यादा मज़बूत है। ये कहता है कि meiosis में chromosomes की movement Mendel के laws जैसी नहीं है — वो उन laws की physical machinery ही है।

आख़िरी line ध्यान से पढ़िए, क्योंकि पूरी theory उसी एक वाक्य में है। Chromosomes का pair बनाना और फिर अलग होना, हर pair से एक हर gamete में — ये segregation की analogy नहीं है। ये segregation ही है, बस दिखती हुई।

board_events.text: An analogy that will carry the whole subtopic
Imagine a fleet of local trains (chromosomes), each carrying a fixed list of passengers (genes) in a fixed seating order.

board_events.text: Mendel had been studying the passengers' arrival patterns at stations, without ever realising they travelled on trains.
Sutton and Boveri pointed at the trains.
Suddenly, two passengers who always arrive together make sense — they were sharing a coach.
Genes on the same chromosome cannot assort independently. That shared coach is what we call linkage.
So Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment was never universal. It quietly required the two genes to be on different trains.
Linkage, discovered in a fruit fly
Independent assortment works beautifully — if the two genes ride different chromosomes.
Thomas Hunt Morgan, working on the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, found gene pairs that refused to assort independently.
They were inherited together far more often than chance allowed.

<text x="270" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">Genes that refuse to assort independently</text>
<text x="130" y="52" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#6b7280">Two genes, one chromosome</text>
<rect x="46" y="66" width="168" height="16" rx="8" fill="#e5e7eb" stroke="#9ca3af"/>
<circle cx="86" cy="74" r="7" fill="#7c3aed"/><text x="86" y="100" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#7c3aed">A</text>
<circle cx="122" cy="74" r="7" fill="#2563eb"/><text x="122" y="100" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#2563eb">B</text>
<text x="130" y="124" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">physically tied together</text>
<text x="390" y="52" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#6b7280">Test-cross offspring</text>
<rect x="290" y="66" width="34" height="90" fill="#7c3aed"/><text x="307" y="172" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2937">parental</text>
<rect x="336" y="70" width="34" height="86" fill="#7c3aed"/><text x="353" y="172" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2937">parental</text>
<rect x="404" y="138" width="34" height="18" fill="#dc2626"/><text x="421" y="172" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2937">recombinant</text>
<rect x="450" y="138" width="34" height="18" fill="#dc2626"/><text x="467" y="172" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2937">recombinant</text>
<line x1="284" y1="156" x2="492" y2="156" stroke="#1f2937"/>
<text x="390" y="196" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">Parentals dominate; recombinants stay rare</text>
<text x="270" y="228" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#dc2626">Independent assortment predicted four equal classes. It did not happen.</text>
<text x="270" y="254" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#16a34a">Morgan, working on Drosophila melanogaster, named this linkage</text>
<text x="270" y="280" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#6b7280">Inherited together far more often than chance allows</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: His explanation: those genes sit on the same chromosome, physically tied together. He called this linkage.
Body colour and eye colour, lying close together on the X chromosome: parental combinations dominated, recombinants were rare — tight linkage.
Eye colour and wing size, lying farther apart on the same chromosome: recombinants appeared far more often — loose linkage.
Same chromosome in both cases. The only thing that changed was the distance between the genes.
How linked genes still get separated
Linkage is not a life sentence. Occasionally, the combinations do get reshuffled.
Crossing over: the physical exchange of corresponding segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, during meiosis, at the pachytene stage.
