<rect x="70" y="204" width="140" height="10" rx="5" fill="#e5e7eb" stroke="#9ca3af"/>
<circle cx="100" cy="209" r="6" fill="#7c3aed"/><circle cx="120" cy="209" r="6" fill="#2563eb"/>
<text x="140" y="236" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">small target for a crossover</text>
<text x="140" y="256" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#16a34a">tight linkage, low recombination</text>
<text x="400" y="194" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">Genes far apart</text>

<circle cx="345" cy="209" r="6" fill="#7c3aed"/><circle cx="455" cy="209" r="6" fill="#2563eb"/>
<text x="400" y="236" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">wide target for a crossover</text>
<text x="400" y="256" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">loose linkage, high recombination</text>

board_events.text: Recombination: the production of non-parental (new) combinations of alleles. Crossing over is the mechanism behind it.
The closer two genes lie on a chromosome, the harder they are to separate: tight linkage, low recombination.
The farther apart they lie, the easier: loose linkage, high recombination.
Recombination frequency tracks distance faithfully. That single fact turns it into a ruler.
Morgan's student Alfred Sturtevant used exactly this to draw the first genetic map.
The terms this subtopic is built on
Linkage: the tendency of genes located on the same chromosome to be inherited together rather than assorting independently (Morgan, 1910).
Linked genes: genes on the same chromosome. They produce more parental-type than recombinant-type offspring.

board_events.caption: Complete linkage versus incomplete linkage
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 540 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">
<text x="270" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">Complete versus incomplete linkage</text>
<rect x="24" y="40" width="230" height="170" rx="8" fill="#f3f4f6" stroke="#86efac"/>
<text x="139" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">Complete linkage</text>
<rect x="60" y="80" width="158" height="12" rx="6" fill="#e5e7eb" stroke="#9ca3af"/>
<circle cx="90" cy="86" r="6" fill="#7c3aed"/><circle cx="106" cy="86" r="6" fill="#2563eb"/>
<text x="139" y="116" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">No crossover between them</text>
<rect x="70" y="132" width="60" height="44" fill="#7c3aed"/><rect x="148" y="132" width="60" height="44" fill="#7c3aed"/>
<text x="139" y="196" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">Zero recombinants</text>
<rect x="286" y="40" width="230" height="170" rx="8" fill="#f3f4f6" stroke="#fca5a5"/>
<text x="401" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">Incomplete linkage</text>
<rect x="322" y="80" width="158" height="12" rx="6" fill="#e5e7eb" stroke="#9ca3af"/>
<circle cx="352" cy="86" r="6" fill="#7c3aed"/><circle cx="430" cy="86" r="6" fill="#2563eb"/>
<text x="401" y="116" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Crossing over sometimes happens</text>
<rect x="322" y="132" width="46" height="44" fill="#7c3aed"/><rect x="374" y="132" width="46" height="44" fill="#7c3aed"/>
<rect x="426" y="164" width="20" height="12" fill="#dc2626"/><rect x="452" y="164" width="20" height="12" fill="#dc2626"/>
<text x="401" y="196" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">Some recombinants appear</text>
<text x="270" y="240" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#6b7280">Linked genes always give more parental-type than recombinant-type offspring</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Complete linkage: no recombinants are formed — the genes never separate.
Incomplete linkage: some recombinants are formed, because crossing over sometimes happens.
More parentals than recombinants is the signature of linkage. Four equal classes means no linkage at all.
Linkage group: all the genes on a single chromosome, inherited as a unit.
Two arrangements of the same linked genes
Coupling and repulsion are the two ways linked alleles can be arranged, depending on how they arrived from the parents.

board_events.caption: Coupling versus repulsion
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 540 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">
<text x="270" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">Coupling and repulsion: how the alleles arrived</text>
<rect x="24" y="40" width="230" height="150" rx="8" fill="#ecfdf5" stroke="#86efac"/>
<text x="139" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">Coupling</text>
<rect x="50" y="82" width="178" height="12" rx="6" fill="#e5e7eb" stroke="#9ca3af"/>
<circle cx="90" cy="88" r="7" fill="#16a34a"/><text x="90" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">A</text>
<circle cx="150" cy="88" r="7" fill="#16a34a"/><text x="150" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">B</text>
<rect x="50" y="126" width="178" height="12" rx="6" fill="#e5e7eb" stroke="#9ca3af"/>
<circle cx="90" cy="132" r="7" fill="#d1d5db" stroke="#9ca3af"/><text x="90" y="156" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">a</text>
<circle cx="150" cy="132" r="7" fill="#d1d5db" stroke="#9ca3af"/><text x="150" y="156" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">b</text>
<text x="139" y="180" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#16a34a">Both dominants from the same parent</text>
<rect x="286" y="40" width="230" height="150" rx="8" fill="#fef2f2" stroke="#fca5a5"/>
<text x="401" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">Repulsion</text>
<rect x="312" y="82" width="178" height="12" rx="6" fill="#e5e7eb" stroke="#9ca3af"/>
<circle cx="352" cy="88" r="7" fill="#16a34a"/><text x="352" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">A</text>
<circle cx="412" cy="88" r="7" fill="#d1d5db" stroke="#9ca3af"/><text x="412" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">b</text>
<rect x="312" y="126" width="178" height="12" rx="6" fill="#e5e7eb" stroke="#9ca3af"/>
<circle cx="352" cy="132" r="7" fill="#d1d5db" stroke="#9ca3af"/><text x="352" y="156" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">a</text>
<circle cx="412" cy="132" r="7" fill="#16a34a"/><text x="412" y="156" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">B</text>
<text x="401" y="180" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">A dominant arrives beside a recessive</text>
<text x="270" y="220" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">Whatever is on one chromosome tends to stay together in a gamete</text>
<text x="270" y="244" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#6b7280">Noticed by Bateson and Punnett, before Morgan named linkage</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Coupling: both dominant alleles arrive from the same parent, on the same chromosome, and tend to stay together in a gamete.
Repulsion: a dominant and a recessive arrive together, so the two dominants tend to remain apart.
The phenomenon was first noticed by Bateson and Punnett — before Morgan named linkage.
Same two genes, same linkage, same distance. Only the starting arrangement differs.
Which alleles travel together is set by the parents, not by the genes themselves.
Recombination frequency becomes a measuring tape
Recombination frequency (RF): the fraction of offspring that are recombinant, expressed as a percentage.
RF = (recombinant offspring / total offspring) × 100.

board_events.caption: RF, and the same number read as a distance
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 540 270" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">
<text x="270" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">Recombination frequency becomes a measuring tape</text>
<rect x="90" y="40" width="360" height="56" rx="8" fill="#f5f3ff" stroke="#7c3aed"/>
<text x="285" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">recombinant offspring</text>
<line x1="200" y1="70" x2="370" y2="70" stroke="#1f2937"/>
<text x="285" y="88" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">total offspring</text>
<text x="150" y="76" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#7c3aed">RF =</text>
<text x="410" y="76" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937">× 100</text>
<rect x="60" y="130" width="420" height="12" rx="6" fill="#e5e7eb" stroke="#9ca3af"/>
<circle cx="120" cy="136" r="8" fill="#7c3aed"/><text x="120" y="166" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#7c3aed">gene A</text>
<circle cx="280" cy="136" r="8" fill="#2563eb"/><text x="280" y="166" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#2563eb">gene B</text>
<circle cx="440" cy="136" r="8" fill="#16a34a"/><text x="440" y="166" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#16a34a">gene C</text>
<line x1="120" y1="110" x2="280" y2="110" stroke="#6b7280"/>
<line x1="120" y1="106" x2="120" y2="114" stroke="#6b7280"/><line x1="280" y1="106" x2="280" y2="114" stroke="#6b7280"/>
<text x="200" y="102" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">8 cM, so RF = 8%</text>
<line x1="280" y1="110" x2="440" y2="110" stroke="#6b7280"/>
<line x1="440" y1="106" x2="440" y2="114" stroke="#6b7280"/>
<text x="360" y="102" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">12 cM, so RF = 12%</text>
<text x="270" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">1 cM (centiMorgan) = 1% recombination frequency</text>
<text x="270" y="226" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">RF is directly proportional to distance, for small distances</text>
<text x="270" y="250" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#6b7280">Sturtevant used exactly this to draw the first genetic map</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Map unit, the centiMorgan (cM): the unit of genetic distance. 1 cM = 1% recombination frequency.
RF is directly proportional to the distance between two genes, for small distances.
Genetic or linkage map: a linear diagram of the relative positions and distances of genes along a chromosome, built from recombination frequencies.
The centiMorgan is a genetic distance, not a physical one. It measures how often, not how many nanometres.
Sturtevant built the first such map from exactly these numbers.
Procedure A: sort the offspring by frequency
Test-cross the heterozygote against the homozygous recessive. The offspring fall into two groups.
Parental types: the allele combinations the parent itself inherited. Recombinant types: new combinations made by crossing over.

board_events.caption: Two tall classes, two short ones
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 540 280" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">
<text x="270" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">Reading a linkage cross: sort by frequency</text>
<text x="270" y="46" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#6b7280">Heterozygote test-crossed against the homozygous recessive</text>
<rect x="70" y="64" width="60" height="120" fill="#7c3aed"/><text x="100" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#7c3aed">AB</text>
<rect x="160" y="70" width="60" height="114" fill="#7c3aed"/><text x="190" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#7c3aed">ab</text>
<rect x="290" y="158" width="60" height="26" fill="#dc2626"/><text x="320" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">Ab</text>
<rect x="380" y="160" width="60" height="24" fill="#dc2626"/><text x="410" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">aB</text>
<line x1="50" y1="184" x2="480" y2="184" stroke="#1f2937"/>
<text x="145" y="224" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">Step 1: two most frequent</text>
<text x="145" y="242" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#7c3aed">= parental types</text>
<text x="365" y="224" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">Step 2: two least frequent</text>
<text x="365" y="242" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">= recombinant types</text>
<text x="270" y="270" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#16a34a">Step 3: recombinants far fewer than parentals, so the genes are linked</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Step 1: identify the parental classes — they are the two most frequent phenotypes.
Step 2: identify the recombinant classes — the two least frequent.
Step 3: if recombinants are far fewer than parentals, the genes are linked. The rarer the recombinants, the tighter the linkage.
Crossing over between two close-together genes is a rare event, so few recombinant gametes form.
Procedure B: compute it, then read it as a distance
RF = (number of recombinant offspring / total offspring) × 100.
The result, read in percent, IS the map distance in centiMorgans. An RF of 8% means the two genes sit 8 cM apart.
Why this works: the chance that a crossover falls between two genes increases steadily with the physical gap between them.

board_events.caption: The ceiling, and why long distances read short
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 540 270" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">
<text x="270" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">The tape has a ceiling at fifty percent</text>
<rect x="60" y="46" width="330" height="24" rx="12" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#16a34a"/>
<rect x="390" y="46" width="90" height="24" rx="12" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#dc2626"/>
<line x1="390" y1="40" x2="390" y2="76" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="62" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">0%</text>
<text x="225" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">tight linkage to loose linkage</text>
<text x="390" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">50%</text>
<text x="452" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">impossible</text>
<text x="270" y="124" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">At or beyond 50%, genes assort as if on different chromosomes</text>
<text x="270" y="148" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">A 60% recombination option is always wrong</text>
<rect x="60" y="166" width="420" height="80" rx="8" fill="#fff7ed" stroke="#f59e0b"/>
<text x="270" y="188" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#b45309">Why long distances read short</text>
<rect x="110" y="202" width="320" height="10" rx="5" fill="#e5e7eb" stroke="#9ca3af"/>
<circle cx="130" cy="207" r="6" fill="#7c3aed"/><circle cx="410" cy="207" r="6" fill="#2563eb"/>
<path d="M200,207 L200,196" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M340,207 L340,196" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="270" y="236" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Two crossovers restore the parental arrangement and go uncounted</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Limiting condition: this tape is accurate only over short distances.
For genes far apart, double crossovers restore the parental arrangement and go uncounted, so the measured RF underestimates the true distance.
The ceiling is 50%. At or beyond that, the genes assort as if they were on different chromosomes entirely.
So a 60% recombination option is always wrong.
Procedure C: order three genes in five seconds
Given the three pairwise map distances between genes A, B and C, find their linear order.
Step 1: find the largest of the three distances. The two genes in that pair are the outermost genes.

board_events.caption: Largest distance names the ends; the missing gene is central
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 540 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">
<text x="270" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">Three-point ordering: the biggest distance names the ends</text>
<text x="270" y="50" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#6b7280">On a straight line, the two end points are always the farthest apart</text>
<text x="60" y="80" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">Step 1. Find the largest of the three pairwise distances.</text>
<text x="76" y="100" font-size="12" fill="#dc2626">Those two genes are the outermost.</text>
<text x="60" y="126" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">Step 2. The gene missing from that pair sits in the middle.</text>
<text x="60" y="152" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">Step 3. Sanity check: the two short segments must add to the long one.</text>
<line x1="90" y1="196" x2="450" y2="196" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2"/>
<circle cx="90" cy="196" r="9" fill="#2563eb"/><text x="90" y="226" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">end</text>
<circle cx="240" cy="196" r="9" fill="#7c3aed"/><text x="240" y="226" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#7c3aed">middle</text>
<circle cx="450" cy="196" r="9" fill="#16a34a"/><text x="450" y="226" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">end</text>
<line x1="90" y1="178" x2="450" y2="178" stroke="#dc2626"/>
<line x1="90" y1="174" x2="90" y2="182" stroke="#dc2626"/><line x1="450" y1="174" x2="450" y2="182" stroke="#dc2626"/>
<text x="270" y="170" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">largest distance</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Step 2: the third gene — the one missing from the largest pair — sits in the middle.
Step 3: sanity check. The two middle-gene distances should add up to the outer distance.
On a straight line, the two end points are always the farthest apart, and the two short segments must sum to the long one.
Do not Punnett anything. This is a five-second check, not a cross.

segments.text: <curious>Hold on to one analogy for the rest of this subtopic, because everything that follows — linkage, crossing over, mapping — is just this picture, extended.
Imagine a fleet of Mumbai local trains. Each train is a chromosome. Each train carries a fixed list of passengers, in a fixed seating order — and those passengers are the genes.
There is the picture. The train, the coaches, the passengers in their fixed seats. Nothing about a passenger's identity changes; what matters is which train they are on.

Now here is what Mendel was doing. He had been studying the passengers' arrival patterns at stations — who shows up with whom, in what proportions — without ever realising they travelled on trains at all.
Sutton and Boveri pointed at the trains. That is the entire contribution, and it is enormous: they gave a physical vehicle to a statistical pattern.

And the moment you can see the trains, something Mendel could not explain suddenly makes sense. Two passengers who always arrive together are not obeying some mysterious rule. They were sharing a coach.

That is the second big idea of this subtopic, arriving early. Genes sitting on the same chromosome cannot assort independently — they are physically tied to the same vehicle. That shared coach is what we call linkage.

Which forces an uncomfortable rereading of the last subtopic. Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment was never universal. It quietly required the two genes to be riding different trains — and nature does not always oblige.
Linkage was not proposed from a blackboard. It was forced on genetics by data that would not behave — so let us follow the man who collected it.

Mendel's independent assortment works beautifully — on one condition. The two genes have to ride different chromosomes. Nobody had tested what happens when they do not, until a man started breeding flies.
Thomas Hunt Morgan worked on the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster — small, fast-breeding, and easy to score in thousands. And he found gene pairs that flatly refused to assort independently.
They were inherited together far more often than chance allowed. Independent assortment predicts four classes in equal numbers. Morgan kept getting two big classes and two tiny ones.
Look at the bars. Two tall columns, the parental combinations, and two stubs, the recombinants. That shape is the fingerprint of linkage, and you should learn to recognise it instantly.

Morgan's explanation was physical, not statistical. Those genes sit on the same chromosome, tied together, so they travel as a package. He called this linkage — genes inherited together rather than assorting freely.

And then he did the experiment that proved distance was the variable. He followed two genes lying close together on the X chromosome — body colour and eye colour. Parental combinations dominated, recombinants were rare. Tight linkage.
Then he followed two genes lying farther apart on the same chromosome — eye colour and wing size. Now recombinants appeared far more often. Loose linkage.

<excited>Sit with that for a second. Same chromosome in both cases. Same organism, same method. The only thing that changed was the distance between the genes — and the recombinant percentage tracked that distance faithfully.
Linkage ties genes together. This section is about the one process that unties them — and, in doing so, hands genetics a ruler.

If linked genes were welded together forever, this subtopic would end here. But Morgan's rare classes prove they are not. Linkage is not a life sentence — occasionally, the combinations do get reshuffled.

The mechanism is crossing over: the physical exchange of corresponding segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, during meiosis, at the pachytene stage. Learn that sentence with its details — non-sister chromatids, homologous chromosomes, pachytene. Examiners pick exactly those words.
Watch the top of the picture. Two homologues come together, chromatids overlap and swap matching segments, and four chromatids walk away: two still parental, two now carrying new combinations.

Those new combinations have a name. Recombination is the production of non-parental — that is, new — combinations of alleles. Crossing over is the physical mechanism; recombination is the result you count.

Now the bottom half, which is the part that makes this whole subtopic work. When two genes lie close together, the stretch between them is a small target, so a crossover rarely falls there. Hard to separate: tight linkage, low recombination.
When they lie far apart, the stretch between them is a wide target, so a crossover lands there often. Easy to separate: loose linkage, high recombination.

So recombination frequency does not merely correlate with distance in a vague way. It tracks distance faithfully — and that single fact quietly turns a breeding experiment into a measuring instrument.

<excited>Morgan's student, Alfred Sturtevant, saw it first. If recombination frequency rises with distance, then measuring how often two genes recombine tells you how far apart they are. He used exactly that to draw the first genetic map — chromosomes mapped without ever seeing a gene.
Now fix the vocabulary, because the numerical questions in this subtopic are really vocabulary questions with arithmetic attached.

Linkage is the tendency of genes located on the same chromosome to be inherited together, rather than assorting independently. Morgan, nineteen ten. Note the word tendency — it is a tendency, not a guarantee, and crossing over is why.

Linked genes are simply genes on the same chromosome. And they have one reliable behavioural signature: they produce more parental-type than recombinant-type offspring. Always more. That is what being linked does.
The two panels show the two flavours. Left, the genes never come apart. Right, they sometimes do.
Complete linkage means no recombinants are formed at all — the genes never separate. Zero recombinant classes in the offspring.
Incomplete linkage means some recombinants are formed, because crossing over sometimes happens between them. This is the common, realistic case, and it is the one every numerical is built on.

And here is the diagnostic to carry into any data table. More parentals than recombinants is the signature of linkage. Four classes in roughly equal numbers means no linkage at all — the genes assorted independently.

One more term, which becomes a formula in a few minutes. A linkage group is all the genes on a single chromosome, inherited as a unit. One chromosome, one linkage group — remember that phrasing exactly.
This pair of terms is small, but it is a favourite one-line recall item, and it also sharpens what linkage actually claims.
Coupling and repulsion are the two ways linked alleles can be arranged on the pair of chromosomes — and which arrangement you get depends entirely on how the alleles arrived from the parents.
Look at the two panels. Same two genes in both, same chromosome, same distance apart. The only difference is which alleles happen to be sitting on which chromosome.

Coupling: both dominant alleles arrived from the same parent, so they sit together on one chromosome, and they tend to stay together in a gamete. The recessives likewise ride together on the other one.

Repulsion: a dominant and a recessive arrived together on the same chromosome. So now the two dominants sit on opposite chromosomes and tend to remain apart — they repel, in the sense of not travelling together.
For the recall question: the phenomenon was first noticed by Bateson and Punnett, before Morgan gave linkage its name. Bateson and Punnett saw the effect; Morgan explained it and named it.

And here is the conceptual point hiding behind the vocabulary. Same two genes, same linkage, same distance. Only the starting arrangement differs — so linkage is about which chromosome an allele is on, not about which alleles like each other.
Which is why the arrangement is set by the parents, not by the genes themselves. The genes do not choose their companions; they simply keep whatever company they arrived with.
This section contains the only quantity you will ever measure in this subtopic, and the only unit. Get both exact.
Recombination frequency, written R F, is the fraction of offspring that are recombinant, expressed as a percentage. Not a count — a fraction, turned into a percent.

The formula is one line: R F equals recombinant offspring divided by total offspring, times one hundred. Note the denominator: total offspring, not the parental ones. Students drop that and lose the mark.
Now look at the tape. The same two genes carry two readings: a percentage on one side and a distance on the other. That is the trick of this whole subtopic — one number, two names.
The map unit is the centiMorgan, written c M, and its definition is a straight conversion: one centiMorgan equals one percent recombination frequency. Named for Morgan, naturally.

And the reason that conversion is allowed: R F is directly proportional to the distance between two genes — for small distances. Keep that qualifier attached; it is a limiting condition we will come back to.

Once you can convert frequencies into distances, you can draw a genetic map, also called a linkage map: a linear diagram of the relative positions and distances of genes along a chromosome, built entirely from recombination frequencies.

One point that catches students. The centiMorgan is a genetic distance, not a physical one. It does not tell you how many nanometres apart the genes are — it tells you how often they get separated. How often, not how far in space.
And that is exactly what Sturtevant did. First genetic map, built from nothing but these numbers, at a time when nobody knew what a gene was made of.
Here is the reading procedure. Given a table of offspring numbers, you should be able to say — in seconds — which classes are which, and whether the genes are linked.

The setup is always the same: the heterozygote is test-crossed against the homozygous recessive. That partner contributes only recessive alleles, so the offspring phenotypes are a direct read-out of the heterozygote's gametes. And those offspring fall into two groups.

Parental types are the allele combinations the parent itself inherited — the gametes made without any crossover. Recombinant types are the new combinations, made by crossing over. Everything in this procedure is about telling those two apart.
And the picture makes it trivial. Two tall bars, two short ones. You are not deriving anything — you are sorting by height.
Step one: identify the parental classes. They are the two most frequent phenotypes. Always the two biggest — because gametes without a crossover are the default outcome.
Step two: identify the recombinant classes. They are the two least frequent. The two stubs.

Step three, the conclusion: if recombinants are far fewer than parentals, the genes are linked. And the finer reading — the rarer the recombinants, the tighter the linkage, because rarity means the crossover almost never lands between them.

The reason sits underneath all three steps. Crossing over between two close-together genes is a rare event, so few recombinant gametes form. Rarity of recombinants is not an accident of the data; it is the physical fact being measured.
Procedure B is the numerical engine of this subtopic, and it is genuinely two steps: compute a percentage, then rename it.
The formula again: R F equals the number of recombinant offspring, divided by total offspring, times one hundred. Recombinants on top; everybody on the bottom.

And then the step students overthink. The result, read in percent, is the map distance in centiMorgans. An R F of eight percent means the two genes sit eight centiMorgans apart. Same number, new unit. There is no second calculation.

The justification is worth one line in a board answer: the chance that a crossover falls between two genes increases steadily with the physical gap between them, so recombination frequency acts as a measuring tape.
Now look at the gauge, because every measuring tape has a range, and this one has a hard end.

The limiting condition first: this tape is accurate only over short distances. That is not a technicality — it is the reason genetic maps are built from many small intervals rather than one long measurement.

Here is the mechanism. For genes far apart, two crossovers can occur between them. The second one undoes the first, restoring the parental arrangement, so that gamete gets counted as parental. Those double crossovers go uncounted, and the measured R F underestimates the true distance.
And the ceiling: fifty percent. At or beyond fifty percent, the genes assort as if they were on different chromosomes entirely — the data cannot tell linked-but-distant apart from unlinked.
Which gives you a free mark whenever you see it. A sixty percent recombination option is always wrong. Recombination frequency cannot exceed fifty percent, ever.
This procedure looks intimidating in a question and is trivial in practice. You are given three pairwise map distances between three genes, and asked for their linear order along the chromosome.
Step one: find the largest of the three distances. The two genes in that pair are the outermost genes — the two ends.
Look at the line. Two ends and a middle. Once you know which two genes are the ends, there is literally one place left for the third.
Step two says exactly that. The third gene — the one missing from the largest pair — sits in the middle. No working required; it is the only position available.
Step three is your sanity check, and in a board answer it earns a mark. The two middle-gene distances should add up to the outer distance. If they do, tick it and move on.

The reason is pure geometry, which is why it is safe. On a straight line, the two end points are always the farthest apart, and the two short segments must sum to the long one. Genes on a chromosome sit on a line, so the logic transfers exactly.
So do not Punnett anything. Students see three genes and start drawing crosses. There is no cross here — this is a five-second check on three numbers.

One caution to carry: the additivity in step three holds cleanly only for short distances, because double crossovers make large R F values underestimate the true distance. On a real map with big gaps, the sum comes out slightly off — and that is expected, not an error.
<curious>पूरे subtopic के लिए एक analogy पकड़ कर रखिए, क्योंकि आगे जो कुछ आता है — linkage, crossing over, mapping — वो सब इसी तस्वीर का विस्तार है।
सोचिए Mumbai की local trains का एक बेड़ा। हर train एक chromosome है। हर train में passengers की एक तय list है, तय seating order में — और वही passengers genes हैं।
तस्वीर सामने है। Train, coaches, और अपनी तय seats पर बैठे passengers। किसी passenger की पहचान नहीं बदलती; मायने ये रखता है कि वो किस train पर है।
अब देखिए Mendel क्या कर रहे थे। वो stations पर passengers के arrival patterns पढ़ रहे थे — कौन किसके साथ आता है, किस proportion में — बिना ये जाने कि वो trains से चलते हैं।
Sutton और Boveri ने trains की तरफ़ इशारा किया। बस यही उनका योगदान है, और ये बहुत बड़ा है: उन्होंने एक statistical pattern को physical vehicle दे दिया।
और जैसे ही trains दिखने लगती हैं, वो चीज़ समझ आ जाती है जो Mendel explain नहीं कर पाए। जो दो passengers हमेशा साथ आते हैं, वो किसी रहस्यमय rule को नहीं मान रहे। वो एक ही coach में सफ़र कर रहे थे।
यही इस subtopic का दूसरा बड़ा idea है, जो जल्दी आ गया। एक ही chromosome पर बैठे genes independently assort कर ही नहीं सकते — वो एक ही vehicle से बँधे हैं। वही shared coach linkage कहलाता है।

और इससे पिछले subtopic को दोबारा पढ़ना पड़ता है। Mendel का Law of Independent Assortment कभी universal था ही नहीं। वो चुपचाप ये माँग रहा था कि दोनों genes अलग trains पर हों — और nature हमेशा ये नहीं मानती।
Linkage किसी blackboard पर नहीं गढ़ा गया। इसे genetics पर उस data ने थोपा जो मानने से इनकार कर रहा था — तो चलिए उस आदमी के पीछे चलते हैं जिसने वो data इकट्ठा किया।

Mendel का independent assortment बहुत अच्छे से काम करता है — एक शर्त पर। दोनों genes अलग chromosomes पर होने चाहिए। जब ऐसा न हो तो क्या होता है, ये किसी ने test नहीं किया था — जब तक एक आदमी ने मक्खियाँ पालनी शुरू नहीं कीं।

Thomas Hunt Morgan ने fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster पर काम किया — छोटी, तेज़ी से बढ़ने वाली, और हज़ारों में गिनने में आसान। और उन्हें ऐसे gene pairs मिले जो independently assort करने से साफ़ मना कर रहे थे।
वो chance से कहीं ज़्यादा बार साथ inherit हो रहे थे। Independent assortment चार बराबर classes predict करता है। Morgan को बार-बार दो बड़ी classes और दो बहुत छोटी मिल रही थीं।
Bars देखिए। दो ऊँचे columns, यानी parental combinations, और दो ठूँठ, यानी recombinants। यही shape linkage की पहचान है, और इसे तुरंत पहचानना सीख लीजिए।

Morgan की explanation physical थी, statistical नहीं। वो genes एक ही chromosome पर बैठे हैं, आपस में बँधे हुए, इसलिए एक package की तरह चलते हैं। उन्होंने इसे linkage कहा — genes जो साथ inherit होते हैं, आज़ादी से assort नहीं करते।

और फिर उन्होंने वो experiment किया जिसने साबित किया कि असली variable distance है। उन्होंने X chromosome पर पास-पास बैठे दो genes देखे — body colour और eye colour। Parental combinations हावी रहे, recombinants कम। Tight linkage।
फिर उन्होंने उसी chromosome पर दूर बैठे दो genes देखे — eye colour और wing size। अब recombinants कहीं ज़्यादा दिखे। Loose linkage।
<excited>एक पल रुक कर सोचिए। दोनों बार chromosome वही। Organism वही, method वही। बदला सिर्फ genes के बीच का distance — और recombinant percentage ने उस distance का ईमानदारी से पीछा किया।
Linkage genes को बाँध देता है। ये section उस एक process के बारे में है जो उन्हें खोलती है — और ऐसा करते हुए genetics के हाथ में एक ruler थमा देती है।

अगर linked genes हमेशा के लिए वेल्ड हो जाते, तो ये subtopic यहीं ख़त्म हो जाता। पर Morgan की rare classes साबित करती हैं कि ऐसा नहीं है। Linkage उम्र क़ैद नहीं है — कभी-कभी combinations दोबारा shuffle हो ही जाते हैं।

Mechanism है crossing over: meiosis के दौरान, pachytene stage पर, homologous chromosomes के non-sister chromatids के बीच corresponding segments का physical exchange। ये वाक्य इसकी सारी details के साथ याद कीजिए — non-sister chromatids, homologous chromosomes, pachytene। Examiners ठीक यही शब्द उठाते हैं।
तस्वीर का ऊपरी हिस्सा देखिए। दो homologues पास आते हैं, chromatids overlap कर के matching segments आपस में बदलते हैं, और चार chromatids निकलते हैं: दो अब भी parental, दो नए combinations वाले।
इन नए combinations का नाम है। Recombination मतलब non-parental — यानी नए — allele combinations का बनना। Crossing over physical mechanism है; recombination वो नतीजा है जो आप गिनते हैं।
अब नीचे का हिस्सा, जो पूरे subtopic को चलाता है। जब दो genes पास-पास हों, तो उनके बीच का हिस्सा छोटा target है, इसलिए crossover वहाँ कम गिरता है। अलग करना मुश्किल: tight linkage, low recombination।
जब वो दूर हों, तो बीच का हिस्सा चौड़ा target है, इसलिए crossover वहाँ अक्सर गिरता है। अलग करना आसान: loose linkage, high recombination।
तो recombination frequency distance से किसी धुँधले तरीक़े से जुड़ी नहीं है। वो distance का ईमानदारी से पीछा करती है — और यही एक बात चुपचाप एक breeding experiment को measuring instrument बना देती है।

<excited>Morgan के student, Alfred Sturtevant, ने ये पहले देखा। अगर recombination frequency distance के साथ बढ़ती है, तो ये नापना कि दो genes कितनी बार recombine करते हैं, बता देगा कि वो कितनी दूर हैं। उन्होंने इसी से पहला genetic map बनाया — बिना कोई gene देखे chromosomes का नक़्शा।
अब vocabulary पक्की कर लीजिए, क्योंकि इस subtopic के numerical questions असल में vocabulary के सवाल हैं, जिनके साथ थोड़ी arithmetic जुड़ी है।

Linkage मतलब एक ही chromosome पर स्थित genes का साथ inherit होने का रुझान, बजाय independently assort करने के। Morgan, उन्नीस सौ दस। शब्द देखिए — tendency, यानी रुझान, guarantee नहीं — और इसकी वजह crossing over है।

Linked genes बस वो genes हैं जो एक ही chromosome पर हैं। और उनका एक भरोसेमंद behavioural signature है: वो recombinant-type से ज़्यादा parental-type offspring बनाते हैं। हमेशा ज़्यादा। Linked होने का यही मतलब है।
दोनों panels दो रूप दिखाते हैं। बाएँ, genes कभी अलग नहीं होते। दाएँ, कभी-कभी होते हैं।
Complete linkage मतलब recombinants बनते ही नहीं — genes कभी अलग नहीं होते। Offspring में शून्य recombinant classes।
Incomplete linkage मतलब कुछ recombinants बनते हैं, क्योंकि उनके बीच कभी-कभी crossing over हो जाता है। यही आम और realistic case है, और हर numerical इसी पर बना होता है।
और ये रहा वो diagnostic जो किसी भी data table में काम आएगा। Recombinants से ज़्यादा parentals = linkage का signature। चारों classes लगभग बराबर = linkage है ही नहीं, genes independently assort कर गए।

एक और term, जो कुछ ही देर में formula बन जाएगी। Linkage group मतलब एक ही chromosome के सारे genes, जो एक unit की तरह inherit होते हैं। एक chromosome, एक linkage group — ये phrasing ठीक ऐसे ही याद रखिए।
ये terms की जोड़ी छोटी है, पर एक-line recall के लिए favourite है, और ये साफ़ भी करती है कि linkage असल में दावा क्या करता है।
Coupling और repulsion linked alleles के chromosomes की जोड़ी पर बैठने के दो तरीक़े हैं — और कौन सा arrangement मिलेगा, ये पूरी तरह इस पर है कि alleles parents से कैसे आए।
दोनों panels देखिए। दोनों में वही दो genes, वही chromosome, वही distance। फ़र्क़ सिर्फ़ इतना कि कौन सा allele किस chromosome पर बैठा है।
Coupling: दोनों dominant alleles एक ही parent से आए, तो वो एक chromosome पर साथ बैठे हैं, और gamete में साथ ही रहते हैं। Recessives भी वैसे ही दूसरे chromosome पर साथ चलते हैं।
Repulsion: एक dominant और एक recessive एक ही chromosome पर साथ आए। तो अब दोनों dominants उल्टे chromosomes पर बैठे हैं और अलग-अलग रहते हैं — यानी साथ सफ़र नहीं करते।
Recall question के लिए: ये phenomenon सबसे पहले Bateson और Punnett ने देखा था, Morgan के linkage नाम देने से पहले। Bateson और Punnett ने असर देखा; Morgan ने उसे समझाया और नाम दिया।

और vocabulary के पीछे छुपा conceptual point ये है। वही दो genes, वही linkage, वही distance। फ़र्क़ सिर्फ़ starting arrangement का — यानी linkage इस बारे में है कि allele किस chromosome पर है, इस बारे में नहीं कि कौन से alleles एक-दूसरे को पसंद करते हैं।
इसीलिए arrangement parents तय करते हैं, genes ख़ुद नहीं। Genes अपने साथी नहीं चुनते; वो बस उसी संगत में रहते हैं जिसके साथ आए थे।
इस section में इस पूरे subtopic की इकलौती measurable quantity है, और इकलौती unit। दोनों बिलकुल सही याद कीजिए।
Recombination frequency, यानी R F, offspring का वो fraction है जो recombinant हैं, percentage में लिखा हुआ। गिनती नहीं — fraction, जिसे percent बना दिया गया।
Formula एक line का है: R F बराबर recombinant offspring बटा total offspring, into सौ। Denominator पर ध्यान दीजिए: total offspring, parental नहीं। Students यहीं चूकते हैं और mark जाता है।
अब tape देखिए। वही दो genes दो readings देते हैं: एक तरफ़ percentage, दूसरी तरफ़ distance। पूरे subtopic का यही खेल है — एक number, दो नाम।
Map unit है centiMorgan, यानी c M, और इसकी definition सीधा conversion है: एक centiMorgan बराबर एक percent recombination frequency। नाम, ज़ाहिर है, Morgan पर।
और ये conversion allowed क्यों है: R F दो genes के बीच के distance के directly proportional है — छोटे distances के लिए। ये शर्त साथ चिपका कर रखिए; ये एक limiting condition है जिस पर हम लौटेंगे।

जब आप frequencies को distances में बदल सकते हैं, तो genetic map बना सकते हैं, जिसे linkage map भी कहते हैं: chromosome पर genes की relative positions और distances का linear diagram, जो पूरी तरह recombination frequencies से बनता है।

एक बात जिसमें students फँसते हैं। centiMorgan एक genetic distance है, physical नहीं। ये नहीं बताता कि genes कितने nanometre दूर हैं — ये बताता है कि वो कितनी बार अलग होते हैं। कितनी बार, न कि जगह में कितनी दूर।
और Sturtevant ने ठीक यही किया। पहला genetic map, सिर्फ़ इन्हीं numbers से बना, उस वक़्त जब किसी को पता ही नहीं था कि gene बना किस चीज़ का है।
ये रहा reading procedure। Offspring के numbers की table मिले, तो आपको सेकंडों में बता देना चाहिए कि कौन सी class क्या है, और genes linked हैं या नहीं।

Setup हमेशा वही: heterozygote का homozygous recessive से test cross। वो partner सिर्फ़ recessive alleles देता है, इसलिए offspring के phenotypes सीधे heterozygote के gametes का read-out हैं। और वो offspring दो groups में बँटते हैं।

Parental types वो allele combinations हैं जो parent ने ख़ुद inherit किए — यानी बिना crossover वाले gametes। Recombinant types नए combinations हैं, जो crossing over से बने। इस पूरे procedure का काम बस इन दोनों को अलग पहचानना है।
और तस्वीर इसे आसान बना देती है। दो ऊँची bars, दो छोटी। आप कुछ derive नहीं कर रहे — आप ऊँचाई से sort कर रहे हैं।
Step one: parental classes पहचानिए। वो दो सबसे ज़्यादा frequent phenotypes हैं। हमेशा सबसे बड़े दो — क्योंकि बिना crossover वाले gametes ही default नतीजा हैं।
Step two: recombinant classes पहचानिए। वो दो सबसे कम frequent हैं। यानी दोनों ठूँठ।

Step three, नतीजा: अगर recombinants parentals से बहुत कम हैं, तो genes linked हैं। और बारीक़ पढ़ाई — recombinants जितने कम, linkage उतनी tight, क्योंकि कम होने का मतलब है crossover उनके बीच लगभग कभी नहीं गिरता।

तीनों steps के नीचे वजह यही है। पास-पास बैठे दो genes के बीच crossing over एक rare event है, इसलिए recombinant gametes कम बनते हैं। Recombinants का कम होना data का इत्तेफ़ाक़ नहीं है; वही तो असल physical fact है जो नापा जा रहा है।
Procedure B इस subtopic का numerical engine है, और ये सच में दो steps है: percentage निकालिए, फिर उसका नाम बदल दीजिए।
Formula दोबारा: R F बराबर recombinant offspring की संख्या, बटा total offspring, into सौ। ऊपर recombinants; नीचे सब।

और फिर वो step जिस पर students ज़्यादा सोचते हैं। नतीजा, percent में पढ़ा जाए, तो वही map distance है centiMorgans में। R F आठ percent मतलब दोनों genes आठ centiMorgan दूर। वही number, नई unit। दूसरी कोई calculation है ही नहीं।

Board answer में justification की एक line ज़रूरी है: दो genes के बीच crossover गिरने की संभावना उनके बीच के physical gap के साथ लगातार बढ़ती है, इसलिए recombination frequency measuring tape की तरह काम करती है।
अब gauge देखिए, क्योंकि हर measuring tape की एक range होती है, और इसका एक सख़्त सिरा है।
पहले limiting condition: ये tape सिर्फ़ छोटे distances पर सही है। ये कोई technicality नहीं — यही वजह है कि genetic maps एक लंबे measurement से नहीं, कई छोटे intervals से बनाए जाते हैं।

Mechanism ये है। दूर बैठे genes के बीच दो crossovers हो सकते हैं। दूसरा पहले को उलट देता है, parental arrangement लौटा देता है, तो वो gamete parental गिना जाता है। ऐसे double crossovers गिने ही नहीं जाते, और मापी गई R F असली distance को कम आँक देती है।
और ceiling: पचास percent। पचास percent पर या उससे आगे, genes ऐसे assort करते हैं जैसे वो अलग chromosomes पर हों — data linked-पर-दूर और unlinked में फ़र्क़ बता ही नहीं सकता।
और इससे एक मुफ़्त mark मिल जाता है। साठ percent recombination वाला option हमेशा ग़लत है। Recombination frequency पचास percent से ज़्यादा हो ही नहीं सकती।
ये procedure question में डरावना लगता है और practice में बहुत आसान है। आपको तीन genes के बीच तीन pairwise map distances दिए जाते हैं, और chromosome पर उनका linear order पूछा जाता है।
Step one: तीनों में से सबसे बड़ा distance ढूँढिए। उस pair के दोनों genes ही सबसे बाहरी genes हैं — यानी दोनों सिरे।
Line देखिए। दो सिरे और एक बीच। जैसे ही पता चला कि कौन से दो genes सिरे हैं, तीसरे के लिए सचमुच एक ही जगह बचती है।
Step two यही कहता है। तीसरा gene — जो सबसे बड़े pair में नहीं है — बीच में बैठता है। कोई working नहीं चाहिए; बस वही एक जगह ख़ाली है।
Step three आपका sanity check है, और board answer में इसका mark मिलता है। बीच वाले gene के दोनों distances जुड़कर बाहरी distance के बराबर होने चाहिए। हो जाएँ, तो tick कीजिए और आगे बढ़िए।

वजह शुद्ध geometry है, इसीलिए ये भरोसेमंद है। सीधी line पर दोनों सिरे हमेशा सबसे दूर होते हैं, और दोनों छोटे segments जुड़कर बड़ा segment बनाते हैं। Chromosome पर genes एक line पर बैठे हैं, तो logic हूबहू लागू होती है।
तो कुछ भी Punnett मत कीजिए। Students तीन genes देखकर crosses बनाने लगते हैं। यहाँ cross है ही नहीं — ये तीन numbers पर पाँच सेकंड का check है।

एक सावधानी साथ रखिए: step three वाली additivity साफ़-साफ़ सिर्फ़ छोटे distances पर चलती है, क्योंकि double crossovers बड़ी R F values को कम आँकवा देते हैं। बड़े gaps वाले असली map पर sum थोड़ा हट जाता है — और ये अपेक्षित है, ग़लती नहीं।

sections.title: The X-body: where sex determination begins... & Example three: recombination frequency and...

board_events.text: Henking's mysterious structure, 1891
Third big idea of this subtopic: sex determination — how an organism ends up male or female.
Henking, in 1891, spotted a mysterious structure in insect sperm.

board_events.text: It went into only half the sperm.
He could not say what it was, so he simply called it the X-body.
That was the first hint that a specific chromosome decides sex.
It was the X chromosome — and different animal groups solved the sex problem in four different ways.
The four sex-determination systems

board_events.text: XX to XO: females are XX; males are XO — they simply lack the second sex chromosome. Grasshopper, cockroach.
XX to XY: females are XX; males are XY. Human, Drosophila.
In both of those systems, the male is the heterogametic sex.
ZZ to ZW: birds and butterflies flip it. Males are ZZ, females are ZW — so the FEMALE is heterogametic.
Haplodiploidy: honeybees use no sex chromosomes at all. Females are diploid (2n), from fertilised eggs; males are haploid (n), from unfertilised eggs.
XO is not XY. In XX to XO there is no Y chromosome at all — the male has a single, unpaired X.
Temperature-dependent determination, as in the crocodile, is a further variation worth knowing by name.
Procedure D: find the heterogametic parent
Homogametic sex: produces only one type of gamete with respect to sex chromosomes. The human female, XX, gives all X.
Heterogametic sex: produces two types. The human male, XY, gives half X and half Y.

board_events.text: Step 1: identify the heterogametic parent — the one producing two kinds of sex-chromosome gamete.
Step 2: that parent's gamete decides the offspring's sex. The homogametic parent contributes the same sex chromosome every time.
Human: the mother (XX) always gives an X; the father (XY) gives X, making an XX daughter, or Y, making an XY son, with equal probability.
Hence the father determines the child's sex, and P(son) = P(daughter) = 1/2.
In birds the logic flips: the mother (ZW) is heterogametic, so the mother determines the chick's sex.
Procedure E: trace a recessive X-linked allele
Sex-linked inheritance: inheritance of genes carried on the sex chromosomes. X-linked genes lie on the X; Y-linked (holandric) genes lie on the Y.
A gene on the X with no counterpart on the Y shows a distinctive zig-zag transmission.

board_events.text: Step 1: an affected father ($X^aY$) passes his $X^a$ to ALL his daughters, and to NONE of his sons — sons receive his Y.
Step 2: those daughters become unaffected carriers ($X^AX^a$). The trait skips them: the allele is recessive and their second X is normal.
Step 3: a carrier daughter then passes $X^a$ to half her sons, who — having only one X — express it.
The trait travels grandfather to carrier daughter to grandson, appearing to criss-cross between the sexes and skip a generation.
Why males are affected more often: a male needs only a single recessive X-linked allele, because he is hemizygous — one X. A female needs two.
Procedure F: always halve to the haploid number
Linkage group: all the genes on a single chromosome, inherited as a unit.

segments.text: The third big idea of this subtopic is sex determination: how an organism ends up male or female. It sits here, next to linkage, for a good reason — the answer turned out to be chromosomal too.

It starts with an observation nobody could interpret. Henking, in eighteen ninety one, was looking at insect sperm being formed, and he spotted a mysterious structure that was there in some cells and not others.
Watch what he saw. Sperm being made, and this structure sorting itself into some of them and not the rest.
That was the striking part: it went into only half the sperm. Not all of them, not a random scatter — a clean half. Something was being distributed, deliberately, into fifty percent of the gametes.
<curious>He could not say what it was. So he did the honest thing and gave it a placeholder name: the X-body. That X was not a symbol for anything — it was literally an unknown.
And that unknown was the first hint that a specific chromosome decides sex. Not the whole genome, not some vague vital force — one identifiable structure, present in half the sperm.
It was, of course, the X chromosome, and Henking's placeholder letter stuck permanently — which is why we say X chromosome today.
But the story does not have one ending. Different animal groups solved the sex problem in genuinely different ways, and the next section lays out all four systems side by side.
Four systems, and the examiners' favourite column is not female or male — it is the heterogametic one. Read the table with that column in mind.
Here they all are. Four rows, and the only thing that really changes across them is who produces two kinds of gamete.
First: X X to X O. Females are X X. Males are X O — and that O is not a letter, it is an absence. The male simply lacks the second sex chromosome. Grasshopper and cockroach are the standard examples.
Second: X X to X Y. Females are X X, males are X Y. Human and Drosophila. This is the one everybody knows, which is exactly why it gets over-applied.
In both of those systems, the male is the heterogametic sex — he makes two kinds of gamete with respect to sex chromosomes, and the female makes only one.

Third: Z Z to Z W, and here the whole thing flips. Birds and butterflies. Males are Z Z, females are Z W — so the female is the heterogametic sex. The letters change from X and Y to Z and W precisely to warn you that the roles have swapped.

Fourth: haplodiploidy, in the honeybee, which abandons sex chromosomes altogether. Females are diploid, developing from fertilised eggs; males are haploid, developing from unfertilised eggs. Sex is decided by how many full chromosome sets an individual has.

<excited>And the trap that catches people every year: X O is not X Y. In the X X to X O system there is no Y chromosome anywhere — the male has a single, unpaired X. Grasshopper males are X O, and writing X Y there is simply wrong.

One more name to hold: temperature-dependent sex determination, as in the crocodile, where the incubation temperature decides. It is worth knowing by name, because it shows sex determination is not always chromosomal at all.
Two definitions, then a two-step procedure that answers every who-decides-sex question in the syllabus, in any species.
Homogametic sex: produces only one type of gamete with respect to the sex chromosomes. The human female is X X, so every egg carries an X. One type, every time.
Heterogametic sex: produces two types. The human male is X Y, so half his sperm carry X and half carry Y. Two types — and that variety is the entire deciding mechanism.
Look at both panels. Left, the human case. Right, the bird case. Notice the structure is identical; only the label on the heterogametic parent moves.
Step one: identify the heterogametic parent — the one producing two kinds of sex-chromosome gamete. Not the mother, not the father, by default. Whichever one makes two kinds.

Step two: that parent's gamete decides the offspring's sex. And the reason is that the other parent contributes the same sex chromosome every single time, so it carries no information — it cannot decide anything.

Run it on humans. The mother is X X and always gives an X. The father gives X, making an X X daughter, or Y, making an X Y son, with equal probability. The mother's contribution is fixed; the father's is the variable.

Hence the father determines the child's sex, and the probability of a son equals the probability of a daughter equals one half. Notice what that sentence actually rests on — not on the father being male, but on the father being heterogametic.

Which is why in birds the logic flips completely. The mother is Z W and therefore heterogametic, so the mother determines the chick's sex. Same procedure, opposite answer — and that is exactly the question examiners set.
Sex-linked inheritance means the inheritance of genes carried on the sex chromosomes. X-linked genes lie on the X chromosome; Y-linked genes, also called holandric genes, lie on the Y.
The interesting case is a gene on the X that has no counterpart on the Y. That asymmetry — two copies in females, one in males — produces a transmission pattern you can recognise on sight.
Follow the pedigree from the top left, and watch the allele zig-zag down the generations.

Step one: an affected father passes his affected X to all of his daughters, and to none of his sons. Every daughter gets his only X; every son gets his Y instead. So the trait never goes father to son — that is a hard rule, and it is testable.

Step two: those daughters become unaffected carriers. The trait skips them, because the allele is recessive and their second X, from the mother, is normal. They carry it silently and look completely unaffected.
Step three: a carrier daughter then passes the affected X to half her sons. And those sons, having only one X, have nothing to mask it with — so they express it.

Put the three steps together and you get the pattern. The trait travels grandfather, to carrier daughter, to grandson — appearing to criss-cross between the sexes and to skip a generation entirely. It did not skip; it was hiding in the daughter.

And this explains the observation that makes X-linked disorders famous. Males are affected far more often, because a male needs only a single recessive X-linked allele to show the trait. He is hemizygous — he has one X, and no second copy to hide behind.
A female needs two copies, which is a much rarer event. Keep that asymmetry in your head; in the next part, on genetic disorders, it decides almost every probability question you will meet.
This is the shortest procedure in the chapter and the one that costs the most marks. It is one division, and students still get it wrong.
Start from the definition. A linkage group is all the genes on a single chromosome, inherited as a unit. One chromosome carries many genes; all of them together are one linkage group.
Look at the picture and count what is countable. Five genes on that chromosome, but one linkage group — because a linkage group is a chromosome's worth of genes, not a gene count.
So the number of linkage groups in a species equals its haploid chromosome number, n. Not the diploid number, two n. That sentence is the whole procedure.

The reason is worth saying out loud, because it makes the rule impossible to forget. Each distinct chromosome is one linkage group. A diploid cell has two copies of each chromosome — but the two homologues are not two different linkage groups, they are two copies of the same one. A haploid set contains one of each, so the haploid number is the count of distinct chromosomes.
Run it once. For an organism with two n equal to twenty four, linkage groups equal n, which is twelve. Halve, then answer.
And memorise the standard values, because they get asked directly: pea has seven, Drosophila has four, maize has ten, human has twenty three. All haploid numbers, all linkage-group counts.
This is the single most common slip in the subtopic. The question hands you two n, the option list contains that same number, and the reflex is to circle it. Always halve to the haploid number first.
Every tool in this subtopic has an edge, and the questions live at those edges. Three conditions, and each one is a ready-made two-mark answer.
Condition one concerns the map tape. Recombination frequency approximates map distance only for small distances. It is an approximation with a working range, not an identity.

Over long stretches, double crossovers occur and go undetected — the second crossover undoes the first, the gamete looks parental, and you never count it. So the true distance is underestimated. Large maps are always built from short intervals for exactly this reason.
The picture puts all three edges side by side: the tape, the father rule, and the theory itself.

The same condition has a hard ceiling attached: the maximum observable recombination frequency is fifty percent. Beyond that, genes behave as if unlinked — the method cannot distinguish far-apart-but-linked from genuinely independent.

Condition two is about a sentence students over-generalise. The rule that the father determines the child's sex is specific to systems where the male is heterogametic. It is not a fact about fatherhood; it is a fact about who makes two kinds of gamete.
In birds it is the mother — the Z W sex — who decides. So before you answer any sex-determination question, read which system you are in. The species is not decoration; it is the data.
Condition three is historical and conceptual at once. The chromosomal theory was framed before anyone knew genes were made of D N A. Sutton and Boveri had no idea what a gene was chemically.

<curious>And that is worth pausing on, because it says something about how science works. The theory correctly located genes on chromosomes without explaining their chemistry at all. A model can be right about where something is long before anyone knows what it is.
A board favourite, and a question that is really testing whether you understand independence — dressed up as a family story.
A couple has four daughters. What is the probability that their fifth child is a son? And note the word explain: this is not a one-line answer, the reasoning is where the marks are.
Look at the picture. Four daughters behind, one question mark ahead. The temptation is to feel that the question mark is somehow owed a son. It is not.
Start with the mother. She is X X, which makes her homogametic, so every egg she produces carries an X. Her contribution is fixed and carries no information about the child's sex.
Now the father. He is X Y, heterogametic, so he contributes X or Y with equal chance. The entire outcome rides on which sperm arrives.

And here is the load-bearing sentence: each fertilisation is independent of every previous one. The sperm that fertilises the fifth egg does not know, and cannot know, what happened in the first four.
So the probability of a son equals the probability that the father contributes a Y, which is one half. Full stop. The answer would have been one half before any of the children were born.

<chuckle>The four previous daughters do not change this at all. Biology has no memory of past births — and if you write that sentence in a board answer, you have written exactly what the examiner is looking for.
A speed trap, which in N E E T means the wrong answer is printed right there in the options, waiting for your reflex.
A plant species has a diploid chromosome number, two n, equal to twenty four. How many linkage groups does it possess?
Look at what the halving actually does. On the left, twenty four chromosomes — but they are twelve pairs. On the right, one of each: twelve distinct chromosomes.
So the speed logic is one line: linkage groups equal the haploid number, which is two n divided by two, which is twenty four divided by two, which is twelve.
Answer: twelve linkage groups. Two seconds, if the halving is automatic.

Now the traps, and there are two of them sitting in the option list. Twenty four is there, for anyone who uses two n directly without halving. And twenty three is there too — the human haploid number — for anyone who has memorised a number instead of a method.
So make the halving reflexive. Read two n, halve it, then answer. Never let the number in the question walk straight onto your answer sheet.
This is the standard numerical of the subtopic, and it is two parts that are secretly one calculation.

In a test cross of a dihybrid, one thousand offspring are scored, and eighty of them are recombinant types. Part a: find the recombination frequency. Part b: state the map distance between the two genes.
Look at the bar. Nearly all parental, a thin sliver recombinant. Before computing anything, that shape already tells you these genes are linked.
Now the arithmetic. R F equals eighty divided by one thousand, times one hundred, which is eight percent. Recombinants on top, total offspring on the bottom — not the parental count.
So part a is answered: R F equals eight percent.
And part b: since one centiMorgan corresponds to one percent recombination, the genes are eight centiMorgans apart. Same eight, different unit.

One line of interpretation earns the extra mark. Only eighty of a thousand are recombinant — far below a fifty-fifty split. That confirms the genes are linked, not assorting independently. If they were unlinked, you would expect roughly five hundred.
And the exam habit to take away: part b is part a with the unit changed. Students recompute, second-guess, and lose time. Read the percent, write the same number in centiMorgans, move on.
इस subtopic का तीसरा बड़ा idea है sex determination: कोई जीव male बनता है या female, ये तय कैसे होता है। ये यहाँ linkage के बग़ल में है, और वजह अच्छी है — जवाब भी chromosomal ही निकला।
शुरुआत एक ऐसे observation से होती है जिसे कोई समझ नहीं पाया। Henking ने, अठारह सौ इक्यानवे में, insect sperm बनते हुए देखे, और उन्हें एक रहस्यमय structure दिखा जो कुछ cells में था और कुछ में नहीं।
देखिए उन्होंने क्या देखा। Sperm बन रहे हैं, और ये structure ख़ुद को कुछ में डाल रहा है, बाक़ी में नहीं।
यही चौंकाने वाली बात थी: वो सिर्फ़ आधे sperm में जाता था। सबमें नहीं, बेतरतीब भी नहीं — साफ़ आधे में। कुछ था जो जानबूझ कर पचास percent gametes में बाँटा जा रहा था।
<curious>वो बता नहीं पाए कि ये है क्या। तो उन्होंने ईमानदारी वाला काम किया और एक placeholder नाम दे दिया: X-body। वो X किसी चीज़ का symbol नहीं था — वो सचमुच एक unknown था।
और वही unknown पहला इशारा था कि sex कोई एक ख़ास chromosome तय करता है। पूरा genome नहीं, कोई धुँधली vital force नहीं — एक पहचानी जा सकने वाली structure, जो आधे sperm में है।
वो, ज़ाहिर है, X chromosome था, और Henking का placeholder letter हमेशा के लिए चिपक गया — इसीलिए आज हम X chromosome कहते हैं।
पर कहानी का एक ही अंत नहीं है। अलग-अलग animal groups ने sex की समस्या सच में अलग-अलग तरीक़ों से हल की, और अगला section चारों systems साथ रख कर दिखाता है।
चार systems, और examiners का favourite column female या male नहीं है — वो heterogametic वाला है। Table इसी column को ध्यान में रखकर पढ़िए।
यहाँ चारों हैं। चार rows, और इनमें असल में बदलता सिर्फ़ ये है कि दो तरह के gametes कौन बनाता है।
पहला: X X to X O। Females X X हैं। Males X O — और वो O कोई letter नहीं, वो अनुपस्थिति है। Male के पास दूसरा sex chromosome है ही नहीं। Grasshopper और cockroach standard examples हैं।
दूसरा: X X to X Y। Females X X, males X Y। Human और Drosophila। यही सबको पता है, और इसीलिए इसे हर जगह लगा दिया जाता है।
इन दोनों systems में male ही heterogametic sex है — वो sex chromosomes के हिसाब से दो तरह के gametes बनाता है, और female सिर्फ़ एक तरह के।

तीसरा: Z Z to Z W, और यहाँ पूरा मामला पलट जाता है। Birds और butterflies। Males Z Z हैं, females Z W — यानी female heterogametic sex है। Letters का X और Y से बदलकर Z और W होना ही आपको चेतावनी देता है कि roles बदल गए हैं।

चौथा: haplodiploidy, honeybee में, जो sex chromosomes को पूरी तरह छोड़ देता है। Females diploid हैं, fertilised eggs से; males haploid हैं, unfertilised eggs से। Sex इस बात से तय होता है कि individual के पास कितने पूरे chromosome sets हैं।

<excited>और वो trap जो हर साल लोगों को पकड़ता है: X O, X Y नहीं है। X X to X O system में Y chromosome कहीं है ही नहीं — male के पास एक अकेला, बिना जोड़ी वाला X होता है। Grasshopper males X O हैं, और वहाँ X Y लिखना बस ग़लत है।

एक और नाम पकड़ लीजिए: temperature-dependent sex determination, जैसे crocodile में, जहाँ incubation temperature तय करता है। नाम से जानना ज़रूरी है, क्योंकि ये दिखाता है कि sex determination हमेशा chromosomal होता ही नहीं।
दो definitions, फिर दो-step procedure जो syllabus के हर who-decides-sex सवाल का जवाब देता है, किसी भी species में।
Homogametic sex: sex chromosomes के हिसाब से सिर्फ़ एक तरह का gamete बनाता है। Human female X X है, तो हर egg में X। एक ही तरह, हर बार।
Heterogametic sex: दो तरह के बनाता है। Human male X Y है, तो आधे sperm में X और आधे में Y। दो तरह — और यही variety पूरा deciding mechanism है।
दोनों panels देखिए। बाएँ human case। दाएँ bird case। ध्यान दीजिए structure बिलकुल वही है; सिर्फ़ heterogametic parent का label जगह बदलता है।
Step one: heterogametic parent पहचानिए — जो दो तरह के sex-chromosome gametes बनाता है। By default न mother, न father। जो भी दो तरह के बनाता हो।
Step two: उसी parent का gamete offspring का sex तय करता है। वजह ये कि दूसरा parent हर बार वही sex chromosome देता है, तो उसमें कोई information है ही नहीं — वो कुछ तय कर ही नहीं सकता।
Humans पर चलाइए। Mother X X है और हमेशा X देती है। Father X देता है, तो X X daughter, या Y देता है, तो X Y son — बराबर probability से। Mother का contribution fixed है; father का variable।

इसलिए father बच्चे का sex तय करता है, और son की probability बराबर daughter की probability बराबर आधा। ध्यान दीजिए ये वाक्य किस पर टिका है — इस पर नहीं कि father male है, बल्कि इस पर कि father heterogametic है।
इसीलिए birds में logic पूरी तरह पलट जाती है। Mother Z W है, यानी heterogametic, तो chick का sex mother तय करती है। वही procedure, उल्टा जवाब — और examiners ठीक यही सवाल पूछते हैं।
Sex-linked inheritance मतलब sex chromosomes पर मौजूद genes की inheritance। X-linked genes X chromosome पर होते हैं; Y-linked genes, जिन्हें holandric genes भी कहते हैं, Y पर।
दिलचस्प case वो gene है जो X पर है और जिसका Y पर कोई जोड़ीदार नहीं। यही asymmetry — females में दो copies, males में एक — ऐसा transmission pattern बनाती है जिसे आप देखते ही पहचान लें।
Pedigree को ऊपर बाएँ से देखिए, और allele को generations में zig-zag करते हुए देखिए।

Step one: एक affected father अपना affected X अपनी सारी daughters को देता है, और किसी बेटे को नहीं। हर बेटी को उसका इकलौता X मिलता है; हर बेटे को उसका Y। तो trait कभी father से son तक नहीं जाता — ये सख़्त rule है, और यही पूछा जाता है।

Step two: वो daughters unaffected carriers बन जाती हैं। Trait उन्हें छोड़ देता है, क्योंकि allele recessive है और उनका दूसरा X, mother से आया हुआ, normal है। वो उसे चुपचाप carry करती हैं और बिलकुल unaffected दिखती हैं।
Step three: फिर carrier daughter वो affected X अपने आधे बेटों को दे देती है। और उन बेटों के पास सिर्फ़ एक X है, उसे छुपाने के लिए कुछ है ही नहीं — तो वो उसे express कर देते हैं।

तीनों steps जोड़िए और pattern मिल जाता है। Trait चलता है grandfather से carrier daughter तक, फिर grandson तक — sexes के बीच criss-cross करता हुआ, और एक generation छोड़ता हुआ। वो छोड़ा नहीं था; वो daughter में छुपा था।

और इससे वो observation समझ आता है जिससे X-linked disorders मशहूर हैं। Males कहीं ज़्यादा affected होते हैं, क्योंकि male को trait दिखाने के लिए सिर्फ़ एक recessive X-linked allele चाहिए। वो hemizygous है — एक X, और छुपने के लिए दूसरी copy नहीं।
Female को दो copies चाहिए, जो कहीं ज़्यादा दुर्लभ है। ये asymmetry दिमाग़ में रखिए; अगले part में, genetic disorders में, यही लगभग हर probability question तय करती है।
ये chapter का सबसे छोटा procedure है और सबसे ज़्यादा marks खाने वाला। एक division है, और फिर भी students ग़लत करते हैं।
Definition से शुरू कीजिए। Linkage group मतलब एक ही chromosome के सारे genes, जो एक unit की तरह inherit होते हैं। एक chromosome पर कई genes होते हैं; वो सब मिलकर एक linkage group हैं।
तस्वीर देखिए और जो गिनने लायक़ है वो गिनिए। उस chromosome पर पाँच genes हैं, पर linkage group एक — क्योंकि linkage group एक chromosome भर के genes हैं, genes की गिनती नहीं।
तो किसी species में linkage groups की संख्या उसके haploid chromosome number n के बराबर होती है। Diploid number two n के नहीं। यही एक वाक्य पूरा procedure है।

वजह ज़ोर से बोलने लायक़ है, क्योंकि इसके बाद rule भूलना मुश्किल है। हर distinct chromosome एक linkage group है। Diploid cell में हर chromosome की दो copies होती हैं — पर दोनों homologues दो अलग linkage groups नहीं हैं, वो एक ही की दो copies हैं। Haploid set में हर एक की एक copy होती है, इसलिए haploid number ही distinct chromosomes की गिनती है।
एक बार चलाइए। जिस जीव में two n बराबर चौबीस है, उसमें linkage groups बराबर n, यानी बारह। पहले आधा कीजिए, फिर जवाब दीजिए।
और standard values याद कर लीजिए, क्योंकि ये सीधे पूछे जाते हैं: pea में सात, Drosophila में चार, maize में दस, human में तेईस। सब haploid numbers, सब linkage-group counts।
यही इस subtopic की सबसे आम चूक है। Question आपको two n देता है, options में वही number रखा होता है, और reflex उसी पर गोला लगा देता है। पहले हमेशा haploid number तक आधा कीजिए।
इस subtopic के हर tool का एक किनारा है, और सवाल उन्हीं किनारों पर बैठे होते हैं। तीन conditions, और हर एक बना-बनाया दो-mark का जवाब है।
Condition one map tape के बारे में है। Recombination frequency map distance के बराबर सिर्फ़ छोटे distances पर होती है। ये एक approximation है जिसकी working range है, कोई identity नहीं।

लंबे हिस्सों में double crossovers होते हैं और पकड़ में नहीं आते — दूसरा crossover पहले को उलट देता है, gamete parental दिखता है, और आप उसे गिनते ही नहीं। इसलिए असली distance कम आँका जाता है। बड़े maps इसीलिए हमेशा छोटे intervals से बनते हैं।
तस्वीर तीनों किनारे साथ रखती है: tape, father rule, और ख़ुद theory।

इसी condition के साथ एक सख़्त ceiling जुड़ी है: सबसे ज़्यादा दिखने वाली recombination frequency पचास percent है। उससे आगे genes ऐसे बर्ताव करते हैं जैसे unlinked हों — method दूर-पर-linked और सच में independent में फ़र्क़ बता ही नहीं सकता।

Condition two एक ऐसे वाक्य के बारे में है जिसे students हर जगह लगा देते हैं। Father बच्चे का sex तय करता है — ये rule सिर्फ़ उन systems के लिए है जहाँ male heterogametic है। ये fatherhood के बारे में fact नहीं है; ये इस बारे में है कि दो तरह के gametes कौन बनाता है।
Birds में mother — यानी Z W sex — तय करती है। तो किसी भी sex-determination question का जवाब देने से पहले पढ़िए कि आप किस system में हैं। Species सजावट नहीं है; वही data है।
Condition three एक साथ historical भी है और conceptual भी। Chromosomal theory तब बनी जब किसी को पता नहीं था कि genes D N A के बने हैं। Sutton और Boveri को gene की chemistry का कोई अंदाज़ा नहीं था।

<curious>और यहाँ रुकना चाहिए, क्योंकि ये science के काम करने के तरीक़े के बारे में कुछ कहता है। Theory ने genes को chromosomes पर सही जगह बिठा दिया, बिना उनकी chemistry समझाए। कोई model ये सही बता सकता है कि चीज़ कहाँ है, उससे बहुत पहले कि कोई जाने वो है क्या।
Board का favourite, और ये सवाल असल में ये जाँच रहा है कि आप independence समझते हैं या नहीं — बस उसे family story बना दिया गया है।
एक जोड़े की चार बेटियाँ हैं। पाँचवाँ बच्चा बेटा होने की probability क्या है? और शब्द देखिए — explain: ये एक-line का जवाब नहीं है, marks reasoning में हैं।
तस्वीर देखिए। पीछे चार बेटियाँ, आगे एक सवालिया निशान। मन कहता है कि उस सवालिया निशान पर अब बेटा बनता है। ऐसा है नहीं।
Mother से शुरू कीजिए। वो X X हैं, यानी homogametic, तो उनका हर egg X लेकर चलता है। उनका contribution fixed है और बच्चे के sex के बारे में कोई information नहीं रखता।
अब father। वो X Y हैं, heterogametic, तो वो बराबर chance से X या Y देते हैं। पूरा नतीजा इसी पर टिका है कि कौन सा sperm पहुँचता है।

और ये रहा वो वाक्य जिस पर सब टिका है: हर fertilisation पिछली हर fertilisation से independent है। पाँचवें egg को fertilise करने वाले sperm को नहीं पता, और पता हो ही नहीं सकता, कि पहले चार में क्या हुआ।
तो बेटा होने की probability बराबर father के Y देने की probability, यानी आधा। बस। जवाब आधा ही होता, चाहे कोई बच्चा पैदा हुआ ही न होता।
<chuckle>पिछली चार बेटियाँ इसमें ज़रा भी बदलाव नहीं करतीं। Biology को पिछले जन्मों की याद नहीं होती — और अगर आप ये वाक्य board answer में लिख दें, तो आपने ठीक वही लिखा है जो examiner ढूँढ रहा है।
ये speed trap है, और N E E T में इसका मतलब है कि ग़लत जवाब options में छपा बैठा है, आपके reflex का इंतज़ार करता हुआ।
एक plant species का diploid chromosome number, two n, चौबीस है। उसमें कितने linkage groups हैं?
देखिए आधा करने से होता क्या है। बाएँ चौबीस chromosomes — पर वो बारह pairs हैं। दाएँ हर एक की एक copy: बारह distinct chromosomes।
तो speed logic एक line है: linkage groups बराबर haploid number, यानी two n बटा दो, यानी चौबीस बटा दो, यानी बारह।
जवाब: बारह linkage groups। दो सेकंड, अगर आधा करना automatic हो।

अब traps, और option list में दो बैठे हैं। चौबीस वहाँ है, उनके लिए जो two n सीधे इस्तेमाल कर लेते हैं। और तेईस भी वहाँ है — human haploid number — उनके लिए जिन्होंने method की जगह एक number रट लिया है।
तो आधा करना reflex बना लीजिए। Two n पढ़िए, आधा कीजिए, फिर जवाब दीजिए। Question का number सीधे answer sheet पर मत चलने दीजिए।
ये इस subtopic का standard numerical है, और ये दो parts हैं जो असल में एक ही calculation हैं।
एक dihybrid के test cross में एक हज़ार offspring गिने गए, और उनमें से अस्सी recombinant types हैं। Part a: recombination frequency निकालिए। Part b: दोनों genes के बीच map distance बताइए।
Bar देखिए। लगभग सब parental, एक पतली सी पट्टी recombinant। कुछ गिनने से पहले ही ये shape बता देती है कि ये genes linked हैं।
अब arithmetic। R F बराबर अस्सी बटा एक हज़ार, into सौ, यानी आठ percent। ऊपर recombinants, नीचे total offspring — parental count नहीं।
तो part a का जवाब हो गया: R F बराबर आठ percent।
और part b: चूँकि एक centiMorgan बराबर एक percent recombination है, दोनों genes आठ centiMorgan दूर हैं। वही आठ, अलग unit।

Interpretation की एक line extra mark दिलाती है। हज़ार में सिर्फ़ अस्सी recombinant हैं — पचास-पचास से बहुत कम। यही पक्का करता है कि genes linked हैं, independently assort नहीं कर रहे। Unlinked होते तो लगभग पाँच सौ की उम्मीद होती।
और exam की आदत ये लीजिए: part b, part a ही है बस unit बदली हुई। Students दोबारा गिनते हैं, शक करते हैं, और समय गँवाते हैं। Percent पढ़िए, वही number centiMorgan में लिखिए, आगे बढ़िए।

sections.title: Example four: ordering three linked genes... & Aneuploidy, karyotype, and the language of...

board_events.text: Example four [N E E T high difficulty]
For three linked genes the map distances are: A to B = 5 cM, B to C = 13 cM, A to C = 8 cM. Determine the linear order of the genes.

board_events.caption: Largest distance first, then the missing gene
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 540 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">
<text x="270" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">Given three distances, find the order</text>
<rect x="60" y="38" width="130" height="30" rx="6" fill="#f3f4f6" stroke="#9ca3af"/><text x="125" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">A to B = 5 cM</text>
<rect x="205" y="38" width="130" height="30" rx="6" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#dc2626"/><text x="270" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">B to C = 13 cM</text>
<rect x="350" y="38" width="130" height="30" rx="6" fill="#f3f4f6" stroke="#9ca3af"/><text x="415" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">A to C = 8 cM</text>
<text x="270" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">Step 1: the largest is B to C, so B and C are the two ends</text>
<text x="270" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">Step 2: the gene missing from that pair is A, so A is central</text>
<line x1="90" y1="156" x2="450" y2="156" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2"/>
<circle cx="90" cy="156" r="9" fill="#2563eb"/><text x="90" y="186" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">B</text>
<circle cx="228" cy="156" r="9" fill="#7c3aed"/><text x="228" y="186" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#7c3aed">A</text>
<circle cx="450" cy="156" r="9" fill="#16a34a"/><text x="450" y="186" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">C</text>
<text x="159" y="144" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">5 cM</text>
<text x="339" y="144" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">8 cM</text>
<text x="270" y="212" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">Step 3: 5 + 8 = 13, so additivity checks out</text>
<text x="270" y="238" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#dc2626">Trap: assuming the first-listed pair, A and B, defines the ends</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Step 1 — largest distance: B to C = 13 cM is the largest, so B and C are the two outermost genes.
Step 2 — middle gene: the gene missing from that pair is A, so A lies in the middle.
Step 3 — additivity check: A to B plus A to C = 5 + 8 = 13 = B to C.
Order: B — A — C, with A central.
The classic trap is to assume the first-listed pair, A and B, defines the ends. The order is dictated by the largest distance, not the order of listing.
Common student pitfalls
Pitfall 1: linkage groups = haploid (n), not diploid (2n). For 2n = 24, the answer is 12, not 24. The single most common slip here.
Pitfall 2: assuming the mother determines the child's sex. It is the heterogametic parent — the father in humans (XY), but the mother in birds (ZW).

board_events.caption: Four slips, each with a trap option waiting
board_events.svg:

<text x="32" y="104" font-size="12" fill="#16a34a">2n = 24 gives 12</text>
<text x="32" y="126" font-size="12" fill="#dc2626">not 24</text>

<text x="32" y="212" font-size="12" fill="#16a34a">Grasshopper male = XO</text>
<text x="32" y="234" font-size="12" fill="#dc2626">a single unpaired X</text>
<rect x="274" y="146" width="248" height="98" rx="8" fill="#fff7ed" stroke="#f59e0b"/>

<text x="288" y="212" font-size="12" fill="#16a34a">At 50%, effectively unlinked</text>
<text x="288" y="234" font-size="12" fill="#dc2626">A 60% option is always wrong</text>
