</svg>

board_events.text: Pitfall 3: confusing XX to XO with XX to XY. In XX to XO there is no Y chromosome at all; the male simply has a single, unpaired X. Grasshopper males are XO, not XY.
Pitfall 4: forgetting the 50% recombination ceiling. Recombination frequency can never exceed 50%; genes showing 50% are effectively unlinked.
A 60% recombination option is always wrong.
Read the system before answering. Every one of these four has a trap option sitting in the paper.
Pro-tips and memory aids
For three-point gene ordering, do not Punnett anything. Just spot the largest of the three pairwise distances.
Those two genes are the ends; the third gene sits between them; and the two short distances must add to the long one.
It turns a confusing problem into a five-second check.
Remember the limiting condition: this additivity holds cleanly only for short distances, because double crossovers make large RF values underestimate true distance.
Memory aids: "Linkage groups go haploid." "Birds break the rule — the mother makes the call." "Biggest distance = the two ends."
Carry forward: RF is proportional to distance, 1 cM = 1% recombination, and the ceiling is 50%.
Next: what happens when a single gene, or a whole chromosome, goes wrong — genetic disorders.
Two families of genetic disorder
Why does one illness run through a family for generations, while another appears in a single child whose parents are perfectly healthy?
The answer lies in WHERE in the genome the problem sits — and that splits genetic disorders into two big families.

board_events.caption: Mendelian versus chromosomal disorders

board_events.text: Mendelian disorders: caused by a change (mutation) in a single gene. Because a single gene obeys Mendel's rules, these are inherited in predictable ratios.
Chromosomal disorders: caused not by a faulty gene but by the wrong NUMBER of whole chromosomes.
These usually arise fresh, by an accident during gamete formation — so they usually appear with no prior family history.
Where the problem sits decides everything else: the ratios, the family history, and the questions you will be asked.
Mendelian disorders and the silent carrier
Most Mendelian disorders are recessive: you need TWO faulty copies to be affected.
A person with one faulty and one normal copy is an unaffected carrier — healthy, but able to pass the faulty allele on.

<text x="270" y="276" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">This is why consanguineous marriage raises the risk</text>

board_events.text: This is exactly why two visibly healthy parents can have an affected child: both are silent carriers, and the child inherits the faulty allele from each.
Think of a recessive disorder allele as a hidden debt in a joint family ledger. One parent carrying it quietly causes no trouble.
But when two carriers marry, and a child inherits the hidden entry from both sides, the debt finally comes due.
This is also why consanguineous marriage raises the risk: relatives are more likely to carry the same hidden allele.
Chromosomal disorders arise fresh
Chromosomal disorders are caused by the wrong number of whole chromosomes, and usually arise by an accident during gamete formation.
Non-disjunction: a pair of chromosomes fails to separate during meiosis.

board_events.text: So one gamete ends up with an extra chromosome, and another with one too few.
Fertilisation then produces an individual with 47 chromosomes (one extra) or 45 (one missing), instead of the usual 46.
An extra copy of chromosome 21 gives Down syndrome; an extra X in a male gives Klinefelter; a missing X in a female gives Turner.
The error happens in a single egg or sperm, not in the family ledger. That is why there is usually no family history.
The risk rises with the mother's age: eggs have been paused mid-meiosis for decades, and the separating machinery grows less reliable.
You cannot cross humans
Mendel chose his parents, made thousands of offspring, and predicted forwards.
Human families give none of that: no controlled crosses, very few children, and long generation times.

board_events.text: So geneticists work backwards, using pedigree analysis.
Pedigree analysis: the study of the inheritance of a trait across several generations of a family, using a standardised family-tree diagram.
You read who is affected across the generations, and then deduce the rules.
From the pattern you deduce two things: dominant or recessive, and autosomal or X-linked.
Terms every question here is built from
Genetic disorder: an illness caused by one or more abnormalities in the genome — either a single-gene mutation (Mendelian) or an abnormality in chromosome number or structure (chromosomal).
Mendelian disorder: caused by alteration or mutation in a single gene; inherited in Mendelian ratios.

board_events.text: A Mendelian disorder may be autosomal (the gene lies on a non-sex chromosome) or sex-linked (the gene lies on a sex chromosome).
Chromosomal disorder: caused by the excess, absence, or abnormal arrangement of one or more whole chromosomes.

Non-disjunction: failure of a chromosome pair to separate during meiosis, producing gametes with an abnormal chromosome number.
Counting chromosomes precisely

board_events.text: Trisomy = one extra chromosome ($2n+1$). Monosomy = one missing chromosome ($2n-1$).
Karyotype: the complete set of an individual's chromosomes, described by number and sex chromosomes — written like 47, XXY or 45, XO.
Consanguineous mating: mating between close relatives, raising the chance that both partners carry the same recessive allele.
No SI units in this subtopic. The quantities are chromosome counts (whole numbers) and probabilities (pure fractions).
Read a karyotype as two pieces: the total count, then the sex chromosomes. Both carry information.

segments.text: Marked high difficulty, and it takes about five seconds once you stop treating it as a genetics problem and start treating it as a number line.
For three linked genes the map distances are: A to B is five centiMorgans, B to C is thirteen centiMorgans, A to C is eight centiMorgans. Determine the linear order of the genes.
Watch the three boxes. One of them is highlighted, and that is the entire solution — the rest is bookkeeping.
Step one, the largest distance. B to C, at thirteen centiMorgans, is the biggest of the three. So B and C are the two outermost genes — the ends of the line.
Step two, the middle gene. The gene missing from that largest pair is A. There is only one position left on a line with two ends already assigned, so A lies in the middle. No calculation.

Step three, the additivity check, which is where the board mark hides. A to B plus A to C equals five plus eight, which is thirteen, which equals B to C. The two short segments sum to the long one, so the arrangement is consistent.
The order is B, then A, then C, with A central. Write it as a line, not as a sentence — examiners want to see the arrangement.

And the classic trap: assuming the first-listed pair, A and B, defines the ends, simply because it was written first. The order is dictated by the largest distance, never by the order of listing. The question lists A to B first precisely to tempt you.
Four pitfalls, and every one of them has a matching wrong option already printed in the question paper. Run these as a checklist.

Pitfall one: linkage groups equal the haploid number, n, not the diploid number, two n. For two n equal to twenty four, the answer is twelve, not twenty four. This is the single most common slip in the subtopic, and it is one division.

Pitfall two: assuming the mother determines the child's sex, or assuming the father always does. Neither. It is the heterogametic parent — the father in humans, who is X Y, but the mother in birds, who is Z W.
The picture holds all four together. Notice they share a shape: in each case a familiar fact is being applied one step past where it is true.

Pitfall three: confusing X X to X O with X X to X Y. In X X to X O there is no Y chromosome at all — the male simply has a single, unpaired X. Grasshopper males are X O, not X Y, and that O is an absence, not a letter.

Pitfall four: forgetting the fifty percent recombination ceiling. Recombination frequency can never exceed fifty percent, and genes showing fifty percent are effectively unlinked — the method has run out of range.
Which hands you a free elimination in any mapping question. A sixty percent recombination option is always wrong. You do not need to compute anything to strike it out.

And the habit underneath all four: read the system before answering. Which organism, which sex-determination system, diploid or haploid number — the question names it, and the naming is not decoration.
Close this subtopic with the shortcuts, because everything here is fast once you know which tool to reach for.
First, three-point gene ordering. Do not Punnett anything — students see three genes and start drawing grids. Just spot the largest of the three pairwise distances.
Those two genes are the ends. The third gene sits between them. And the two short distances must add to the long one. Three sentences, and the problem is finished.
It genuinely turns a problem that looks like it needs a page into a five-second check. In a paper where time is the binding constraint, that is worth more than the mark itself.

But keep the condition attached, because the honest version of a shortcut includes its range. This additivity holds cleanly only for short distances, because double crossovers make large R F values underestimate the true distance.
Three memory aids, and they are short on purpose. Linkage groups go haploid — use n. Birds break the rule, the mother makes the call. And biggest distance equals the two ends.

Carry three facts forward as a set: R F is proportional to distance; one centiMorgan equals one percent recombination; and the ceiling is fifty percent. Almost every numerical here is one of those three, read in the right direction.

And notice where this subtopic leaves you. We now know genes sit on chromosomes, that they can be linked, and that some of them sit on the X. Next we ask what happens when one of those genes, or an entire chromosome, goes wrong — that is genetic disorders.

<curious>Start with a question you have probably wondered about without framing it genetically. Why does one illness run through a family for generations, appearing in cousins and grandparents, while another appears out of nowhere in a single child whose parents are perfectly healthy?
That is not two unrelated mysteries. It is one question with one answer, and the answer is structural.
The answer lies in where in the genome the problem sits. And that single consideration splits genetic disorders into two big families — which is why this subtopic is organised the way it is.
Look at the split. One branch, a faulty gene. The other branch, a faulty chromosome count. Everything else in this subtopic hangs off that fork.

The first family: Mendelian disorders, caused by a change — a mutation — in a single gene. And because a single gene obeys Mendel's rules, these disorders are inherited in predictable ratios, exactly like tall and dwarf in pea. The last two subtopics were not a detour; they were the toolkit.
The second family: chromosomal disorders, caused not by a single faulty gene but by the wrong number of whole chromosomes. Not a typo in one word — a missing or duplicated page.

And that difference in scale produces the difference in family history. Chromosomal disorders usually arise fresh, by an accident during gamete formation, so they usually appear with no prior family history at all.
So hold the organising idea. Where the problem sits decides everything else: whether you can predict ratios, whether relatives are affected, and which kind of question the examiner can even ask you.
Mendelian disorders are single-gene disorders, so they follow Mendel exactly. But there is a catch that shapes the whole subtopic: most of them are recessive.
Recessive means you need two faulty copies to be affected. One faulty copy is not enough — the normal copy on the other chromosome does the job well enough to keep you healthy.

Which creates a person the whole subtopic revolves around: the carrier. One faulty copy, one normal copy, heterozygous. Healthy themselves, and completely able to pass the faulty allele on. Unaffected, but not neutral.
Now look at what happens when two carriers have children. Four boxes, and you have seen this grid before — it is just a monohybrid cross wearing a medical name.

And there is the answer to the puzzle we opened with. Two visibly healthy parents can have an affected child, because both are silent carriers, and the child inherits the faulty allele from each side. Nothing appeared from nowhere; it was in the family all along, unexpressed.
Think of a recessive disorder allele as a hidden debt in a joint family ledger. One parent carrying it quietly causes no trouble at all — the entry sits there, unnoticed, for a whole generation.

But when two carriers marry, and a child happens to inherit the hidden entry from both sides, the debt finally comes due. Note the word happens — it is a one-in-four chance per child, not a certainty.

And that picture explains one more fact cleanly. This is why marriages between close relatives — consanguineous marriages — raise the risk. Relatives share ancestors, so they are more likely to carry the same hidden allele in the same ledger.
The second family works completely differently, and the difference is worth stating sharply: nothing here is inherited from a carrier. It is an accident, and it happens once.
Chromosomal disorders are caused by the wrong number of whole chromosomes. And they usually arise fresh, by an accident during the formation of an egg or a sperm.
The accident has a name: non-disjunction. During meiosis, a pair of chromosomes fails to separate. They should move apart, one into each cell. Instead they travel together into the same one.
Watch what that does to the two gametes. Follow the pair on the left, and see where each copy ends up.

One gamete ends up with an extra chromosome. The other ends up with one too few. Both gametes are abnormal, from a single failure — and notice, neither parent is a carrier of anything. Their body cells are perfectly normal.
Then fertilisation with a normal gamete does the arithmetic. You get an individual with forty seven chromosomes, one extra, or forty five, one missing, instead of the usual forty six.

And which chromosome it was decides which syndrome you get. An extra copy of chromosome twenty one gives Down syndrome. An extra X in a male gives Klinefelter syndrome. A missing X in a female gives Turner syndrome. Same mechanism, three outcomes.

Which explains the family-history difference completely. The error happens in a single egg or sperm, rather than being carried in the family ledger — so these disorders usually appear with no prior family history at all.

One more fact, and it is asked directly. The accident becomes more likely as eggs age, which is why the chance of a non-disjunction disorder such as Down syndrome rises with the mother's age. Her eggs have been paused mid-meiosis for decades, and the machinery that separates chromosomes grows less reliable over that time.
Before the disorders themselves, one methodological problem has to be solved — and it is a real one, not a formality.
Think about what Mendel actually had. He chose his parents deliberately. He produced thousands of offspring. He got a new generation every season. So he could set up a cross and predict forwards.

Human families give you none of that. You cannot set up controlled crosses — obviously, and rightly. Families have very few children, so your sample is tiny. And generation times are decades, not seasons.
Look at the two columns. Everything that made pea easy is missing on the right. So the method has to be turned around.

So geneticists work backwards. Instead of choosing parents and predicting children, you take the children that exist and deduce what the parents must have carried. That reversal is called pedigree analysis.

Formally: pedigree analysis is the study of the inheritance of a trait across several generations of a family, using a standardised family-tree diagram. Standardised matters — the symbols are fixed, so any geneticist reads the same chart the same way.

The procedure is exactly what it sounds like. You read who is affected across the generations — who is filled in, who is not, which sex — and then you deduce the rules that could have produced that pattern.
And the deduction has two parts, always the same two. Is the trait dominant or recessive? And is it autosomal or X-linked? Answer those two, and the pedigree has told you everything it can.
Four definitions, and they are not decorative. Every question in this subtopic is a request to classify something into one of these boxes.

A genetic disorder is an illness caused by one or more abnormalities in the genome. And the definition itself contains the fork: either a single-gene mutation, which is Mendelian, or an abnormality in chromosome number or structure, which is chromosomal.

A Mendelian disorder is caused by alteration or mutation in a single gene, and is inherited in Mendelian ratios. Single gene, Mendel's rules. If you can compute a probability with a Punnett square, you are in this family.
Here they are laid out together. Notice the bar across the bottom — the Mendelian box splits again, and that second split is where most exam questions live.

That second split: a Mendelian disorder may be autosomal, meaning the gene lies on a non-sex chromosome, or sex-linked, meaning the gene lies on a sex chromosome. Same single-gene logic, but the sex-linked ones inherit in that criss-cross pattern you already know.

A chromosomal disorder is caused by the excess, absence, or abnormal arrangement of one or more whole chromosomes. Excess, absence, arrangement — three words, and each one is a different way to be wrong.

A carrier is a heterozygous individual who carries one copy of a recessive disorder allele but is phenotypically unaffected — and who can transmit the allele. Read that definition as two clauses, because examiners test the second one: unaffected, yet transmitting.

And non-disjunction is the failure of a chromosome pair to separate during meiosis, producing gametes with an abnormal chromosome number. One term, and it is the cause of every chromosomal disorder in your syllabus.
This section is the counting language. Get it exact, because a karyotype question is answered entirely by reading two numbers correctly.

Aneuploidy is the gain or loss of one or a few chromosomes — two n plus one, or two n minus one — caused by non-disjunction. Note the scale: one or a few. Whole extra sets are a different word, and that word belongs to the next part.
Three columns, three counts. Normal, one extra, one missing. That is the entire vocabulary of aneuploidy, in pictures.

Trisomy means one extra chromosome, two n plus one — three copies of one particular chromosome instead of two. Monosomy means one missing chromosome, two n minus one. Tri for three copies, mono for one copy left.

A karyotype is the complete set of an individual's chromosomes, described by number and sex chromosomes. It is written as a count, then the sex chromosomes — like forty seven comma X X Y, or forty five comma X O.

And one more term that belongs with the Mendelian half: consanguineous mating, meaning mating between close relatives, which raises the chance that both partners carry the same recessive allele. In a pedigree it is drawn as a double line — that is a deliberate flag.

A housekeeping point examiners like to test sideways: there are no S I units anywhere in this subtopic. The quantities are chromosome counts, which are whole numbers, and probabilities, which are pure fractions. Nothing to dimension-check.

And the habit to build: read a karyotype as two pieces. First the total count — is it forty six, forty seven, or forty five? Then the sex chromosomes — X X, X Y, X X Y, X O? Both pieces carry information, and most questions hand you both and expect you to use both.
ये high difficulty लिखा है, और जैसे ही आप इसे genetics problem मानना छोड़कर number line मानने लगें, ये पाँच सेकंड का हो जाता है।
तीन linked genes के map distances हैं: A to B पाँच centiMorgan, B to C तेरह centiMorgan, A to C आठ centiMorgan। Genes का linear order बताइए।
तीनों boxes देखिए। उनमें से एक highlight है, और वही पूरा solution है — बाक़ी सब हिसाब-किताब है।
Step one, सबसे बड़ा distance। B to C, तेरह centiMorgan पर, तीनों में सबसे बड़ा है। तो B और C ही सबसे बाहरी genes हैं — line के दोनों सिरे।
Step two, बीच वाला gene। उस सबसे बड़े pair में जो gene नहीं है, वो A है। जिस line के दोनों सिरे तय हो चुके हों, उसमें एक ही जगह बचती है, तो A बीच में है। कोई calculation नहीं।

Step three, additivity check, और यहीं board का mark छुपा है। A to B plus A to C बराबर पाँच plus आठ, यानी तेरह, जो B to C के बराबर है। दोनों छोटे segments जुड़कर बड़ा बनाते हैं, तो arrangement consistent है।
Order है B, फिर A, फिर C — A बीच में। इसे line की तरह लिखिए, वाक्य की तरह नहीं — examiners arrangement देखना चाहते हैं।

और classic trap: ये मान लेना कि पहले लिखा गया pair, A और B, सिरे तय करता है, सिर्फ़ इसलिए कि वो पहले लिखा था। Order सबसे बड़े distance से तय होता है, listing के order से कभी नहीं। Question A to B पहले लिखता ही इसलिए है कि आप फिसलें।
चार pitfalls, और हर एक के लिए एक मिलता-जुलता ग़लत option question paper में पहले से छपा है। इन्हें checklist की तरह चलाइए।
Pitfall one: linkage groups बराबर haploid number n, diploid two n नहीं। Two n बराबर चौबीस के लिए जवाब बारह है, चौबीस नहीं। यही इस subtopic की सबसे आम चूक है, और ये सिर्फ़ एक division है।

Pitfall two: ये मान लेना कि बच्चे का sex mother तय करती है, या ये कि father हमेशा तय करता है। दोनों ग़लत। तय heterogametic parent करता है — humans में father, जो X Y है, पर birds में mother, जो Z W है।
तस्वीर चारों को साथ रखती है। ध्यान दीजिए इनकी shape एक है: हर बार एक जानी-पहचानी बात को वहाँ तक खींच दिया गया है जहाँ वो सच नहीं रहती।

Pitfall three: X X to X O को X X to X Y समझ लेना। X X to X O में Y chromosome है ही नहीं — male के पास बस एक अकेला, बिना जोड़ी वाला X है। Grasshopper males X O हैं, X Y नहीं, और वो O एक अनुपस्थिति है, कोई letter नहीं।

Pitfall four: पचास percent वाली recombination ceiling भूल जाना। Recombination frequency पचास percent से ज़्यादा हो ही नहीं सकती, और पचास percent दिखाने वाले genes असरदार तौर पर unlinked हैं — method की range ख़त्म हो चुकी है।
और इससे किसी भी mapping question में एक मुफ़्त elimination मिल जाता है। साठ percent recombination वाला option हमेशा ग़लत है। उसे काटने के लिए कुछ गिनना ही नहीं पड़ता।
और चारों के नीचे की आदत: जवाब देने से पहले system पढ़िए। कौन सा organism, कौन सा sex-determination system, diploid या haploid number — question ये बताता है, और ये बताना सजावट नहीं है।
इस subtopic को shortcuts के साथ बंद कीजिए, क्योंकि यहाँ सब कुछ तेज़ है — बस पता होना चाहिए कौन सा tool उठाना है।
पहला, three-point gene ordering। कुछ भी Punnett मत कीजिए — students तीन genes देखकर grids बनाने लगते हैं। बस तीनों pairwise distances में से सबसे बड़ा पहचानिए।
वो दोनों genes सिरे हैं। तीसरा gene बीच में बैठता है। और दोनों छोटे distances जुड़कर बड़े के बराबर होने चाहिए। तीन वाक्य, और problem ख़त्म।
ये सच में उस problem को, जो पूरा पन्ना माँगती लगती है, पाँच सेकंड के check में बदल देता है। जिस paper में समय ही सबसे बड़ी अड़चन है, वहाँ ये mark से भी ज़्यादा क़ीमती है।

पर condition साथ रखिए, क्योंकि shortcut का ईमानदार version उसकी range भी बताता है। ये additivity साफ़-साफ़ सिर्फ़ छोटे distances पर चलती है, क्योंकि double crossovers बड़ी R F values को असली distance से कम दिखा देते हैं।
तीन memory aids, और ये जानबूझ कर छोटे हैं। Linkage groups haploid पर चलते हैं — n लगाइए। Birds rule तोड़ते हैं, वहाँ mother तय करती है। और सबसे बड़ा distance बराबर दोनों सिरे।

तीन facts एक set की तरह आगे ले जाइए: R F distance के proportional है; एक centiMorgan बराबर एक percent recombination; और ceiling पचास percent। यहाँ का लगभग हर numerical इन्हीं तीन में से एक है, बस सही दिशा में पढ़ा हुआ।

और देखिए ये subtopic आपको कहाँ छोड़ता है। अब हम जानते हैं कि genes chromosomes पर बैठते हैं, कि वो linked हो सकते हैं, और कि कुछ X पर होते हैं। आगे हम पूछेंगे कि जब उनमें से कोई एक gene, या पूरा chromosome, ग़लत हो जाए तो क्या होता है — यही है genetic disorders।

<curious>एक ऐसे सवाल से शुरू करते हैं जो शायद आपके मन में आया हो, बिना genetics की भाषा में। कोई बीमारी एक परिवार में पीढ़ियों तक क्यों चलती है, cousins और दादा-दादी तक, जबकि दूसरी कहीं से भी एक ऐसे बच्चे में आ जाती है जिसके माँ-बाप बिलकुल स्वस्थ हैं?
ये दो अलग पहेलियाँ नहीं हैं। ये एक सवाल है जिसका एक जवाब है, और वो जवाब structural है।
जवाब इसमें है कि problem genome में कहाँ बैठी है। और यही एक बात genetic disorders को दो बड़े परिवारों में बाँट देती है — इसीलिए ये subtopic इसी तरह सजा है।
बँटवारा देखिए। एक शाख़ पर faulty gene। दूसरी पर faulty chromosome count। इस subtopic का बाक़ी सब कुछ इसी दोराहे से लटका है।

पहला परिवार: Mendelian disorders, जो किसी एक gene में बदलाव — यानी mutation — से होते हैं। और चूँकि एक अकेला gene Mendel के rules मानता है, ये disorders predictable ratios में inherit होते हैं, बिलकुल वैसे जैसे pea में tall और dwarf। पिछले दो subtopics कोई चक्कर नहीं थे; वो toolkit थे।
दूसरा परिवार: chromosomal disorders, जो किसी एक faulty gene से नहीं, बल्कि पूरे chromosomes की ग़लत संख्या से होते हैं। एक शब्द की टाइपिंग ग़लती नहीं — पूरा पन्ना ग़ायब या दोगुना।

और scale का यही फ़र्क़ family history का फ़र्क़ बनाता है। Chromosomal disorders आमतौर पर नए सिरे से पैदा होते हैं, gamete बनने के दौरान हुई एक दुर्घटना से — इसलिए उनमें अक्सर कोई पुरानी family history होती ही नहीं।
तो organising idea पकड़ लीजिए। Problem कहाँ बैठी है, यही बाक़ी सब तय करता है: ratios निकाल सकते हैं या नहीं, रिश्तेदार affected हैं या नहीं, और examiner आपसे किस तरह का सवाल पूछ भी सकता है।
Mendelian disorders single-gene disorders हैं, इसलिए वो Mendel को हूबहू मानते हैं। पर एक पेच है जो पूरे subtopic की shape बनाता है: इनमें से ज़्यादातर recessive होते हैं।
Recessive मतलब affected होने के लिए दो faulty copies चाहिए। एक faulty copy काफ़ी नहीं — दूसरे chromosome की normal copy इतना काम कर देती है कि आप स्वस्थ रहें।

और इससे वो इंसान बनता है जिसके इर्द-गिर्द पूरा subtopic घूमता है: carrier। एक faulty copy, एक normal copy, heterozygous। ख़ुद स्वस्थ, और faulty allele आगे देने में पूरी तरह सक्षम। Unaffected, पर neutral नहीं।
अब देखिए दो carriers के बच्चे होने पर क्या होता है। चार boxes, और ये grid आप पहले देख चुके हैं — ये बस monohybrid cross है, medical नाम पहन कर।

और यही उस पहेली का जवाब है जिससे हमने शुरुआत की। दो दिखने में स्वस्थ माँ-बाप का बच्चा affected हो सकता है, क्योंकि दोनों silent carriers हैं, और बच्चे को faulty allele दोनों तरफ़ से मिल जाता है। कुछ कहीं से नहीं आया; वो परिवार में पहले से था, बस express नहीं हो रहा था।

Recessive disorder allele को ऐसे सोचिए जैसे संयुक्त परिवार के बही-खाते में छुपा कोई क़र्ज़। एक parent उसे चुपचाप carry करे तो कोई परेशानी नहीं — entry वहीं पड़ी रहती है, पूरी एक पीढ़ी तक, बिना ध्यान में आए।

पर जब दो carriers की शादी होती है, और किसी बच्चे को वो छुपी entry दोनों तरफ़ से मिल जाती है, तब क़र्ज़ वसूली पर आ जाता है। शब्द पर ध्यान दीजिए — मिल जाती है — ये हर बच्चे के लिए चार में से एक का मौक़ा है, पक्की बात नहीं।

और यही तस्वीर एक और बात साफ़ कर देती है। इसीलिए क़रीबी रिश्तेदारों की शादियाँ — consanguineous marriages — जोखिम बढ़ाती हैं। रिश्तेदारों के पूर्वज साझा होते हैं, इसलिए उनके एक ही बही-खाते में वही छुपा allele होने की संभावना ज़्यादा है।
दूसरा परिवार बिलकुल अलग तरीक़े से चलता है, और ये फ़र्क़ साफ़ कहने लायक़ है: यहाँ कुछ भी किसी carrier से inherit नहीं होता। ये एक दुर्घटना है, और एक ही बार होती है।
Chromosomal disorders पूरे chromosomes की ग़लत संख्या से होते हैं। और वो आमतौर पर नए सिरे से पैदा होते हैं, egg या sperm बनने के दौरान हुई एक दुर्घटना से।
उस दुर्घटना का नाम है: non-disjunction। Meiosis के दौरान chromosomes की एक जोड़ी अलग होने में नाकाम रहती है। उन्हें अलग-अलग cells में जाना चाहिए था। बजाय इसके वो साथ ही एक में चले जाते हैं।
देखिए इससे दोनों gametes का क्या होता है। बाईं तरफ़ की जोड़ी को follow कीजिए, और देखिए हर copy कहाँ पहुँचती है।

एक gamete के पास एक extra chromosome आ जाता है। दूसरे के पास एक कम रह जाता है। एक ही चूक से दोनों gametes असामान्य — और ध्यान दीजिए, कोई parent किसी चीज़ का carrier नहीं है। उनकी body cells बिलकुल normal हैं।
फिर normal gamete से fertilisation बाक़ी हिसाब कर देता है। ऐसा individual बनता है जिसके पास सैंतालीस chromosomes हैं, एक ज़्यादा, या पैंतालीस, एक कम — आम छियालीस की जगह।

और कौन सा chromosome था, यही तय करता है कि कौन सा syndrome होगा। Chromosome इक्कीस की एक extra copy देती है Down syndrome। Male में एक extra X देता है Klinefelter। Female में एक ग़ायब X देता है Turner। एक ही mechanism, तीन नतीजे।

और इससे family-history वाला फ़र्क़ पूरी तरह समझ आ जाता है। ग़लती एक अकेले egg या sperm में होती है, family के बही-खाते में नहीं चलती — इसलिए ये disorders अक्सर बिना किसी पुरानी family history के दिखते हैं।

एक और बात, और ये सीधे पूछी जाती है। Eggs की उम्र बढ़ने के साथ ये दुर्घटना ज़्यादा संभव हो जाती है, इसीलिए Down syndrome जैसे non-disjunction disorder का ख़तरा माँ की उम्र के साथ बढ़ता है। उनके eggs दशकों से meiosis के बीच में रुके हुए हैं, और chromosomes को अलग करने वाली machinery उतने समय में कम भरोसेमंद हो जाती है।
Disorders से पहले एक methodological समस्या हल करनी है — और ये असली है, कोई औपचारिकता नहीं।
सोचिए Mendel के पास असल में क्या था। उन्होंने parents जानबूझ कर चुने। हज़ारों offspring बनाए। हर मौसम में नई generation मिली। तो वो cross लगा कर आगे की भविष्यवाणी कर सकते थे।

Human families में से आपको इनमें कुछ नहीं मिलता। आप controlled crosses लगा नहीं सकते — ज़ाहिर है, और ठीक ही है। परिवारों में बहुत कम बच्चे होते हैं, तो sample बहुत छोटा। और generation times दशकों में हैं, मौसमों में नहीं।
दोनों columns देखिए। जो कुछ pea को आसान बनाता था, वो दाईं तरफ़ ग़ायब है। तो method को उल्टा करना पड़ता है।
इसलिए geneticists उल्टा चलते हैं। Parents चुनकर बच्चों की भविष्यवाणी करने की जगह, आप मौजूद बच्चों से ये निकालते हैं कि parents ने क्या carry किया होगा। इसी उलटाव को pedigree analysis कहते हैं।

औपचारिक तौर पर: pedigree analysis किसी trait की inheritance का अध्ययन है, कई पीढ़ियों में, एक standardised family-tree diagram की मदद से। Standardised मायने रखता है — symbols तय हैं, तो कोई भी geneticist वही chart वैसे ही पढ़ता है।
Procedure बिलकुल वैसा ही है जैसा सुनने में लगता है। आप पीढ़ियों में पढ़ते हैं कि कौन affected है — कौन भरा हुआ है, कौन नहीं, कौन सा sex — और फिर वो rules निकालते हैं जो इस pattern को बना सकते थे।
और उस deduction के दो हिस्से हैं, हमेशा वही दो। Trait dominant है या recessive? और autosomal है या X-linked? इन दोनों का जवाब मिल गया, तो pedigree ने आपको सब बता दिया जो वो बता सकता था।
चार definitions, और ये सजावट नहीं हैं। इस subtopic का हर सवाल असल में यही कहता है कि किसी चीज़ को इन्हीं डिब्बों में से एक में डालिए।

Genetic disorder वो बीमारी है जो genome में एक या ज़्यादा असामान्यताओं से होती है। और definition के अंदर ही दोराहा है: या तो single-gene mutation, जो Mendelian है, या chromosome की संख्या या structure में असामान्यता, जो chromosomal है।

Mendelian disorder किसी एक gene में बदलाव या mutation से होता है, और Mendelian ratios में inherit होता है। एक gene, Mendel के rules। अगर आप Punnett square से probability निकाल सकते हैं, तो आप इसी परिवार में हैं।
यहाँ सब साथ रखे हैं। नीचे की पट्टी देखिए — Mendelian डिब्बा दोबारा बँटता है, और उसी दूसरे बँटवारे में ज़्यादातर exam questions रहते हैं।

वो दूसरा बँटवारा: Mendelian disorder autosomal हो सकता है, यानी gene किसी non-sex chromosome पर है, या sex-linked, यानी gene किसी sex chromosome पर है। Single-gene logic वही, पर sex-linked वाले उसी criss-cross pattern में चलते हैं जो आप जानते हैं।
Chromosomal disorder एक या ज़्यादा पूरे chromosomes की अधिकता, अनुपस्थिति, या असामान्य arrangement से होता है। अधिकता, अनुपस्थिति, arrangement — तीन शब्द, और हर एक ग़लत होने का अलग तरीक़ा।

Carrier वो heterozygous individual है जो recessive disorder allele की एक copy carry करता है पर phenotypically unaffected है — और उस allele को आगे दे सकता है। इस definition को दो हिस्सों में पढ़िए, क्योंकि examiners दूसरा हिस्सा पूछते हैं: unaffected, फिर भी transmit करने वाला।

और non-disjunction मतलब meiosis में chromosome की जोड़ी का अलग होने में नाकाम रहना, जिससे असामान्य chromosome number वाले gametes बनते हैं। एक term, और आपके syllabus के हर chromosomal disorder की वजह यही है।
ये section गिनती की भाषा है। इसे बिलकुल सही रखिए, क्योंकि karyotype वाला सवाल पूरी तरह दो numbers सही पढ़ने से हल हो जाता है।

Aneuploidy मतलब एक या कुछ chromosomes का बढ़ना या घटना — two n plus one, या two n minus one — जिसकी वजह non-disjunction है। Scale पर ध्यान दीजिए: एक या कुछ। पूरे extra sets के लिए अलग शब्द है, और वो शब्द अगले part का है।
तीन columns, तीन counts। Normal, एक ज़्यादा, एक कम। Aneuploidy की पूरी vocabulary यही है, तस्वीरों में।
Trisomy मतलब एक extra chromosome, two n plus one — किसी एक ख़ास chromosome की दो की जगह तीन copies। Monosomy मतलब एक ग़ायब chromosome, two n minus one। Tri यानी तीन copies, mono यानी एक ही बची।

Karyotype किसी individual के chromosomes का पूरा set है, जो संख्या और sex chromosomes से बताया जाता है। इसे count, फिर sex chromosomes की तरह लिखते हैं — जैसे सैंतालीस comma X X Y, या पैंतालीस comma X O।

और एक term जो Mendelian आधे के साथ जाती है: consanguineous mating, यानी क़रीबी रिश्तेदारों के बीच विवाह, जो इस संभावना को बढ़ाता है कि दोनों साथी वही recessive allele carry करें। Pedigree में इसे double line से खींचते हैं — ये जानबूझ कर लगाया गया संकेत है।

एक छोटी बात जो examiners घुमा कर पूछते हैं: इस पूरे subtopic में कोई S I units हैं ही नहीं। Quantities हैं chromosome counts, जो पूर्ण संख्याएँ हैं, और probabilities, जो शुद्ध भिन्न हैं। Dimension check का सवाल ही नहीं।

और जो आदत बनानी है: karyotype को दो हिस्सों में पढ़िए। पहले कुल count — छियालीस, सैंतालीस, या पैंतालीस? फिर sex chromosomes — X X, X Y, X X Y, X O? दोनों हिस्सों में information है, और ज़्यादातर सवाल दोनों देते हैं और दोनों का इस्तेमाल चाहते हैं।

board_events.text: Sickle-cell anaemia, P K U, thalassaemia

board_events.caption: The three autosomal recessive Mendelian disorders
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 540 280" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">
<text x="270" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">Autosomal recessive Mendelian disorders</text>
<rect x="18" y="36" width="504" height="30" fill="#e5e7eb"/>

<rect x="18" y="66" width="504" height="66" fill="#f9fafb"/>

<text x="30" y="108" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">anaemia</text>
<text x="190" y="86" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Point mutation in the beta-globin gene</text>
<text x="190" y="104" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Glutamic acid replaced by valine at the 6th position</text>
<text x="190" y="122" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">Red cells sickle under low oxygen</text>
<rect x="18" y="132" width="504" height="66" fill="#ffffff"/>
<text x="30" y="156" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#7c3aed">Phenylketonuria</text>
<text x="30" y="174" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#7c3aed">(P K U)</text>
<text x="190" y="152" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Lacks the enzyme converting phenylalanine to tyrosine</text>
<text x="190" y="170" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Phenylpyruvic acid accumulates</text>
<text x="190" y="188" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">Impairs cognitive development</text>
<rect x="18" y="198" width="504" height="56" fill="#f9fafb"/>
<text x="30" y="230" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">Thalassaemia</text>
<text x="190" y="218" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Reduced synthesis of alpha- or beta-globin chains</text>
<text x="190" y="240" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">A quantitative defect: too little normal globin</text>
<rect x="18" y="36" width="504" height="218" fill="none" stroke="#9ca3af"/>
<line x1="180" y1="36" x2="180" y2="254" stroke="#9ca3af"/>

</svg>

board_events.text: Sickle-cell anaemia: a point mutation in the beta-globin gene; glutamic acid becomes valine at the 6th position; red cells sickle under low oxygen.
Phenylketonuria (PKU): lack of the enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine; phenylpyruvic acid accumulates, impairing cognitive development.
Thalassaemia: reduced synthesis of alpha- or beta-globin chains — a quantitative defect, meaning too little normal globin.
All three are autosomal: the gene is on a non-sex chromosome, so males and females are affected roughly equally.
All three are recessive: two faulty copies are needed, so carriers are healthy and common.
Memorising which bucket each disorder falls into is worth more marks than any mechanism. Examiners test exactly this.
Haemophilia and colour blindness

board_events.caption: The X-linked recessive pair, and who gets affected
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 540 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">
<text x="270" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">X-linked recessive Mendelian disorders</text>
<rect x="18" y="36" width="504" height="30" fill="#e5e7eb"/>
<text x="30" y="56" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">Disorder</text>
<text x="200" y="56" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">Defect</text>
<rect x="18" y="66" width="504" height="56" fill="#f9fafb"/>
<text x="30" y="98" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">Haemophilia</text>
<text x="200" y="88" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">A blood-clotting protein is non-functional</text>
<text x="200" y="110" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">Minor cuts bleed for a long time</text>
<rect x="18" y="122" width="504" height="56" fill="#ffffff"/>
<text x="30" y="146" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">Colour blindness</text>
<text x="30" y="164" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">(red-green)</text>
<text x="200" y="144" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Defect in the red and green cones</text>
<text x="200" y="166" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">Cannot distinguish red from green</text>
<rect x="18" y="36" width="504" height="142" fill="none" stroke="#9ca3af"/>
<line x1="190" y1="36" x2="190" y2="178" stroke="#9ca3af"/>
<rect x="18" y="192" width="248" height="56" rx="8" fill="#eff6ff" stroke="#2563eb"/>
<text x="142" y="214" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">Affected son</text>
<text x="142" y="236" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">needs only a carrier mother</text>
<rect x="274" y="192" width="248" height="56" rx="8" fill="#fef2f2" stroke="#dc2626"/>
<text x="398" y="214" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">Affected daughter</text>
<text x="398" y="236" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">needs an AFFECTED father</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Haemophilia: a blood-clotting protein is non-functional, so minor cuts bleed for a long time. X-linked recessive.
Colour blindness (red-green): a defect in the red and green cones, so the affected person cannot distinguish red from green. X-linked recessive.
Both genes lie on the X chromosome, so the criss-cross pattern from the last subtopic applies directly.
An affected son needs only a carrier mother — he is hemizygous, with one X and nothing to mask it.
An affected daughter requires an AFFECTED father, because she needs a faulty X from both parents.
This is why males are affected far more often than females for both disorders.
The three chromosomal disorders

board_events.caption: Karyotype, sex, and key features

<text x="270" y="172" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">male</text>
<text x="330" y="158" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Overall masculine, with some feminine</text>
<text x="330" y="176" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">development (gynaecomastia)</text>

<rect x="18" y="200" width="504" height="64" fill="#fdf2f8"/>

<text x="150" y="228" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">45, XO</text><text x="150" y="244" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">monosomy X</text>
<text x="270" y="236" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#db2777">female</text>
<text x="330" y="222" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Short stature, rudimentary ovaries</text>
<text x="330" y="240" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Sterile; lack of secondary sexual characters</text>
<rect x="18" y="36" width="504" height="228" fill="none" stroke="#9ca3af"/>
<line x1="140" y1="36" x2="140" y2="264" stroke="#9ca3af"/><line x1="260" y1="36" x2="260" y2="264" stroke="#9ca3af"/><line x1="320" y1="36" x2="320" y2="264" stroke="#9ca3af"/>
<text x="270" y="284" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">Extra X in a male = Klinefelter. Missing X in a female = Turner.</text>

board_events.text: Down syndrome: 47 chromosomes, trisomy of chromosome 21. Either sex.
Features: characteristic facial features, short stature, impaired cognitive development. Risk rises with maternal age.
Klinefelter syndrome: 47, XXY — an extra X. Always male.
Features: overall masculine but with some feminine development (gynaecomastia); sterile.
Turner syndrome: 45, XO — monosomy of X. Always female.
Features: short stature, rudimentary ovaries, sterile; lack of secondary sexual characters.
Extra X in a male gives Klinefelter. Missing X in a female gives Turner. Lock that pairing in.
Procedure A: symbols first, then two questions
Standard symbols: a square is male, a circle is female. A filled symbol is affected, an open symbol unaffected.
A horizontal line joins a mating pair; a double horizontal line marks a consanguineous mating; a vertical line drops to the offspring.

board_events.caption: The symbols, and the two classification questions
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 540 290" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">
<text x="270" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">Reading a pedigree: symbols first, then two questions</text>
<rect x="18" y="34" width="504" height="72" rx="8" fill="#f3f4f6" stroke="#9ca3af"/>
<rect x="40" y="52" width="24" height="24" fill="none" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="52" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">male</text>

<rect x="196" y="52" width="24" height="24" fill="#1f2937"/><text x="208" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">affected</text>

<rect x="18" y="118" width="248" height="126" rx="8" fill="#f5f3ff" stroke="#c4b5fd"/>
<text x="142" y="140" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#7c3aed">Q1: dominant or recessive?</text>
<text x="30" y="164" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Two AFFECTED parents give an</text>
<text x="30" y="180" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">unaffected child</text>
<text x="30" y="198" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#7c3aed">→ trait is DOMINANT</text>
<text x="30" y="220" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Two UNAFFECTED parents give an</text>
<text x="30" y="236" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">affected child → RECESSIVE</text>
<rect x="274" y="118" width="248" height="126" rx="8" fill="#ecfdf5" stroke="#86efac"/>
<text x="398" y="140" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">Q2: autosomal or X-linked?</text>
<text x="286" y="164" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Affected roughly equal across sexes</text>
<text x="286" y="182" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">→ suspect AUTOSOMAL</text>
<text x="286" y="206" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Overwhelmingly male, skipping via</text>
<text x="286" y="222" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">a carrier daughter</text>
<text x="286" y="238" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">→ X-LINKED RECESSIVE</text>
<text x="270" y="272" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#6b7280">An affected child from unaffected parents means both parents hid the allele</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Question 1 — dominant or recessive? If two AFFECTED parents ever produce an unaffected child, the trait is dominant.
If two UNAFFECTED parents produce an affected child, the trait is recessive.
Why: an affected child from unaffected parents means both parents hid the allele — only possible if the disorder allele is recessive.
Question 2 — autosomal or X-linked? If affected individuals are roughly equal across the sexes, suspect autosomal.
If affected individuals are overwhelmingly male, and the trait skips from an affected grandfather through an unaffected carrier daughter to a grandson, suspect X-linked recessive.
Procedure B: it is a monohybrid cross
For two carriers, Aa × Aa, where a is the recessive disorder allele:

board_events.caption: The carrier × carrier cross, read three ways
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 480 290" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">
<text x="240" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">Two carriers: Aa × Aa</text>
<text x="240" y="46" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#6b7280">It is just a monohybrid cross wearing a medical name</text>
<text x="190" y="76" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">A</text>
<text x="290" y="76" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">a</text>
<text x="118" y="126" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">A</text>
<text x="118" y="206" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">a</text>
<rect x="140" y="86" width="100" height="70" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#1f2937"/><text x="190" y="122" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" fill="#1f2937">AA</text><text x="190" y="142" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#16a34a">normal</text>
<rect x="240" y="86" width="100" height="70" fill="#fff7ed" stroke="#1f2937"/><text x="290" y="122" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" fill="#1f2937">Aa</text><text x="290" y="142" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#b45309">carrier</text>
<rect x="140" y="156" width="100" height="70" fill="#fff7ed" stroke="#1f2937"/><text x="190" y="192" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" fill="#1f2937">Aa</text><text x="190" y="212" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#b45309">carrier</text>
<rect x="240" y="156" width="100" height="70" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#1f2937"/><text x="290" y="192" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" fill="#1f2937">aa</text><text x="290" y="212" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">affected</text>
<text x="240" y="252" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#1f2937">1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa</text>
<text x="240" y="278" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">1/4 affected · 1/2 carrier · 1/4 normal</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: The genotype ratio is 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa.
So 1/4 of children are affected (aa), 1/2 are unaffected carriers (Aa), and 1/4 are unaffected non-carriers (AA).
Why: this is just a monohybrid cross — the disorder allele follows Mendel's law of segregation exactly.
1/4 is the AFFECTED risk. 1/2 is the CARRIER risk. 3/4 is the chance of being unaffected. Read which one is asked.
The same three numbers answer sickle-cell, P K U and thalassaemia questions alike, because all three sit in the same bucket.
Procedure C: track only the X
Track only the X chromosomes, because the Y carries no allele for these genes.
A son's phenotype is decided entirely by the single X he receives from his mother.

board_events.caption: The two crosses that matter

<rect x="18" y="34" width="248" height="212" rx="8" fill="#eff6ff" stroke="#2563eb"/>

<rect x="274" y="34" width="248" height="212" rx="8" fill="#fef2f2" stroke="#dc2626"/>
<text x="398" y="56" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">Affected father × carrier mother</text>
<text x="366" y="82" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">X<tspan font-size="9" dy="-4">a</tspan><tspan dy="4">Y × X</tspan><tspan font-size="9" dy="-4">A</tspan><tspan dy="4">X</tspan><tspan font-size="9" dy="-4">a</tspan></text>
<rect x="296" y="96" width="94" height="60" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#1f2937"/>
<text x="343" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">Sons</text>
<text x="343" y="140" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">1/2 affected</text>
<rect x="406" y="96" width="98" height="60" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#1f2937"/>
<text x="455" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">Daughters</text>
<text x="455" y="140" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">1/2 affected</text>
<text x="398" y="180" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Daughters now receive the father’s</text>
<text x="398" y="196" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">affected X, so they CAN be affected</text>
<text x="398" y="222" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">The only common route to an</text>
<text x="398" y="238" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">affected daughter</text>
<text x="270" y="274" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#6b7280">A daughter needs a faulty X from BOTH parents, which requires an affected father</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Carrier mother ($X^AX^a$) × normal father ($X^AY$): sons are 1/2 affected and 1/2 normal.
All daughters are unaffected — they always receive the father's normal $X^A$ — and half of them are carriers.
Affected father ($X^aY$) × carrier mother ($X^AX^a$): now daughters CAN be affected ($X^aX^a$), because they receive the father's $X^a$.
This is the only common route to an affected daughter.
Why daughters are usually spared: a daughter needs two faulty X copies, so she needs a faulty X from both parents — which requires an affected father.
Procedure D: four steps from accident to syndrome
Step 1: during meiosis in one parent, a chromosome pair — or the sex chromosomes — fails to separate.
Step 2: one resulting gamete carries an extra chromosome; another is missing one.

board_events.text: Step 3: after fertilisation with a normal gamete, the zygote is trisomic ($2n+1$) or monosomic ($2n-1$).
Step 4: name it by which chromosome was involved.
Trisomy 21 gives Down syndrome. An extra X in a male (XXY) gives Klinefelter. A missing X in a female (XO) gives Turner.
These are not inherited from a carrier parent. They are accidents of meiosis, in one gamete.
One base, one amino acid, one disease
A single base change in the beta-globin gene: the 6th codon changes from GAG to GUG.
That swaps one amino acid — glutamic acid becomes valine — at the 6th position of the beta-globin chain.

board_events.text: That one substitution makes haemoglobin (now called HbS) clump when oxygen is low, deforming red cells into a sickle shape.
Genotypes: $Hb^AHb^A$ = normal; $Hb^AHb^S$ = unaffected carrier (sickle-cell trait); $Hb^SHb^S$ = affected.
Notably, carriers have some resistance to malaria.
A classic example of why a harmful allele persists in malaria-endemic populations.
And because only a single base pair changes, this is a point mutation — not a frameshift. That distinction returns in the next part.
Bad haemoglobin versus too little haemoglobin
Both are autosomal recessive blood disorders involving globin. But the defect is fundamentally different in KIND.

board_events.text: In sickle-cell anaemia the defect is QUALITATIVE: a normal amount of globin is made, but it is the wrong globin.
A single amino-acid substitution gives the abnormal HbS.
In thalassaemia the defect is QUANTITATIVE: the globin made is structurally normal, but too little of it is produced.
The rate of synthesis of the alpha-chain (alpha-thalassaemia) or the beta-chain (beta-thalassaemia) is reduced.
Put simply: sickle-cell makes BAD haemoglobin; thalassaemia makes TOO LITTLE haemoglobin.
This single distinction is the most commonly tested contrast in the whole subtopic.
Three honest edges
Condition 1: the clean Mendelian ratios — such as a one-in-four risk — are probabilities PER CHILD, not guarantees.
A carrier couple can have four affected children in a row, or none at all. Each conception is independent.
