<text x="139" y="84" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Arises naturally, with no</text>
<text x="139" y="100" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">external agent</text>
<text x="139" y="126" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">a copying error during</text>
<text x="139" y="142" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">DNA replication</text>
<rect x="286" y="38" width="230" height="120" rx="8" fill="#fef2f2" stroke="#dc2626"/>
<text x="401" y="60" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">Induced</text>
<text x="401" y="84" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Caused by an external agent</text>
<text x="401" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">called a MUTAGEN</text>
<text x="401" y="132" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">Mutant: the organism or cell</text>
<text x="401" y="148" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">carrying the mutation</text>
<rect x="24" y="172" width="230" height="76" rx="8" fill="#eff6ff" stroke="#2563eb"/>
<text x="139" y="194" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">Physical mutagens</text>
<text x="139" y="216" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">U V rays</text>
<text x="139" y="236" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">X-rays · gamma rays</text>
<rect x="286" y="172" width="230" height="76" rx="8" fill="#f5f3ff" stroke="#7c3aed"/>
<text x="401" y="194" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#7c3aed">Chemical mutagens</text>
<text x="401" y="216" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">mustard gas</text>
<text x="401" y="238" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">many mutagens are also carcinogens</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Induced mutation: caused by an external agent, called a mutagen.
Mutagen: any physical or chemical agent that induces mutation.
Physical mutagens: UV rays, X-rays, gamma rays.
Chemical mutagens: mustard gas is the standard example.
Many mutagens are also carcinogens — agents that cause cancer. That link is examinable, and it is not a coincidence.
Mutant: the organism or cell that carries the mutation. The mutation is the change; the mutant is the carrier.
One base pair changes
Point mutation: a change in a single base pair of DNA. Also called a substitution — one base is swapped for another.

board_events.caption: Substitution, and its two sub-types
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 540 280" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">
<defs><marker id="pt1" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 z" fill="#6b7280"/></marker></defs>
<text x="270" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">Point mutation: one base pair changes</text>
<text x="270" y="46" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#6b7280">Also called a substitution. The reading frame is untouched.</text>
<rect x="70" y="60" width="150" height="40" rx="6" fill="#ecfdf5" stroke="#16a34a"/>
<text x="145" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-family="monospace" fill="#1f2937">G A G</text>
<line x1="228" y1="80" x2="264" y2="80" stroke="#6b7280" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#pt1)"/>
<rect x="272" y="60" width="150" height="40" rx="6" fill="#fef2f2" stroke="#dc2626"/>
<text x="347" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-family="monospace" fill="#1f2937">G <tspan fill="#dc2626" font-weight="bold">U</tspan> G</text>
<text x="440" y="86" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">sickle-cell</text>
<text x="145" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#16a34a">glutamic acid</text>
<text x="347" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">valine</text>
<rect x="24" y="136" width="230" height="106" rx="8" fill="#eff6ff" stroke="#2563eb"/>
<text x="139" y="158" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">Transition</text>
<text x="139" y="182" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">purine ↔ purine</text>
<text x="139" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">or pyrimidine ↔ pyrimidine</text>
<text x="139" y="224" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#2563eb">A to G, or C to T</text>
<rect x="286" y="136" width="230" height="106" rx="8" fill="#f5f3ff" stroke="#7c3aed"/>
<text x="401" y="158" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#7c3aed">Transversion</text>
<text x="401" y="182" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">purine ↔ pyrimidine</text>
<text x="401" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">the class itself changes</text>
<text x="401" y="224" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#7c3aed">A to C, or G to T</text>
<text x="270" y="268" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">Only ONE codon is affected. Every codon after it is read normally.</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: The reading frame is untouched, because nothing was added or removed. Only ONE codon is affected.
Substitutions come in two sub-types, defined by the CLASS of base involved.
Transition: a purine is replaced by a purine, or a pyrimidine by a pyrimidine — for example A to G, or C to T. The class stays the same.
Transversion: a purine is replaced by a pyrimidine, or vice versa — for example A to C, or G to T. The class itself changes.
Sickle-cell anaemia is the standard example: GAG becomes GUG, so glutamic acid becomes valine at the 6th position of beta-globin.
Insert or delete, and the frame slips
Frameshift mutation: an insertion or deletion of bases that shifts the reading frame.

board_events.caption: One base gone, and every later codon is re-cut
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 540 280" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">
<text x="270" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">Frameshift: insert or delete, and the frame slips</text>
<text x="40" y="52" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">Original</text>

<rect x="224" y="38" width="46" height="24" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#16a34a"/><text x="247" y="55" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-family="monospace" fill="#1f2937">GAA</text>
<rect x="276" y="38" width="46" height="24" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#16a34a"/><text x="299" y="55" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-family="monospace" fill="#1f2937">UCA</text>

<rect x="172" y="84" width="46" height="24" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#dc2626"/><text x="195" y="101" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-family="monospace" fill="#1f2937">CUG</text>
<rect x="224" y="84" width="46" height="24" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#dc2626"/><text x="247" y="101" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-family="monospace" fill="#1f2937">AAU</text>
<rect x="276" y="84" width="46" height="24" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#dc2626"/><text x="299" y="101" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-family="monospace" fill="#1f2937">CA?</text>
<text x="360" y="101" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">everything downstream is wrong</text>
<text x="270" y="132" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">One base gone, and every codon after it is re-cut in the wrong place</text>
<rect x="24" y="148" width="230" height="94" rx="8" fill="#fef2f2" stroke="#dc2626"/>
<text x="139" y="170" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">NOT a multiple of 3</text>
<text x="139" y="194" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">1, 2, 4, 5 bases added</text>
<text x="139" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">or removed</text>
<text x="139" y="232" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">FRAMESHIFT occurs</text>
<rect x="286" y="148" width="230" height="94" rx="8" fill="#ecfdf5" stroke="#16a34a"/>
<text x="401" y="170" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">A multiple of 3</text>
<text x="401" y="194" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">3, 6, 9 bases added</text>
<text x="401" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">or removed</text>
<text x="401" y="232" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">NO frameshift</text>
<text x="270" y="268" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#7c3aed">A multiple of three removes whole codons and leaves the frame intact</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Because the reader counts in threes from a fixed start, removing or adding a base re-cuts every codon downstream.
So the damage is not local. Every codon after the mutation is read in the wrong place, and the protein is usually destroyed.
But there is a crucial exception, and it is the most tested fact here.
If the number of bases inserted or deleted is a MULTIPLE OF 3, there is NO frameshift — whole codons are added or removed, and the frame stays intact.
So 1, 2, 4 or 5 bases shift the frame. But 3, 6 or 9 bases do not.
Four ways to rearrange a chromosome
Chromosomal mutations happen at a much larger scale — whole segments, or whole chromosomes.

board_events.text: Deletion: a segment of the chromosome is lost.
Duplication: a segment is repeated, so those genes are present in extra copies.
Inversion: a segment breaks out, flips end to end, and rejoins — the genes are all still there, in reverse order.
Translocation: a segment moves to a NON-homologous chromosome — a different chromosome altogether.
Translocations are common in cancer cells. The gene count may be unchanged; what altered is the ARRANGEMENT.
A few chromosomes, or whole sets?
Numerical changes split by scale, and this split is worth memorising exactly.

board_events.caption: Aneuploidy versus polyploidy
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 540 270" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">
<defs><marker id="nm1" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 z" fill="#6b7280"/></marker></defs>
<text x="270" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">Numerical mutations: a few, or whole sets?</text>
<rect x="200" y="36" width="140" height="30" rx="8" fill="#e5e7eb" stroke="#6b7280"/>
<text x="270" y="56" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">Numerical change</text>
<line x1="236" y1="66" x2="150" y2="92" stroke="#6b7280" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#nm1)"/>
<line x1="304" y1="66" x2="390" y2="92" stroke="#6b7280" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#nm1)"/>
<rect x="24" y="98" width="230" height="132" rx="8" fill="#f5f3ff" stroke="#c4b5fd"/>
<text x="139" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#7c3aed">Aneuploidy</text>
<text x="139" y="142" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">A FEW chromosomes gained</text>
<text x="139" y="158" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">or lost</text>
<text x="139" y="182" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#7c3aed">2n + 1 or 2n − 1</text>
<text x="139" y="204" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">Cause: NON-DISJUNCTION</text>
<text x="139" y="222" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">trisomy 2n+1 · monosomy 2n−1</text>
<rect x="286" y="98" width="230" height="132" rx="8" fill="#ecfdf5" stroke="#86efac"/>
<text x="401" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">Polyploidy</text>
<text x="401" y="142" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">WHOLE extra sets of</text>
<text x="401" y="158" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">chromosomes</text>
<text x="401" y="182" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">3n, 4n and beyond</text>
<text x="401" y="204" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">Cause: FAILURE OF CYTOKINESIS</text>
<text x="401" y="222" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#16a34a">common and useful in plants</text>
<text x="270" y="256" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">A few chromosomes = aneuploidy. Whole sets = polyploidy.</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Aneuploidy: gain or loss of a FEW chromosomes — $2n+1$ or $2n-1$.
Its cause is non-disjunction, the failure of a chromosome pair to separate during meiosis. Trisomy is $2n+1$; monosomy is $2n-1$.
This is exactly the mechanism behind Down, Klinefelter and Turner syndromes from Part 3.
Polyploidy: the presence of WHOLE extra sets of chromosomes — 3n, 4n and beyond.
Its cause is different: failure of cytokinesis, so the duplicated chromosomes stay in one cell instead of being divided into two.
A few chromosomes means aneuploidy. Whole sets means polyploidy. Different scale, different cause.
Autopolyploidy and allopolyploidy
Autopolyploidy: the extra sets come from the SAME species — auto meaning self. One genome, multiplied.

board_events.caption: Same species, or different species
board_events.svg:

<rect x="24" y="38" width="230" height="150" rx="8" fill="#f5f3ff" stroke="#c4b5fd"/>
<text x="139" y="60" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#7c3aed">Autopolyploidy</text>
<text x="139" y="80" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">auto = self</text>
<rect x="80" y="94" width="10" height="30" rx="5" fill="#7c3aed"/>
<rect x="98" y="94" width="10" height="30" rx="5" fill="#7c3aed"/>
<rect x="116" y="94" width="10" height="30" rx="5" fill="#7c3aed"/>
<rect x="134" y="94" width="10" height="30" rx="5" fill="#7c3aed"/>
<text x="139" y="146" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Extra sets from the SAME</text>
<text x="139" y="162" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">species</text>
<text x="139" y="180" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#7c3aed">one genome, multiplied</text>
<rect x="286" y="38" width="230" height="150" rx="8" fill="#ecfdf5" stroke="#86efac"/>
<text x="401" y="60" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">Allopolyploidy</text>
<text x="401" y="80" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">allo = other</text>
<rect x="340" y="94" width="10" height="30" rx="5" fill="#16a34a"/>
<rect x="358" y="94" width="10" height="30" rx="5" fill="#16a34a"/>
<rect x="386" y="94" width="10" height="30" rx="5" fill="#f59e0b"/>
<rect x="404" y="94" width="10" height="30" rx="5" fill="#f59e0b"/>
<text x="401" y="146" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Sets from DIFFERENT species,</text>
<text x="401" y="162" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">combined after hybridisation</text>
<text x="401" y="180" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#16a34a">two genomes, joined</text>
<rect x="60" y="204" width="420" height="44" rx="8" fill="#fff7ed" stroke="#f59e0b"/>
<text x="270" y="224" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#b45309">Polyploidy is common in plants and often useful</text>
<text x="270" y="240" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">bigger fruits and grains — but it is usually lethal in animals</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Allopolyploidy: the sets come from DIFFERENT species, combined after hybridisation — allo meaning other. Two genomes, joined.
Polyploidy is common in plants, and often useful: it gives bigger fruits and grains, and many crop plants are polyploid.
But polyploidy is usually lethal in animals. This asymmetry between plants and animals is directly examinable.
Read the prefixes and the definitions follow: auto is self, allo is other.
Somatic versus germinal; forward versus reverse
The definition of mutation said 'inheritable'. But that needs a qualification, and it is the most important one in this subtopic.

board_events.caption: Where the mutation happened decides whether it is passed on
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 540 270" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">
<text x="270" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">Which mutations actually get inherited?</text>
<rect x="24" y="38" width="230" height="128" rx="8" fill="#fff7ed" stroke="#f59e0b"/>
<text x="139" y="60" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#b45309">Somatic mutation</text>
<text x="139" y="84" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Occurs in a BODY cell</text>

board_events.text: Somatic mutation: occurs in a body cell. It is NOT inherited — it dies with the individual.
Germinal mutation: occurs in a gamete-forming cell. It IS inherited — it enters the next generation.
So only germinal mutations matter for inheritance. Somatic mutations matter medically — cancer — but they are a different question.
Two more terms, defined by direction. Forward mutation: wild type becomes mutant — the usual direction.
Reverse, or back, mutation: mutant becomes wild type — the original sequence is restored.
Say them the way the marking scheme says them

board_events.text: Mutation: a sudden, stable and inheritable change in the DNA of an organism.
Mutant: an organism or cell carrying a mutation.

Aneuploidy: gain or loss of a few chromosomes. Polyploidy: presence of whole extra chromosome sets.

board_events.text: If bases: it is a GENE mutation. Then question 2 — how many bases?
One base swapped (nothing added or removed) → point mutation. Bases added or removed → frameshift, unless the number is a multiple of 3.
If chromosomes: it is a CHROMOSOMAL mutation. Then question 2 — shape, or number?
Shape changed → structural: deletion, duplication, inversion or translocation.
Number changed → numerical: a few chromosomes is aneuploidy; whole sets is polyploidy.
Scale first, then detail. Every classification question in this subtopic falls out of those two questions.
Procedure B: how much of the protein is destroyed?
Step 1: total codons = total bases ÷ 3. A 300-base mRNA has 100 codons.

board_events.text: Step 2: find which codon holds the mutated base. Base 31 sits in codon 11, since 31 = 3 × 10 + 1 — ten complete codons come before it.
Step 3: altered codons = total codons − the intact codons before the mutation.
So codons 1 to 10 are intact, and codons 11 to 100 are all altered: 100 − 10 = 90.
Only what came BEFORE the mutation survives. Everything after it is re-cut in the wrong place.
Notice how small the cause is and how large the effect: one missing base destroys ninety percent of the protein.

segments.text: Two causes, and the vocabulary around them is high-yield because it is short and definite.

A spontaneous mutation arises naturally, with no external agent at all. Typically it is a copying error during D N A replication — the polymerase is astonishingly accurate, but it is not perfect, and a genome is very long.
Here is the split, with the mutagens underneath. Note there are exactly two classes of mutagen, and each has a small fixed list.
An induced mutation is caused by an external agent, and that agent has a name: a mutagen.
The definition: a mutagen is any physical or chemical agent that induces mutation. Physical or chemical — that phrase is the classification, built into the definition.
Physical mutagens: U V rays, X-rays, and gamma rays. All radiation, and you can see the theme — energetic enough to damage the D N A molecule directly.
Chemical mutagens: mustard gas is the standard example, and it is the one to write if you are asked for one.

Now the connection that carries marks: many mutagens are also carcinogens — agents that cause cancer. And that is not a coincidence. An agent that damages D N A can produce a mutation in a body cell, and cancer is what happens when the wrong body cell mutates. The two lists overlap because they share a mechanism.
One last term, and students blur it constantly. The mutant is the organism or cell that carries the mutation. The mutation is the change; the mutant is the carrier. Do not use one word for the other.
Gene mutations come in two kinds, and this is the first: the point mutation, which is the gentler of the two.
The definition: a point mutation is a change in a single base pair of D N A. It is also called a substitution, because one base is swapped for another — swapped, not added, not removed.
Look at the top row. One letter is different, and the codon is still three letters long. That is the whole event.

And that is why the reading frame is untouched: nothing was added or removed, so the total count is unchanged and every boundary stays where it was. Only one codon is affected — the one containing the swapped base.

Now substitutions split further, and this is the pair examiners like, because the names sound similar and mean opposite things. The sub-types are defined by the class of base involved — purine or pyrimidine.
Transition: a purine is replaced by a purine, or a pyrimidine by a pyrimidine. For example A to G, both purines. Or C to T, both pyrimidines. The class stays the same — transition, same-type.
Transversion: a purine is replaced by a pyrimidine, or the other way round. For example A to C, or G to T. The class itself changes — transversion, crossing over to the other type.

And the example you already know, now properly classified: sickle-cell anaemia. G A G becomes G U G, so glutamic acid becomes valine at the sixth position of beta-globin. One base, one codon, one amino acid — a textbook point mutation, and the reason it is a point mutation is that the base count never changed.
The second kind of gene mutation, and it is the destructive one.

The definition: a frameshift mutation is an insertion or deletion of bases that shifts the reading frame. Insertion or deletion — the base count changes, and that is the whole difference from a substitution.
Follow the two rows. Same start, and then one base disappears — and look at what happens to every box after it.

The mechanism is exactly the sentence analogy. Because the reader counts in threes from a fixed start, removing or adding a base re-cuts every codon downstream. The reader does not know anything went missing; it just keeps counting.

So the damage is not local. Every codon after the mutation is read in the wrong place, and the protein is usually destroyed completely. This is why a frameshift is generally far more severe than a point mutation, despite involving the same one base.
But there is a crucial exception, and it is the single most tested fact in this subtopic. Listen for it.

If the number of bases inserted or deleted is a multiple of three, there is no frameshift. Whole codons are added or removed, the boundaries fall in the same places as before, and the frame stays intact.

So one, two, four or five bases shift the frame. But three, six or nine bases do not. The question is never how many bases — it is whether that number divides by three. Check divisibility first, always.

Now change scale completely. Point mutations and frameshifts are about single bases. Chromosomal mutations are about whole segments, or whole chromosomes — and the arithmetic of bases is irrelevant here.
Structural changes come in exactly four kinds. Read the four bars against the normal one at the top; each shows what happened to the letters A through E.
Deletion: a segment of the chromosome is lost. C is simply gone, and the genes it carried are gone with it.
Duplication: a segment is repeated, so those genes are present in extra copies. C appears twice. Nothing was lost — there is now too much.
Inversion: a segment breaks out, flips end to end, and rejoins. Look carefully — B, C, D are all still present, in reverse order. Nothing gained, nothing lost, and yet the chromosome is changed.

Translocation: a segment moves to a non-homologous chromosome — a completely different chromosome, not its partner. That word non-homologous is what distinguishes it from crossing over, which exchanges between homologues.
And the fact that gets asked: translocations are common in cancer cells. A gene landing beside the wrong neighbours can be switched on when it should be silent.

Notice what inversion and translocation have in common, because it is the deeper point. The gene count may be completely unchanged. What altered is the arrangement — and in genetics, position is information. Where a gene sits can matter as much as whether it is there.
The second half of chromosomal mutations is about number.
And it splits by scale — a split worth memorising exactly, because the two words look alike and mean quite different things.
Look at the fork. Left, a few. Right, whole sets. And notice the causes at the bottom are different too — that is not decoration.
Aneuploidy: gain or loss of a few chromosomes. Two n plus one, or two n minus one. A few — one, or a handful. Not a set.
Its cause is non-disjunction, the failure of a chromosome pair to separate during meiosis. Trisomy is two n plus one; monosomy is two n minus one. All of this you met in Part three.

And that is worth saying out loud: this is exactly the mechanism behind Down, Klinefelter and Turner syndromes. Those were not a separate topic — they were aneuploidy, met before you had the word for it.
Polyploidy: the presence of whole extra sets of chromosomes. Three n, four n, and beyond. Not one extra chromosome — one extra copy of everything.

And its cause is different, which is the part students skip. Polyploidy comes from failure of cytokinesis: the chromosomes duplicate, but the cell never divides, so the duplicated set stays in one cell. Non-disjunction is a failure to separate chromosomes; cytokinesis failure is a failure to separate cells.
So hold the pair: a few chromosomes means aneuploidy. Whole sets means polyploidy. Different scale, different cause, different name — and an exam option will offer you the wrong one of the two.
Polyploidy splits again, into two kinds, and this is a place where the Greek does the work for you.
Autopolyploidy: the extra sets come from the same species. Auto means self. One genome, multiplied — the plant simply has more copies of its own chromosome set.
The two panels show it. Left, all four bars the same colour. Right, two colours. That is the entire distinction, in a picture.
Allopolyploidy: the sets come from different species, combined after hybridisation. Allo means other. Two genomes, joined — a hybrid that then doubled up.

Now the fact that matters biologically and agriculturally. Polyploidy is common in plants, and often useful: it gives bigger fruits and bigger grains, and many of the crop plants on your plate are polyploid. Wheat is a famous case.

But polyploidy is usually lethal in animals. Same event, opposite outcome. This asymmetry between plants and animals is directly examinable, and it is worth being able to state as a contrast rather than two separate facts.

And the memory hook is just the prefix. Auto is self; allo is other. Read the prefix and the definition follows — you are not memorising two definitions, you are memorising two Greek words you already half know.
The definition we started with said mutation is inheritable. That word needs a qualification, and it is the most important qualification in this subtopic.
Because whether a mutation is inherited depends entirely on where in the body it happened.
Look at the two cells. Same red dot, same change — and completely different fates, decided by which cell it landed in.
A somatic mutation occurs in a body cell — a skin cell, a lung cell, a liver cell. It is not inherited. It dies with the individual, because body cells do not make gametes.
A germinal mutation occurs in a gamete-forming cell. It is inherited — it enters the egg or sperm, and from there the next generation.

So only germinal mutations matter for inheritance. Somatic mutations matter enormously in medicine — cancer is largely a somatic mutation story — but they are a different question from the one this chapter is asking. Do not let a cancer example pull you into calling it heritable.
Two more terms, and they are defined by direction rather than by mechanism. A forward mutation is where the wild type becomes the mutant — the usual direction, the one everything so far assumed.

And a reverse mutation, also called a back mutation, is where the mutant becomes the wild type — the original sequence is restored. It is rare, but it is real, and it tells you something quietly reassuring: mutation is not a one-way door.
Consolidate the vocabulary, because this subtopic is unusually definition-heavy and the definitions are unusually short. That combination means easy marks — or easy losses.
All five together. Read them as the marking scheme, because that is effectively what they are.
Mutation: a sudden, stable and inheritable change in the D N A of an organism. Three adjectives, and you should be able to justify each.
Mutant: an organism or cell carrying a mutation. One line, and it exists purely so you do not confuse it with the mutation itself.

Mutagen: any physical or chemical agent that induces mutation. And keep the examples attached — U V, X-rays and gamma rays for physical, mustard gas for chemical. A definition without an example is usually a half mark.
Point mutation: a change in a single base pair, also called a substitution. Single is the key word — one base pair, no more.
Frameshift mutation: an insertion or deletion that shifts the reading frame. And notice what is deliberately absent: no number. The number is what you check against three.

And two from the chromosomal side, which get confused most: aneuploidy is the gain or loss of a few chromosomes. Polyploidy is the presence of whole extra chromosome sets. A few, versus whole sets. If you can say that contrast cleanly, you have the harder half of this subtopic.
This procedure is the spine of the subtopic. Almost every question here is a classification, and classification is two questions asked in the right order.

Question one, and it is always first: what is the scale? Are we talking about bases, or about chromosomes? Do not start with the details — start here, because the details differ completely between the two branches.
The tree does it in one picture. One question at the top, two branches, and a second question inside each branch.
If the answer is bases, it is a gene mutation. Then ask question two: how many bases, and were they swapped or added or removed?

One base swapped, with nothing added or removed, gives a point mutation. Bases added or removed gives a frameshift — unless the number is a multiple of three, in which case the frame survives. That exception is built into the branch; do not forget it just because you reached the right box.
If the answer is chromosomes, it is a chromosomal mutation. Then ask question two differently: has the shape changed, or the number?
Shape changed gives structural — deletion, duplication, inversion or translocation, and you pick among the four by what happened to the segment.
Number changed gives numerical. And within numerical, a few chromosomes is aneuploidy; whole sets is polyploidy. Same question you have already answered twice today.

So the whole thing is: scale first, then detail. Every classification question in this subtopic falls out of those two questions — and if you find yourself unsure, it is almost always because you skipped question one and jumped to a name.
Procedure B is the numerical one for gene mutations, and it is three steps of division and subtraction. No biology in the arithmetic at all.
Step one: total codons equals total bases divided by three. So a three hundred base m R N A has one hundred codons. Always do this first — it gives you the ceiling for everything else.
The picture walks the three steps. Divide, locate, subtract. Notice the green block is small and the red block is nearly everything.

Step two: find which codon holds the mutated base. If base thirty one is deleted, it sits in codon eleven — because thirty one equals three times ten, plus one. Ten complete codons come before it, and then the mutated base starts the eleventh.
Step three: altered codons equals total codons minus the intact codons before the mutation. That subtraction is the whole answer.
So codons one to ten are intact, and codons eleven to one hundred are all altered. One hundred minus ten is ninety.

And the principle underneath the arithmetic, which is worth stating in the answer: only what came before the mutation survives. Everything after it is re-cut in the wrong place, because the reader kept counting in threes past a gap.

<curious>Now notice how small the cause is and how large the effect. One missing base — one letter out of three hundred — destroys ninety percent of the protein. That ratio is why frameshifts are so much more serious than substitutions, and it is worth feeling rather than just calculating.
दो वजहें, और इनके इर्द-गिर्द की vocabulary high-yield है क्योंकि वो छोटी और पक्की है।

Spontaneous mutation क़ुदरती तौर पर पैदा होता है, बिना किसी बाहरी एजेंट के। आमतौर पर ये D N A replication के दौरान copy करने की ग़लती होती है — polymerase हैरतअंगेज़ रूप से सटीक है, पर परफ़ेक्ट नहीं, और genome बहुत लंबा है।
ये रहा बँटवारा, और नीचे mutagens। ध्यान दीजिए mutagens की ठीक दो श्रेणियाँ हैं, और हर एक की छोटी सी तय सूची है।
Induced mutation किसी बाहरी एजेंट से होता है, और उस एजेंट का नाम है mutagen।
Definition: mutagen कोई भी physical या chemical एजेंट है जो mutation पैदा करता है। Physical या chemical — यही वाक्यांश classification है, definition के अंदर ही बना हुआ।
Physical mutagens: U V rays, X-rays, और gamma rays। सब radiation, और theme दिख रही है — इतने ऊर्जावान कि D N A molecule को सीधे नुक़सान पहुँचा दें।
Chemical mutagens: mustard gas standard उदाहरण है, और एक पूछा जाए तो यही लिखिए।

अब वो जोड़ जिसके marks हैं: बहुत से mutagens carcinogens भी हैं — यानी cancer पैदा करने वाले एजेंट। और ये इत्तेफ़ाक़ नहीं है। जो एजेंट D N A को नुक़सान पहुँचाता है वो body cell में mutation कर सकता है, और cancer तब होता है जब ग़लत body cell में mutation हो जाए। दोनों सूचियाँ इसलिए मिलती हैं क्योंकि mechanism साझा है।
आख़िरी term, और students इसे लगातार घुला देते हैं। Mutant वो जीव या cell है जो mutation carry करता है। Mutation बदलाव है; mutant उसे ढोने वाला। एक शब्द दूसरे के लिए मत लिखिए।
Gene mutations दो क़िस्म के होते हैं, और ये पहला है: point mutation, जो दोनों में नरम वाला है।
Definition: point mutation D N A के एक अकेले base pair में बदलाव है। इसे substitution भी कहते हैं, क्योंकि एक base की जगह दूसरा आ जाता है — बदला जाता है, जोड़ा नहीं जाता, हटाया नहीं जाता।
ऊपर की row देखिए। एक अक्षर अलग है, और codon अब भी तीन अक्षरों का है। पूरी घटना बस इतनी है।
और इसीलिए reading frame को कुछ नहीं होता: कुछ जोड़ा या हटाया नहीं गया, तो कुल गिनती वही रही और हर सीमा अपनी जगह रही। सिर्फ़ एक codon प्रभावित होता है — वही जिसमें बदला हुआ base है।
अब substitutions और बँटते हैं, और examiners को यही जोड़ी पसंद है, क्योंकि नाम मिलते-जुलते हैं और मतलब उल्टे। Sub-types शामिल base की श्रेणी से तय होते हैं — purine या pyrimidine।
Transition: purine की जगह purine, या pyrimidine की जगह pyrimidine। जैसे A से G, दोनों purines। या C से T, दोनों pyrimidines। श्रेणी वही रहती है — transition, यानी एक ही क़िस्म।
Transversion: purine की जगह pyrimidine, या उल्टा। जैसे A से C, या G से T। श्रेणी ख़ुद बदल जाती है — transversion, यानी दूसरी क़िस्म में पार जाना।

और वो उदाहरण जो आप जानते हैं, अब ठीक से classify हुआ: sickle-cell anaemia। G A G बनता है G U G, तो beta-globin के छठे position पर glutamic acid की जगह valine। एक base, एक codon, एक amino acid — textbook point mutation, और ये point mutation इसलिए है क्योंकि base की गिनती कभी बदली ही नहीं।
Gene mutation की दूसरी क़िस्म, और यही तबाही वाली है।
Definition: frameshift mutation bases का ऐसा insertion या deletion है जो reading frame को खिसका देता है। Insertion या deletion — base की गिनती बदलती है, और substitution से पूरा फ़र्क़ यही है।
दोनों rows follow कीजिए। शुरुआत वही, फिर एक base ग़ायब — और देखिए उसके बाद के हर box का क्या होता है।

Mechanism बिलकुल वही वाक्य वाली analogy है। चूँकि पढ़ने वाला एक तय शुरुआत से तीन-तीन गिनता है, एक base हटाने या जोड़ने से आगे का हर codon दोबारा कट जाता है। पढ़ने वाले को पता ही नहीं कि कुछ ग़ायब हुआ; वो बस गिनता रहता है।

तो नुक़सान स्थानीय नहीं है। Mutation के बाद का हर codon ग़लत जगह पढ़ा जाता है, और protein आमतौर पर पूरी तरह तबाह हो जाता है। इसीलिए frameshift आमतौर पर point mutation से कहीं ज़्यादा गंभीर है, जबकि base उतना ही एक है।
पर एक अहम अपवाद है, और यही इस subtopic का सबसे ज़्यादा पूछा जाने वाला तथ्य है। ध्यान से सुनिए।
अगर जोड़े या हटाए गए bases की संख्या तीन का गुणज है, तो कोई frameshift नहीं होता। पूरे codons जुड़ते या हटते हैं, सीमाएँ पहले वाली जगहों पर ही पड़ती हैं, और frame सलामत रहता है।
तो एक, दो, चार या पाँच bases frame खिसका देते हैं। पर तीन, छह या नौ नहीं। सवाल कभी ये नहीं होता कि कितने bases — सवाल ये है कि वो संख्या तीन से कटती है या नहीं। हमेशा पहले विभाज्यता जाँचिए।
अब scale पूरी तरह बदलिए। Point mutations और frameshifts अकेले bases की बात हैं। Chromosomal mutations पूरे segments या पूरे chromosomes की बात हैं — और यहाँ bases की arithmetic बेमानी है।
Structural बदलाव ठीक चार क़िस्म के होते हैं। ऊपर वाली normal bar के मुक़ाबले चारों देखिए; हर एक दिखाती है कि A से E तक के अक्षरों का क्या हुआ।
Deletion: chromosome का एक हिस्सा खो जाता है। C बस ग़ायब है, और उसके genes भी उसके साथ गए।
Duplication: एक हिस्सा दोहरा जाता है, तो वो genes अतिरिक्त copies में मौजूद हैं। C दो बार दिखता है। कुछ खोया नहीं — अब ज़्यादा है।

Inversion: एक हिस्सा टूट कर निकलता है, सिरे से सिरे तक पलटता है, और वापस जुड़ जाता है। ध्यान से देखिए — B, C, D तीनों अब भी मौजूद हैं, उल्टे क्रम में। न कुछ मिला, न कुछ गया, और फिर भी chromosome बदल गया।

Translocation: एक हिस्सा किसी non-homologous chromosome पर चला जाता है — बिलकुल अलग chromosome पर, अपने साथी पर नहीं। यही non-homologous शब्द इसे crossing over से अलग करता है, जो homologues के बीच अदला-बदली करता है।
और वो तथ्य जो पूछा जाता है: translocations cancer cells में आम हैं। ग़लत पड़ोसियों के बग़ल में जा गिरा gene तब चालू हो सकता है जब उसे चुप रहना चाहिए।

ध्यान दीजिए inversion और translocation में क्या साझा है, क्योंकि यही गहरी बात है। Gene की गिनती बिलकुल भी नहीं बदली हो सकती। बदला है arrangement — और genetics में स्थिति ख़ुद जानकारी है। Gene कहाँ बैठा है, ये उतना ही मायने रख सकता है जितना कि वो है या नहीं।
Chromosomal mutations का दूसरा आधा संख्या के बारे में है।
और वो scale से बँटता है — और ये बँटवारा ठीक-ठीक याद करने लायक़ है, क्योंकि दोनों शब्द मिलते-जुलते हैं और मतलब काफ़ी अलग।
दोराहा देखिए। बाएँ कुछ चंद। दाएँ पूरे sets। और ध्यान दीजिए नीचे वजहें भी अलग हैं — वो सजावट नहीं है।
Aneuploidy: कुछ chromosomes का बढ़ना या घटना। Two n plus one, या two n minus one। कुछ चंद — एक, या मुट्ठी भर। कोई पूरा set नहीं।
इसकी वजह है non-disjunction, यानी meiosis में chromosome की जोड़ी का अलग न हो पाना। Trisomy है two n plus one; monosomy है two n minus one। ये सब आप Part तीन में मिल चुके हैं।
और ये ज़ोर से कहने लायक़ है: Down, Klinefelter और Turner syndromes के पीछे बिलकुल यही mechanism है। वो कोई अलग topic नहीं थे — वो aneuploidy ही थे, बस तब आपके पास ये शब्द नहीं था।
Polyploidy: chromosomes के पूरे अतिरिक्त sets की मौजूदगी। Three n, four n, और आगे। एक extra chromosome नहीं — हर चीज़ की एक extra copy।

और इसकी वजह अलग है, और यही हिस्सा students छोड़ देते हैं। Polyploidy cytokinesis के नाकाम होने से आती है: chromosomes दोगुने हो जाते हैं, पर cell बँटती ही नहीं, तो दोगुना set एक ही cell में रह जाता है। Non-disjunction chromosomes को अलग करने की नाकामी है; cytokinesis failure cells को अलग करने की नाकामी।
तो जोड़ी पकड़िए: कुछ chromosomes मतलब aneuploidy। पूरे sets मतलब polyploidy। अलग scale, अलग वजह, अलग नाम — और exam का कोई option आपको इन दोनों में से ग़लत वाला ज़रूर देगा।
Polyploidy दोबारा बँटती है, दो क़िस्मों में, और यहाँ Greek आपका काम कर देती है।
Autopolyploidy: अतिरिक्त sets उसी species से आते हैं। Auto मतलब स्वयं। एक genome, गुणित — पौधे के पास बस अपने ही chromosome set की ज़्यादा copies हैं।
दोनों panels दिखा देते हैं। बाएँ चारों bars एक ही रंग की। दाएँ दो रंग। पूरा फ़र्क़ यही है, तस्वीर में।
Allopolyploidy: sets अलग-अलग species से आते हैं, hybridisation के बाद जुड़े हुए। Allo मतलब अन्य। दो genomes, जुड़े हुए — एक hybrid जो फिर दोगुना हो गया।

अब वो तथ्य जो biology और खेती दोनों में मायने रखता है। Polyploidy पौधों में आम है, और अक्सर फ़ायदेमंद: इससे बड़े फल और बड़े अनाज मिलते हैं, और आपकी थाली के बहुत से crop plants polyploid हैं। Wheat मशहूर मिसाल है।
पर जानवरों में polyploidy आमतौर पर जानलेवा होती है। वही घटना, उल्टा नतीजा। पौधों और जानवरों के बीच ये असंतुलन सीधे पूछा जाता है, और इसे दो अलग तथ्यों की जगह एक contrast की तरह कहना आना चाहिए।
और याद रखने का सहारा बस उपसर्ग है। Auto यानी स्वयं; allo यानी अन्य। उपसर्ग पढ़िए और definition अपने आप आ जाती है — आप दो definitions नहीं रट रहे, दो Greek शब्द रट रहे हैं जो आप आधे जानते ही हैं।
जिस definition से हमने शुरू किया था उसने कहा था mutation वंशागत है। उस शब्द को एक शर्त चाहिए, और इस subtopic की सबसे अहम शर्त यही है।
क्योंकि mutation inherit होगा या नहीं, ये पूरी तरह इस पर है कि वो शरीर में कहाँ हुआ।
दोनों cells देखिए। वही लाल बिंदु, वही बदलाव — और बिलकुल अलग अंजाम, सिर्फ़ इस बात से तय कि वो किस cell में गिरा।
Somatic mutation किसी body cell में होता है — कोई skin cell, lung cell, liver cell। ये inherit नहीं होता। ये उसी व्यक्ति के साथ ख़त्म हो जाता है, क्योंकि body cells gametes नहीं बनातीं।
Germinal mutation gamete बनाने वाली cell में होता है। ये inherit होता है — ये egg या sperm में जाता है, और वहाँ से अगली पीढ़ी में।

तो inheritance के लिए सिर्फ़ germinal mutations मायने रखते हैं। Somatic mutations medicine में बेहद मायने रखते हैं — cancer काफ़ी हद तक somatic mutation की कहानी है — पर वो इस chapter के सवाल से अलग सवाल हैं। किसी cancer के उदाहरण को आपको heritable कहलवाने मत दीजिए।
दो और terms, और ये mechanism से नहीं, दिशा से तय होते हैं। Forward mutation वो है जहाँ wild type mutant बन जाता है — आम दिशा, जो अब तक हर बात मान कर चल रही थी।

और reverse mutation, जिसे back mutation भी कहते हैं, वो है जहाँ mutant वापस wild type बन जाता है — मूल अनुक्रम बहाल हो जाता है। ये दुर्लभ है, पर असली है, और ये चुपचाप एक तसल्ली देता है: mutation एकतरफ़ा दरवाज़ा नहीं है।
Vocabulary समेट लीजिए, क्योंकि ये subtopic असामान्य रूप से definition-भारी है और definitions असामान्य रूप से छोटी। इस मेल का मतलब है आसान marks — या आसान नुक़सान।
पाँचों साथ। इन्हें marking scheme की तरह पढ़िए, क्योंकि असल में वो यही हैं।
Mutation: किसी जीव के D N A में अचानक होने वाला, स्थायी और वंशागत बदलाव। तीन विशेषण, और हर एक को आप सही ठहरा सकें।
Mutant: mutation carry करने वाला जीव या cell। एक line, और ये सिर्फ़ इसलिए है कि आप इसे ख़ुद mutation से न घुला दें।

Mutagen: कोई भी physical या chemical एजेंट जो mutation पैदा करता है। और उदाहरण साथ रखिए — physical के लिए U V, X-rays और gamma rays, chemical के लिए mustard gas। बिना उदाहरण की definition आमतौर पर आधा mark है।
Point mutation: एक अकेले base pair में बदलाव, जिसे substitution भी कहते हैं। अकेला अहम शब्द है — एक base pair, इससे ज़्यादा नहीं।
Frameshift mutation: ऐसा insertion या deletion जो reading frame को खिसका दे। और ध्यान दीजिए क्या जानबूझ कर ग़ायब है: कोई संख्या नहीं। संख्या वो है जिसे आप तीन से जाँचते हैं।

और chromosomal तरफ़ से दो, जो सबसे ज़्यादा गड़बड़ाते हैं: aneuploidy कुछ chromosomes का बढ़ना या घटना है। Polyploidy पूरे अतिरिक्त chromosome sets की मौजूदगी है। कुछ चंद, बनाम पूरे sets। अगर ये contrast साफ़ बोल सकें, तो इस subtopic का मुश्किल आधा आपके पास है।
ये procedure इस subtopic की रीढ़ है। यहाँ लगभग हर सवाल classification है, और classification मतलब दो सवाल, सही क्रम में पूछे हुए।
सवाल एक, और ये हमेशा पहले: scale क्या है? बात bases की है, या chromosomes की? Details से शुरू मत कीजिए — यहीं से शुरू कीजिए, क्योंकि दोनों शाखाओं में details बिलकुल अलग हैं।
Tree ये एक तस्वीर में कर देता है। ऊपर एक सवाल, दो शाखाएँ, और हर शाखा के अंदर दूसरा सवाल।
अगर जवाब है bases, तो ये gene mutation है। फिर सवाल दो पूछिए: कितने bases, और वो बदले गए या जोड़े/हटाए गए?

एक base बदला, बिना कुछ जोड़े या हटाए, तो point mutation। Bases जोड़े या हटाए गए, तो frameshift — बशर्ते संख्या तीन का गुणज न हो, वरना frame बच जाता है। वो अपवाद इसी शाखा में बना हुआ है; सही डिब्बे तक पहुँच गए इसलिए उसे भूल मत जाइए।
अगर जवाब है chromosomes, तो ये chromosomal mutation है। फिर सवाल दो अलग तरह से पूछिए: shape बदली है, या number?
Shape बदली तो structural — deletion, duplication, inversion या translocation, और इन चारों में से segment के साथ जो हुआ उससे चुनिए।
Number बदला तो numerical। और numerical के अंदर, कुछ चंद chromosomes मतलब aneuploidy; पूरे sets मतलब polyploidy। वही सवाल जिसका जवाब आप आज दो बार दे चुके हैं।
तो पूरी बात है: पहले scale, फिर detail। इस subtopic का हर classification सवाल इन्हीं दो सवालों से निकल आता है — और अगर आप उलझें, तो लगभग हमेशा इसलिए कि आपने सवाल एक छोड़ कर सीधे नाम पर छलाँग लगा दी।
Procedure B gene mutations वाला numerical है, और ये भाग और घटाव के तीन steps हैं। Arithmetic में biology है ही नहीं।
Step one: कुल codons बराबर कुल bases बटा तीन। तो तीन सौ base वाले m R N A में एक सौ codons हैं। ये हमेशा पहले कीजिए — इससे बाक़ी सब की ऊपरी सीमा मिल जाती है।
तस्वीर तीनों steps चलाती है। भाग, स्थान, घटाव। ध्यान दीजिए हरा हिस्सा छोटा है और लाल हिस्सा लगभग सब कुछ।

Step two: पता कीजिए mutated base किस codon में है। अगर base इकत्तीस हटाया गया, तो वो codon ग्यारह में है — क्योंकि इकत्तीस बराबर तीन into दस, plus एक। उससे पहले दस पूरे codons आते हैं, और फिर mutated base ग्यारहवाँ शुरू करता है।
Step three: बदले हुए codons बराबर कुल codons minus mutation से पहले के सलामत codons। वही घटाव पूरा जवाब है।
तो codons एक से दस सलामत हैं, और codons ग्यारह से सौ तक सब बदले हुए। एक सौ minus दस बराबर नब्बे।

और arithmetic के नीचे का सिद्धांत, जो जवाब में लिखने लायक़ है: सिर्फ़ वही बचता है जो mutation से पहले था। उसके बाद का सब कुछ ग़लत जगह पर दोबारा कट जाता है, क्योंकि पढ़ने वाला एक ख़ाली जगह के पार भी तीन-तीन गिनता रहा।

<curious>अब देखिए कारण कितना छोटा है और असर कितना बड़ा। एक ग़ायब base — तीन सौ में से एक अक्षर — protein का नब्बे प्रतिशत तबाह कर देता है। यही अनुपात है जिससे frameshifts substitutions से कहीं ज़्यादा गंभीर होते हैं, और इसे सिर्फ़ गिनने से बेहतर है महसूस करना।

sections.title: Procedure C: chromosome-number arithmetic & Cheat sheet: the whole chapter on one page

board_events.text: Procedure C: find n first
Step 1: from the given $2n$, find the haploid number n. If $2n = 24$, then $n = 12$.

board_events.caption: Trisomic, triploid and tetraploid for 2n = 24
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 540 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">

<text x="270" y="48" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#6b7280">First find the haploid number: n = 24 ÷ 2 = 12</text>

<text x="99" y="136" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#7c3aed">24 + 1 = 25</text>

<text x="440" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">4n</text>
<text x="440" y="136" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">4 × 12 = 48</text>
<text x="440" y="162" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#16a34a">POLYPLOIDY</text>

<text x="270" y="230" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Trap: computing 3n as 3 × 24 = 72. The n in 3n is the HAPLOID number.</text>

board_events.text: Step 2: trisomic means $2n+1$ — so 24 + 1 = 25. That is aneuploidy.
Step 3: triploid means $3n$ — so 3 × 12 = 36. That is polyploidy.
Step 4: tetraploid means $4n$ — so 4 × 12 = 48. Also polyploidy.
Trisomy ADDS one to 2n. Triploid MULTIPLIES n. The n in 3n is the HAPLOID number, not the diploid one.
The trap is computing 3n as 3 × 24 = 72. Finding n first, before anything else, is what protects you.
What mutation is not
Condition 1: not all mutations are harmful. Most are neutral, and some are beneficial.

<text x="442" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Somatic mutations are</text>
<text x="442" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">NOT inherited</text>
<text x="442" y="134" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">They matter medically</text>
<text x="442" y="150" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">— cancer — but not</text>
<text x="442" y="166" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">for inheritance</text>
<text x="442" y="194" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">two different questions</text>

board_events.text: Mutation is the raw material of evolution. Without it there would be no new alleles to select among — and no variation at all.
Condition 2: cells carry DNA repair machinery, so most damage never becomes a mutation.
A mutation is damage that got PAST repair. The rate you observe is what survived correction, not what occurred.
Condition 3: only germinal mutations are inherited. Somatic mutations matter medically — cancer — but not for inheritance.
"All mutations are harmful" is the single most common wrong sentence in this subtopic. Do not write it.
Example one [C B S E Board]
Define mutation. In sickle-cell anaemia, the codon GAG is replaced by GUG. Classify this mutation and justify your answer.

board_events.caption: One base swapped, frame intact
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 540 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">
<defs><marker id="e51" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 z" fill="#6b7280"/></marker></defs>

<text x="110" y="100" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#16a34a">glutamic acid</text>
<text x="280" y="100" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">valine</text>
<text x="380" y="70" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">at the 6th position</text>
<text x="380" y="88" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">of beta-globin</text>

<text x="150" y="138" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">Only ONE base changed</text>
<text x="150" y="156" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">nothing added, nothing removed</text>
<rect x="280" y="118" width="220" height="46" rx="8" fill="#ecfdf5" stroke="#16a34a"/>
<text x="390" y="138" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">Reading frame intact</text>
<text x="390" y="156" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">every later codon reads normally</text>
<rect x="140" y="180" width="260" height="38" rx="8" fill="#f5f3ff" stroke="#7c3aed"/>
<text x="270" y="204" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#7c3aed">POINT (substitution) mutation</text>
<text x="270" y="240" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#dc2626">Not a frameshift: the base count never changed</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Definition: mutation is a sudden, stable and inheritable change in the DNA of an organism.
Classification: this is a point mutation, also called a substitution.
Justification one: only ONE base changed — the A became a U. Nothing was added, and nothing was removed.
Justification two: because the base count is unchanged, the reading frame is intact, so every later codon is read normally.
It is NOT a frameshift, precisely because no base was inserted or deleted. Consequence: glutamic acid becomes valine at the 6th position of beta-globin.
Example two [C U E T / N E E T speed trap]
Three consecutive bases are deleted from the middle of a gene. Will this cause a frameshift mutation?

board_events.caption: A multiple of three removes a whole codon
board_events.svg:

<text x="40" y="58" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">Original</text>

<rect x="172" y="92" width="46" height="24" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#16a34a"/><text x="195" y="109" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-family="monospace" fill="#1f2937">GAA</text>
<rect x="224" y="92" width="46" height="24" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#16a34a"/><text x="247" y="109" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-family="monospace" fill="#1f2937">UCA</text>
<text x="300" y="109" font-size="11" fill="#16a34a">still cut in the right places</text>
<rect x="60" y="134" width="420" height="42" rx="8" fill="#ecfdf5" stroke="#16a34a"/>
<text x="270" y="152" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">3 is a multiple of 3, so NO frameshift</text>
<text x="270" y="170" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">One whole codon is removed; the remaining codons keep their boundaries</text>
<rect x="60" y="188" width="420" height="46" rx="8" fill="#fff7ed" stroke="#f59e0b"/>
<text x="270" y="208" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#b45309">The protein is short by one amino acid — but the rest is correct</text>
<text x="270" y="226" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">Trap: assuming every deletion is a frameshift. Check divisibility by 3 first.</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Check divisibility by 3 first: 3 ÷ 3 = 1, so 3 IS a multiple of 3.
Answer: NO frameshift occurs.
Why: exactly one whole codon is removed, and the remaining codons keep their original boundaries.
The protein is short by one amino acid — but every other amino acid is correct.
Trap: assuming every deletion causes a frameshift. Check divisibility by 3 BEFORE you answer.
Example three [N E E T]
An mRNA is 300 bases long. A single base is deleted at position 31. How many codons of the resulting protein are altered?

board_events.caption: Ten survive, ninety are destroyed
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 540 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">
<text x="270" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">300-base mRNA, base 31 deleted. How many codons alter?</text>
<rect x="40" y="46" width="150" height="46" rx="6" fill="#f3f4f6" stroke="#9ca3af"/>
<text x="115" y="66" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">Step 1</text>
<text x="115" y="84" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">300 ÷ 3 = 100 codons</text>
<rect x="196" y="46" width="150" height="46" rx="6" fill="#f5f3ff" stroke="#7c3aed"/>
<text x="271" y="66" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">Step 2</text>
<text x="271" y="84" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2937">base 31 sits in codon 11</text>
<rect x="352" y="46" width="150" height="46" rx="6" fill="#fef2f2" stroke="#dc2626"/>
<text x="427" y="66" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#6b7280">Step 3</text>
<text x="427" y="84" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">100 − 10 = 90</text>
<text x="270" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">31 = 3 × 10 + 1, so ten complete codons come before it</text>
<rect x="40" y="134" width="460" height="34" rx="6" fill="#e5e7eb"/>
<rect x="40" y="134" width="46" height="34" rx="6" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#16a34a"/>
<text x="63" y="156" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#16a34a">1 to 10</text>
<rect x="86" y="134" width="414" height="34" rx="6" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#dc2626"/>
<text x="293" y="156" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">codons 11 to 100: every one is altered</text>
<text x="270" y="192" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">Answer: 90 codons altered</text>
<text x="270" y="222" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#7c3aed">A single missing base destroys ninety percent of the protein</text>
<text x="270" y="246" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#16a34a">Only the ten codons BEFORE the deletion survive</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Step 1: total codons = 300 ÷ 3 = 100.
Step 2: base 31 sits in codon 11, since 31 = 3 × 10 + 1 — ten complete codons come before it.
Step 3: codons 1 to 10 are intact; codons 11 to 100 are all altered.
So altered codons = 100 − 10 = 90.
A single missing base destroys ninety percent of the protein. Only the ten codons BEFORE the deletion survive.
Example four [N E E T high difficulty]
A plant has $2n = 24$. Find the chromosome number of a trisomic, a triploid and a tetraploid individual, and name the type of numerical change in each.

board_events.caption: 25, 36 and 48 — and their categories
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 540 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">
<text x="270" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">2n = 24. Trisomic, triploid, tetraploid?</text>
<text x="270" y="46" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#6b7280">n = 24 ÷ 2 = 12. Everything below uses that number.</text>
<rect x="24" y="60" width="150" height="104" rx="8" fill="#f5f3ff" stroke="#7c3aed"/>
<text x="99" y="82" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#7c3aed">Trisomic (2n + 1)</text>
<text x="99" y="108" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">24 + 1 = 25</text>
<text x="99" y="132" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">ANEUPLOIDY</text>
<text x="99" y="152" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#6b7280">from non-disjunction</text>
<rect x="194" y="60" width="150" height="104" rx="8" fill="#ecfdf5" stroke="#86efac"/>
<text x="269" y="82" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">Triploid (3n)</text>
<text x="269" y="108" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">3 × 12 = 36</text>
<text x="269" y="132" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#16a34a">POLYPLOIDY</text>
<text x="269" y="152" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#6b7280">from cytokinesis failure</text>
<rect x="364" y="60" width="152" height="104" rx="8" fill="#ecfdf5" stroke="#86efac"/>
<text x="440" y="82" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">Tetraploid (4n)</text>
<text x="440" y="108" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2937">4 × 12 = 48</text>
<text x="440" y="132" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#16a34a">POLYPLOIDY</text>
<text x="440" y="152" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#6b7280">from cytokinesis failure</text>
<rect x="60" y="184" width="420" height="46" rx="8" fill="#fef2f2" stroke="#dc2626"/>
<text x="270" y="204" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">Trisomy ADDS one to 2n. Triploid MULTIPLIES the haploid number.</text>
<text x="270" y="222" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">Trap: writing 3n as 3 × 24 = 72. The n in 3n is the haploid number, 12.</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Step 1, always first: $n = 24 ÷ 2 = 12$.
Trisomic = $2n+1$ = 24 + 1 = 25. This is aneuploidy, caused by non-disjunction.
Triploid = $3n$ = 3 × 12 = 36. This is polyploidy, caused by failure of cytokinesis.
Tetraploid = $4n$ = 4 × 12 = 48. Also polyploidy.
Trap: computing 3n as 3 × 24 = 72. The n in 3n is the HAPLOID number, 12 — not the diploid number you were handed.
Common student pitfalls
Pitfall 1: assuming every deletion or insertion causes a frameshift. A multiple of 3 causes NO frameshift; anything else does.
